title: What Technologies Will Shape The World Of The Future ?
text:
The US earnings season is now getting underway and focus of attention will be on the mega-cap technology stocks. They have been the decisive factor in portfolio performance of the past year or more, but in recent weeks have started to slip and investors turn attention to small-cap stocks. Indeed, earnings estimates for the ‘magnificent seven’ US technology firms have been slipping.
While investors need to be alert to this as a crucial factor for portfolios, there is also a need to take a much longer view on technology, and here there is a range of useful, recent publications from leading universities and think tanks – notable amongst them are the MIT Technology Review, the World Economic Forum’s Top 10 Emerging Tech Trends and McKinsey’s Technology Trends Outlook.
It is worth noting that many of these trends are nascent, and effectively accessible through venture capital for instance, but even at this early stage, a number of them are worth thinking about in greater detail as their eco-systems begin to develop. I would highlight the following ones.
What’s next after AI?
There is a consensus that AI – at least as far as generative AI is concerned – is in a bubble, in both public and private markets. Notwithstanding this, the next ‘phase’ in AI is beginning, and it will see far more skilled use of AI (by specialists like doctors and soldiers), the use of AI in complex industrial processes – Sanofi uses it in the drug discovery process and Aramco uses AI to manage the complexity of running multiple oil and gas wells. Relatedly, AI will be increasingly applied to very specific, proprietary data-sets in multiple realms from options trading to the production of chemicals.
Greater computing power and connectivity
An interesting, underestimated development that followed the ratification of the EU AI Act this year was the announcement by the EU that it would centre centers of excellence in super-computing. The move reflects the reality that a related trend to the rise of AI is the creation of vastly more powerful forms of computing (quantum) and modes of telecommunication. Quantum computing (the deployment of quantum mechanics to create chips and hardware with hugely superior computing ability (for example potentially strong enough to hack blockchain)) is an area where Europe is arguably ahead of the US and China, and this technology will have many use cases – in the design of chemicals to cybersecurity to complex financial calculations.
In this field, another development that is perhaps more germane to our everyday lives is a range of technologies that aim to enhance the connectivity of telecommunications – the arrival of 6G is already being heralded, the importance of satellites to the space economy is something we will hear more about, not just in terms of private networks like Starlink, but also in terms of the risk of space wars.
In detail, is an exciting area – scientists are developing ‘reconfigurable intelligent surfaces; (RIS) to facilitate the more efficient flow of teleco signals, and there is also a budding industry in what is called HAPS (High Altitude Platform Stations), which in some cases are balloon like structures in space that enhance signal flow (interestingly Ireland has one of the biggest investment HAPS ecosystems, according to the World Economic Forum).
Greener technology
The arrival of cheap Chinese electric vehicles in Europe has started an important debate on competitiveness, and on green technologies. Indeed, the new Labour has made ‘Green Technology’ a centrepiece of its industrial policy with the forthcoming launch of ‘GB Energy’ and the early roll-out of onshore wind energy.
From an Irish point of view there are several innovations to watch, notably alternative animal feeds (sourced from insects, single-cell proteins, algae and food waste, provide viable alternatives to traditional ingredients like soy, maize and wheat. This is one potential innovation that can help Ireland reduce its carbon footprint.
Staying with carbon, there is. fast growing industry in carbon extraction, where already large European firms like Climeworks have built a technology that, in effect ‘hoovers’ carbon out of the air and buries it (in this case there first significant plant is in Iceland). Other scientists are experimenting with carbon capturing microbes.
We also note the rise of more efficient forms of energy such as the growing deployment of energy pumps, innovations in super-efficient solar cells and in many countries the commercialization of small-scale nuclear reactors. In many countries, nuclear energy is ‘off the policy menu’ but advances in technology mean it is a more flexible form of energy, and as. Sector it is spawning new innovations such as the commercialization of the nuclear based power source used in the Mars probe.
Bio-engineering and advanced medicine
Many of the new technological trends we have come across have serious ethical dimensions in the sense that they breach legal and moral barriers that have so far not been countenanced. Bio-engineering, and the use of CRSPR (the editing of DNA sequences). It is a hugely promising area but a potentially controversial one also. In Europe, CRSPR is used commercially in gene therapy for blood disorders, and its business use cases are broad – from enhancing longevity to alternative protein production, to more mundane uses (designing bananas that last longer).
In medicine, the ability to design drugs to the specific DNA of a patient (so that the drugs work better) is a clear trend, and avid newsreaders might also be aware of “xenotransplantation”, which is the transplantation of organs from animals into humans. Given the scarcity of human organs and the difficulty in transporting them, the attraction o this approach is clear.
Next level engineering and supply chains
Anyone who has visited a large industrial plant cannot have missed the role of robots in the manufacturing process. Robotics is now entering the mainstream in manufacturing, the military, chemicals and healthcare (in precision surgery and skeletal structures for instance).
Several developments, such as better batteries for robots, the use of AI to permit robots to think and act more independently (itself quite worrying). Major industrial firms from BMW to Chevron deploy robots in their industrial processes.
Finally, there has been a surge in the use of robots, drones and immersive reality tools in the design and construction of industrial buildings. Granted that construction accounts for 40% of the global carbon dioxide (CO2 ) emissions, this makes the building process much more efficient, with less reliance on scarce labour, and facilitates inspections.

title: Ambient Temperature Rising: Increasing Demand And Competition For AI Scribes
text:
By the time Henry Ford introduced the Model T in 1908, the automotive industry had been around for 15 years, and competition was fierce, with approximately 200 manufacturers.
Just 20 years later, automotive sales had increased by ~10X, but the number of manufacturers had dropped to 24.
What happened?
An industry shakeout, due to a combination of factors: the emergence of dominant technology and design (internal combustion engine, steel body), production efficiency and scale (assembly lines), and lower, more accessible pricing, among others. Survival of the fittest, as it was.
The biggest beneficiaries of the shakeout were consumers and, in the longer term, American society and economy. Affordable automobiles led to increased mobility, extended and expedited trade, and expanded the ability of people to gather for personal, public and commercial purposes.
More than a hundred years later, we may be on the front edge of another industry shakeout in one of the only areas in healthcare where demand for artificial intelligence seems to be materializing: ambient scribe technology. Given the potential of the technology, one can start to imagine how such a shakeout might produce benefits for clinicians, patients, and the healthcare ecosystem as a whole.
The Good News For Clinicians About Ambient Scribe Technology
“No doctor pursued a career in medicine with the hope of spending most of their time on paperwork and documentation,” says Alex LeBrun, Cofounder and CEO of Nabla, an ambient scribe technology company based in Paris, France.
Yet increasingly, that is where doctors are spending their time. As Matthew Holt of The Health Care Blog has written, doctors have always spent time documenting patient histories and their own notes. The burden of this exercise increased substantially in the 2010s as the federal government poured $35 billion of financial incentives into getting doctors and hospitals to adopt electronic health records, or EHRs. Doctors and patients went from face-to-face encounters to face-to-screen encounters, with doctors focusing on navigating the thousand clicks of the EHR.
Add in increasing burdens from health insurance companies (such as the rising use of prior authorizations), reduced autonomy as a result of consolidation, and increased disease burden and associated demand following a global epidemic, and you have the makings of an epidemic of clinician burnout.
Indeed, if there is one thing that every ambient scribe company seems to agree on, it is that the value of the technology lies first and foremost in reducing administrative complexity and addressing factors that contribute to clinician burnout.
How does ambient scribe technology do this? Most solutions leverage smartphone microphones and dictation, natural language processing, and large language models to capture the physician-patient interaction and provide an organized summary of a patient encounter, structured in a manner that allows (at least in an ideal environment) for seamless integration into the EHR.
In short, the ambient scribe potentially does away with much of the note-taking and EHR data entry that make up much of the thousand clicks of a patient encounter, allowing the doctor to speak freely with the patient.
For Ambience Healthcare, an ambient scribe company whose investors include OpenAI (of ChatGPT fame) Startup Fund, reducing clinicians’ burden is part of the mission. Cofounder and CEO Mike Ng notes that today’s doctors spend only 27% of their time on direct patient care, and asks whether it’s possible to flip that so that it looks closer to 73% of their time.
“Clinicians using Ambience’s platform spend 80% less time on EHR documentation. They report lower levels of burnout, and they feel like they’re able to have deeper, more meaningful connections with their patients during the visit,” Ng explains.
That’s good news for clinicians, and good news for Ambience.
The challenge for Ambience: there are a lot of other companies who have begun offering ambient scribe services, too.
The Rise of Ambient Scribes
While there has long been a cottage industry of companies providing medical scribes to reduce the documentation burden on doctors, the demand for scribes increased as EHR adoption increased. In virtually every case, however, these services provided in-person medical scribes to follow a physician through her day.
In 2011, there was only one company leveraging technology to provide speech-to-text services: Nuance Communications.
By 2020 there were a handful of newer entrants combining smartphone, ambient listening and some type of artificial intelligence technology, including Abridge, Nabla, Robin Healthcare, Ambience Healthcare and Suki. These “pure play” ambient scribe companies now have a collective valuation of more than $2B, of which the largest by reported revenue (Augmedix) generates only $44 million in annual sales. Clearly, investor enthusiasm is ahead of where the market is.
These companies face competition not just from each other, but from other, more established and often better funded health technology companies. Commure and Innovaccer are just two among a handful of companies whose core business is not related to ambient scribe technology, but who have recently announced ambient scribe offerings.
Commure and Innovaccer’s underlying reasons for making these announcements, and their approach to the offering themselves, may precipitate or accelerate the coming industry shakeout.
How Ambient Scribe Companies Compete Today
“I believe ambient scribing will become a commodity in healthcare, ultimately being priced very near ZERO,” says Abhinav Shashank, CEO of Innovaccer. Innovaccer, a data activation platform company that has raised more than $600 million to date, released its ambient scribe solution at the JP Morgan Healthcare conference. The company’s ‘Sara Scribe’ will offer up to 200 scribe notes per clinician for free, after which it will charge $1 per note.
Commure released its ambient scribe solution in April of this year, noting in its announcement that the technology would be available for free for 250,000 clinician users of its other software applications. (Just this week, Commure announced it was acquiring Augmedix, a move that likely makes sense for both sides).
What seems clear about both Innovaccer and Commure’s approach is the belief that ambient scribe is a feature, not a product. And with this belief comes the notion that the feature may simply be a lever to help acquire new users or retain existing users; either way, it is incidental, not critical, to the company’s broader value proposition and its underlying economic engine. Accordingly, such an approach to low-cost or free pricing may be part of a cohesive strategy to simultaneously drive volume of customers up (while earning revenue on other products) while draining “pure play” ambient scribe competitors of their core value proposition and pricing power.
One might think of modern technology giants such as Google or Meta, which regularly offer free features (e.g., Google Maps) in order to drive user engagement with other services that can be monetized.
It appears that Innovaccer in particular may subscribe to this approach. “Scribing is just the beginning—akin to how Google search is basic and should be free. The real value lies in a comprehensive support system that leverages AI to its fullest potential,” notes Shashank.
Matthew Holt foresees pricing pressure for ambient scribes as a whole as a result of these factors and other factors, writing that, “...realistically the whole market will have to compress… because the switching costs are going to be very trivial.” Axios reports current monthly prices for AI scribes ranging from $600 down to $119.
It’s not just technology executives and analysts who see this risk. Dr. Spencer Dorn, Vice Chair of Medicine and Professor at UNC Chapel Hill, sees and evaluates a lot of health tech solutions in his capacity. “With so many vendors, AI scribes are becoming commoditized,” he explains.
Price may be an important consideration, but others emphasize other factors as equally or perhaps more salient considerations. “We’re looking at ambient scribes because we’re trying to reduce clinician burnout. We want to help clinicians practice up to their license, and reduce inefficiency and administrative work,” Dr. Scott Cohen, Associate Chief Clinical Officer at Bassett Healthcare Network, says, explaining that the quality of EHR integration and accuracy of scribe output is key to clinician adoption and ultimately the realization of benefits.
Nabla’s CEO puts the matter of accuracy more bluntly. “The real litmus test for clinicians is, do they trust the tool enough to look the patient in the eye, instead of looking at their screen,” LeBrun says.
Key to accuracy is the robustness and reliability of clinically-relevant data that underpin each company’s large language models. Ng of Ambience says, “there’s a massive difference between ‘off-the-shelf’ langage models or a compelling demo, versus a clinical-grade product that works robustly in the clinic across specialties.” Ambience believes its investments in training its data across specialties and care settings is part of what sets it apart.
The ability to demonstrate bottom-line value is also important, and is a reason that Ambience incorporates coding compliance functionality into its scribe technology.
Features, functions and value propositions are not the only way that ambient scribe companies are seeking to differentiate themselves and separate themselves from competitors. Different target markets, messaging and sales approaches also play a role. Nabla, for instance, has largely employed a “product led growth” model, optimizing product design, marketing and sales efforts around organic efforts to attract, reach and retain individual clinicians (rather than large healthcare organizations).
Nabla’s ethos has led it to focus on delivering flexible technology that can be easily customized to the clinician. “We still have clinicians coming to our website, and buying the tool for their own use, on a daily basis…. Over 30,000 clinicians use Nabla, and they are constantly telling us ‘this is the first time I’ve been given tech that I can use in my own way,” explains CEO LeBrun.
Price. Standalone offering vs bundled. Accuracy. EHR integration. Return on investment. Go to market strategy and market focus. All of these reflect ways that ambient scribe companies are already competing and seeking to differentiate themselves in an emerging market but one with clear, strong demand signals.
There is also speculation on what will be important in the near future, and what clinicians will want as the technology and capabilities advance.
Shashank of Innovaccer notes that as costs for scribe services come down, companies will need to offer advanced capabilities such as clinical decision support and patient engagement tools.
LeBrun and Nabla point to the ability of an AI assistant to aid in preparing for a patient encounter, potentially suggesting questions for a clinician. This type of functionality resonates with Cohen of Bassett, who explains, “With an EHR, the clinician has to know where to look in the application for a million different things. Over time, I expect successful scribe vendors will move beyond note-writing to incorporate other related activities, such as summarizing clinical history, serving up insights relevant to the condition, and even entering orders through the clinician’s voice.”
With no shortage of ideas, the product roadmap for ambient scribe companies seems full of possibilities. But for any one company to deliver on that future, they’ll have to survive the current round of competition and the likely winnowing that is coming.
What Has Driven Industry Shake Out Before? And What Is Relevant To Ambient Scribe Companies?
In 1996, a couple of clever entrepreneurs realized they could harness the power of the internet to answer virtually any basic question a person might have. With a first mover advantage, strong brand, a compelling value proposition, and potential to quickly reach prohibitive scale, it raised millions to support a growth plan.
Yet, outside of a handful of aging Gen Xers still raging against the machine, few likely remember AskJeeves.com.
That’s of course because Google came along. While there are many reasons Google came to dominate internet search - beating out not just AskJeeves.com but many others including powerhouse Yahoo! - three primary reasons stand out:
- Search, not answering questions: whereas AskJeeves.com was in the question-and-answer business, Google was in the search business. From a product perspective, Google didn’t need to provide the best response (as AskJeeves did); it utilized algorithms and was able to leverage user data to present results, and constantly could fine-tune based on user feedback loops.
- Business model: by virtue of presenting website links (rather than answers), Google stumbled upon what became a dominant business model: advertising. As Google grew its user base, it was able to grow revenues in a non-linear manner as clicks increased and so too did Google’s ability to charge a premium for each click. A sustainable business model meant increased capacity to raise further capital and reinvest in improving the business.
- Economies of scale: over time, Google was able to reinvest in various areas (product, technology, marketing) in ways to create substantial barriers to entry. Google’s size has also given it enormous advantages over time in terms of ability to drive down supplier costs, thus increasing its economic advantage over potential competitors.
Yet technology evolves, and so Google has adapted to maintain its dominant position. For instance, as internet speeds and underlying internet infrastructure advanced, it became possible for the browser itself to direct users based on their use of the address bar. Identifying that the browser could potentially disconnect consumers from the need to use its search engine (or direct them to a competitors’ search engine), Google introduced its own browser in 2008. Today, Chrome has 66% market share. Second is Safari, Apple’s own browser, to which Google pays a reported $20 billion annually in order to be the default search engine.
It is this dynamic - the ability to control access to or influence users themselves - that presents both promise and peril for ambient scribe companies.
Today it is the EHR that serves as the de facto operating system for clinicians, hospitals and health systems. While clinicians may complain about the EHR, the fact is that, having gone through a massive period of transformation and behavior change prompted by the EHR Incentive Program, clinicians now run their day off of the EHR. And if there is one thing clinicians want, it is consistency in routine; they don’t want to use different systems with different log-ins for discrete clinical tasks. As a result, perhaps the most questions that any health tech company gets are “Do you integrate with my EHR? Is it single sign on? Can you describe how deep the integration is?”
Ambient scribe technology holds the promise of decoupling the bonds that bind clinicians to the EHR itself
Ambient scribe technology holds the promise of decoupling the bonds that bind clinicians to the EHR itself, at least to a large extent. As the technology improves and capabilities expand, it becomes possible to imagine a world in which healthcare delivery innovation can occur outside of the EHR. Where the pivot point and influence shifts from the EHR to the ambient scribe platform. Or said another way, where the ambient scribe technology becomes the browser, the primary interaction method for the user.
Whether it’s building an ‘App Store’ and enabling an ecosystem of innovation - allowing other digital health companies to leverage the data and user experience infrastructure - or connecting clinicians seamlessly to other healthcare constituents, it does seem there are longer term opportunities for ambient scribe companies. Presumably, these are much more lucrative than the business of selling ambient scribe technology to providers, which appears to be a relatively smaller (assuming the Axios numbers and 1M physicians, a ~$1.5B market) and declining market opportunity.
Previous analyses suggest that, in digital markets, business model transformation is critical to how industry shakeouts occur. Others emphasize the importance of quickly reaching economies of scale.
Either way, given market dynamics - apparent market appetite for ambient scribe technology, an abundance of vendors, and resulting price pressure - it seems reasonable to believe that speed to market and identification of a viable long term, sustainable revenue model will be critical to determining industry shakeout.
Yet if part of that long term revenue model is displacing or weakening the role of the EHR, ambient scribe vendors are hesitant to betray that. Innovaccer, Ambience and Nabla all emphasized the role of the EHR and how working productively with EHRs and other IT infrastructure is important to their own success. LeBrun of Nabla seemed to go furthest, explaining that scribe technology can “radically transform” how clinicians perceive the EHR, noting, “That’s great for clinicians, but it’s also great for EHRs.”
A Race To Scale, But With An Unclear Course And Murky Finish Line
Much of the focus regarding the technical and regulatory hurdles that ambient scribe companies (and much of healthcare technology writ large) are likely to face has been on various aspects of artificial intelligence that reflect broader concerns about the fairness, equity, and safety of large language models as well as how they are used responsibly in healthcare. But these are not the only challenges presenting themselves to ambient scribe companies.
Bassett Healthcare Network’s Chief Digital Health Officer, Paul Uhrig (who is also the organization’s Chief Legal Officer) is encouraged to see his clinicians excited about the technology, but as part of his diligence has raised questions that may have profound implications for the ambient scribe landscape.
“For instance, will the audio recordings be considered part of the designated health record under HIPAA or applicable state laws? Since health care providers are required to maintain the designated health record for up to 7 years, if the answer to these questions is yes, that could change the economics of this service since the storage cost of archiving thousands if not millions of audio recordings could be significant. Does the patient have a right of access to the recordings? The law and the policies of health systems need to catch up with the proliferation of this valuable technology,” Uhrig explains.
There are questions regarding how organizations and clinicians should manage the technology and second-order effects. Dorn of UNC Chapel Hill, for instance, is concerned about offloading critical thinking to machines. “While writing notes takes time and effort, the process helps us synthesize information and clarify our thinking,” he notes.
Scott Arnold, Chief Digital and Innovation Officer of Tampa General Hospital, likewise has concerns about the consequences of overreliance on such a powerful technology. “It’s similar to the evolution of EHRs and the ‘missing muscle memory’ for team members to document on paper during an outage,” he says, noting the impact of recent cyber attacks and downtime.
Navigating the regulatory landscape, evolving market needs, and clinician behavior change is a lot for ambient scribe companies to figure out. The companies face enormous internal hurdles as well. For instance, while the world has a plethora of software engineering talent, artificial intelligence is new and requires dramatically different skill sets; combined with the sensitivity of clinical data, talent itself (not customers) may be the scarce resource that ambient scribe companies find themselves competing over.
While many of these companies have been able to raise substantial capital even during a tight market thus far, as competition increases and downward pricing pressure for the core solution manifests itself, unit economics may erode. Combined with an inevitable fall from where the solutions are currently in the hype cycle, and we may see challenges with fundraising.
A Good Time To Be A Doctor
Ambience’s Mike Ng, for one, thinks the level of investment in artificial intelligence and ambient scribing in particular is a good thing for the healthcare system. “Long term, we think this will end up being a great thing for the ecosystem—free and open competition means that we’re more likely to end up with the best possible solutions for clinicians,” Ng says.
There is additional good news for doctors and other clinicians who have been suffering the slings and arrows of “administrivia” and pajama time: the excitement around ambient scribes is not just hype. A recent study published in the New England Journal of Medicine found encouraging results related to the adoption of ambient scribe technology among a large number of Kaiser Permanente physicians in terms of clinician and patient acceptance, clinician satisfaction, scribe accuracy, and a reduction in documentation burden.
Arnold of Tampa General offers additional anecdotal confirmation of his health systems’ experience. “So far, the technology has delivered as promised — in fact, the results are quite amazing so far…. We have an ambulatory specialist [seeing more patients than before] with time now to have dinner with his family without writing notes all night,” Arnold says.
While it’s worth noting that ambient scribes are just a small part of the technology a physician must interact with, it’s perhaps the first example of a technology that actively “abstracts away” the experience of the product itself, enabling and encouraging a return to a more human experience in which the doctor can focus on the patient.
It remains to be seen how widely adopted ambient scribe technology will be or the ultimate impact it will have. But the present moment seems to share a number of similarities with the automotive industry more than a century ago: emerging technology that reflects a fundamental shift from the status quo, strong and growing demand, rapid investment into the development and design of products to meet this demand, and enough externalities to imagine a future that looks brighter and more connected than ever before.
How will the ambient scribe industry shake out? Impossible to answer with any certainty. But who will win regardless? That one seems clear: we all will.

title: Council Post: A 'TsunamAI' Of Change Is Coming To Healthcare
text:
Lee Shapiro is the Cofounder & Managing Partner of 7Wire Ventures.
In the last 50 years, there have been significant developments that have forever improved the delivery of healthcare. Consider imaging (MRI/CT scans), minimally invasive surgery, anti-viral therapies, precision medicine (e.g., CRISPR and gene editing) and near or complete eradication of diseases like polio and smallpox. As we look back 50 years from now, we will have experienced seismic changes from AI. When I've spoken with healthcare leaders, they've pointed to a progression of AI adoption that will occur in the following three categories, which you should consider for your organization: administrative, research and development, and care delivery.
Area 1: Administrative
Administrative spending accounts for 15-30% of total healthcare spending in the U.S., much of which is considered wasteful. Furthermore, administrative tasks drive provider burnout: 2016 data showed that physicians spent 48% of their time on electronic health records (EHR) and desk work compared with 26% on direct clinical face time with patients.
AI is having an impact on clinical notes and medical coding. Microsoft, through Nuance, developed an AI-powered solution that documents patient encounters at the point of care. Abridge also uses AI to generate clinical notes from patient conversations. In your own organization, consider the hours that could be shifted from documenting care to care delivery.
Prior authorization (PA) for medical services is another area ripe for AI disruption. PA is estimated to cost $25 billion yearly, and 93% of physicians have indicated that PA "can delay access to medically necessary care." One health plan operator that received more than 1.5 million prior authorization requests in 2022 implemented an augmented intelligence solution that allowed it to process requests up to 1,400 times faster than in the past. However, there have been challenges to AI denials of PA requests. In response, the House of Delegates directed the AMA to advocate for greater oversight over this process, including whether insurers are requiring a human examination of patient records before a denial.
This is an important point: AI has the potential to reduce time and costs, but successfully rolling it out requires building trust with patients and providers. Consider where human engagement is needed when rolling out such solutions.
Area 2: Research And Development
Jensen Huang, president of NVIDIA, claims that "'digital biology' is going to be the 'next amazing revolution' for AI." It is no exaggeration to say that AI can change the way therapeutics are discovered and developed, with the potential to improve speed, reduce costs and improve access to treatments.
At the stage of target identification, AI could mine -omics data, analyze phenotypic results and identify novel binding sites, among other activities. It could then be used to predict pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties. Companies are pouring funding into the space; recently Xaira, a company using "machine learning, data generation and therapeutic product development to build a platform for drug discovery," emerged from stealth with $1 billion in funding.
AI is also speeding up clinical trials. Up to one-third of the time for clinical trials is spent recruiting patients, and one in five trials do not recruit the required number of people, according to a Nature article. AI can help in designing trial criteria, identifying suitable cohorts for trials and alerting medical staff and patients about trial opportunities. For example, H1 offers an AI-enabled healthcare data platform that, according to its website, aids in R&D pipeline acceleration and trial design. AI can also be used to facilitate diversity within clinical trials; Acclinate uses its analytic platform to identify locations for trials, reach hard-to-find groups and mobilize the recruitment process.
Sixty-eight percent of pharmaceutical businesses "identified pervasive AI as the technological trend with the highest potential impact on their business/market environment." Ask your leadership team how AI can glean new insights from your clinical data or how to partner with clinical research organizations or life sciences companies to bring new products to market.
Area 3: Care Delivery
Within care delivery, I am most excited about the potential of AI to allow providers to uplevel their skills. While your doctor will not be replaced by AI, doctors who use AI may replace those who do not. Clinical adoption of these innovations must first prove efficacy and then fit neatly within the provider’s workflow.
In the near term, AI has the potential to augment how hospitals use data, 97% of which goes unused (registration required). AI-powered diagnostics and predictive analytics can take advantage of this data. Aidoc has developed cardiovascular solutions that consolidate data, generate clinical insights and streamline follow-up conversations with patients. AI can also help interpret medical images, helping patients see results faster and identifying concerns. In breast cancer detection, AI can enable radiologists to better view anatomical structures. It can also enable remote interpretation of imaging, which can help drive equitable access in low-resourced areas.
Care delivery will require a significant human footprint in the near- to medium-term. Leaders should focus on finding ways to leverage AI to provide high-quality, relevant information to providers in a timely manner. As providers become more comfortable using AI on a day-to-day basis, I believe there will be greater opportunities for future use cases.
My three recommendations for leaders are:
1. Balance Impact And Risk: Understand your organization’s risk appetite. Evaluate the potential risks of using AI in any given situation (e.g., bias and lack of accuracy). Think through where a solution may require a “human in the loop.”
2. Build Or Partner For Capabilities: Evaluate where your organization may need its own custom tools and approaches versus where you can partner to leverage existing models.
3. Change Management: Adapting to a new way of working can be challenging. Incorporate end users in your design process and allow for time to increase their overall comfort level with any solution.
AI has the potential to be a positive, transformative force within healthcare—it is up to leaders to ensure we are prepared to harness its power.

title: Council Post: How To Use AI To Improve Operational Excellence
text:
Jeff Brown is the COO at OXOS Medical.
AI is not only for IT and not only for the senior most leadership to consider. If you’re not getting ahead of your competition with AI, then that same competition is working to use AI to move past you. Here are just a few powerful ways to leverage AI to improve your business’s operations.
Challenge ALL Department Leaders To Develop An AI Strategy
It's not enough for AI initiatives to be confined to marketing or IT departments. Every department leader must be challenged to craft a robust AI strategy tailored to the specific operational needs of their department and/or responsibility. This involves setting clear goals, understanding how AI can be leveraged and its potential impact, and aligning these strategies across the organization. You don’t need a “boil the ocean” strategy to do this; there are likely many gold nuggets that will be discovered and all will contribute to benefits across your organization.
The process can be summarized in a few key steps:
- Challenge your department leaders to identify the most promising opportunities to use AI to streamline operations for their respective departments.
- Have these leaders present their findings to their peers and company leadership.
- Look for trends across functions to align efforts and get multiple birds with one stone.
Execute and deliver real, measurable value.
For example, Amazon department heads from operations, customer service and supply chain collaboratively developed AI-driven strategies that standardized route optimization, automated customer interactions and predicted inventory needs. This cross-functional alignment, spearheaded by a designated AI strategy leader, resulted in a significant increase in operational efficiency across the board.
Target AI At Your Most Highly Leveraged Process Workflows
AI solutions are a must to remain competitive in the current market, and certainly for the future. Identifying where exactly a difference can be made in your processes is crucial. Focus on high-return areas, typically those with high labor content or significant strategic value.
Kroger provides a great example of this. As a leading adopter of AI, the company has aimed AI solutions at some of its biggest opportunity areas, particularly food spoilage and sales efficiency. Kroger optimizes its supply chain using AI for online delivery operations. It works to keep food fresher using computer vision and routing and optimizes store efficiency with digital simulations. This approach can be the blueprint for organizations in any sector.
Use AI To Rejuvenate ‘Forgotten’ Portions Of Your Business
Often the most transformative opportunities lie in a business's neglected or routine segments. AI can breathe new life into these areas by automating complex compliance processes or revitalizing outdated practices. For instance, a current process workflow can be fed into an AI large language model and asked to provide a list of the most probable opportunities for improvement given the current process design, risks, staff involvement and so on.
We can again look to Amazon for a great example. Amazon uses machine learning algorithms to analyze existing workflows, identifying inefficiencies such as suboptimal picking routes or their current slotting strategy in their distribution centers. The AI system then suggests improvements such as reorganizing the warehouse layout to minimize travel time between high-demand items or altering staffing levels during peak hours. The result of these AI-driven optimizations was a reduction in operational costs and faster shipping times for sorting and packaging items, improving delivery times and overall customer experience.
Another example comes from an area thought to be “untouchable,” namely regulated industries. AI tools are beginning to be used to ensure both compliance and the effective and timely realization of revenue streams.
For example, there is a large push in the medical device and pharmaceutical industries to develop AI tools to specifically and systematically capture applicable regulatory standards affecting a product. At the same time, AI tools are being used to clearly define a list of compliance requirements from the standards that apply to specific devices, as well as to suggest best practices for how best to comply with and even develop testing strategies.
Leveraging AI in this way can streamline compliance reviews, reduce reliance on costly consultants and accelerate the launch of new products, all of which help deliver revenue faster.
Leverage AI To Remove User Error
Incorporating AI directly into products and services can drastically reduce user error and enhance customer safety and satisfaction. If a user is required to make critical decisions or if safety is a concern during the use of your device, AI can be used to take the guesswork out of the system and ensure your device works safely and as intended.
An example of this is seen at Google Health, which uses a suite of AI tools for image processing, detection and suggested diagnosis. For example, their AI system for ultrasound imaging is trained on thousands of fetal and breast ultrasound images, enabling it to recognize crucial details that could otherwise be missed by users. Leveraging AI in this way has resulted in image recognition accuracy and suggested diagnoses that are comparable to highly trained ultrasonographers. Pairing the use of AI with highly trained users can result in better patient outcomes and faster treatment.
AI is not just a tool for writing papers or ideation; it is a fundamental pillar for operational excellence that can transform every aspect of a business. From enhancing departmental strategies to reinvigorating stale processes and ensuring effective and safe product use, AI empowers businesses to operate smarter, faster and more efficiently. As businesses continue to navigate the complexities of the digital age, those who master the strategic use of AI will survive and thrive.

title: Council Post: A CISO's Guide To Fortifying Your Cybersecurity Posture
text:
Vijay Pitchumani is Director of Product Management at Okta.
The past year has witnessed an explosion in artificial intelligence (AI) adoption. Advancements in generative AI and machine learning (ML) are rapidly reshaping industries and transforming how businesses operate. A 2024 McKinsey study reveals a staggering 72% of surveyed organizations are leveraging AI in some capacity, with a remarkable 65% actively utilizing GenAI to drive efficiency in marketing, sales, product development and support functions.
This transformative technology offers significant benefits beyond business process optimization. It presents a powerful opportunity to fortify an organization's security posture. In today's hyper-connected world, the threat landscape is constantly evolving, demanding a proactive approach to security. The statistics are sobering: Data breaches skyrocketed a concerning 78% year-over-year in 2023, surpassing a staggering 3,200 incidents. Additionally, the average cost of a single breach has reached nearly $4.5 million.
These figures highlight the critical need for robust and adaptable cybersecurity strategies.
Generative AI and machine learning empower security teams and chief information security officers (CISOs) with powerful new tools and capabilities to tackle modern cybersecurity threats. These tools provide deeper insights into an organization's cybersecurity posture, enabling proactive responses and enhanced security. This blog post dives into the critical considerations for CISOs as they develop and implement successful AI strategies to combat modern cyber threats.
Breaking Down Data Silos: A Unified View For Stronger Defense
For CISOs, managing a complex landscape of best-in-breed cybersecurity tools is a common challenge. While these individual products excel in their specific domains, their fragmented data creates blind spots and hinders effective threat analysis.
To unlock the full potential of AI and gain a comprehensive view of their security posture, CISOs need a data unification strategy. This can be achieved by either centralizing data access from these point solutions or by implementing platform-based solutions that address multiple security needs. By eliminating data silos, CISOs can foster a more holistic and proactive approach to cybersecurity. Imagine a central dashboard that provides a real-time view of security across the entire network, highlighting potential threats and vulnerabilities. This unified view empowers CISOs to make informed decisions and prioritize resources effectively.
Locking Down Access: The Least Privilege Principle
Unifying data empowers AI for advanced threat detection, but it also creates a centralized target for attackers. The principle of least privilege becomes crucial here. CISOs must ensure only authorized personnel have access to specific data sets, with the most limited permissions necessary for their roles. This minimizes the attack surface and empowers AI to effectively analyze data without exposing sensitive information.
By following least privilege, CISOs can ensure AI leverages valuable insights for robust security without compromising confidentiality. Imagine a scenario where only security analysts have access to complete network data while other personnel have access to specific sections relevant to their roles. This minimizes the potential damage if a bad actor breaches a single access point.
Deeper Insights, Faster Response
By eliminating data silos and locking down data access, organizations can now leverage generative AI and machine learning capabilities to derive comprehensive visibility into their security landscape. This translates into actionable data that empowers the entire organization to respond swiftly and effectively to emerging threats. Imagine AI analyzing network traffic patterns and identifying a potential intrusion attempt in real time. This early detection allows for immediate response, potentially stopping an attack before it can infiltrate the system.
To take the response to the next level, CISOs must leverage this visibility and implement automation and response playbooks for effective risk remediation. Automated remediation further streamlines the process, automatically addressing identified threats before they can escalate. This frees up valuable resources for CISOs and their teams, allowing them to focus on strategic initiatives and continuous improvement. Imagine automated systems patching vulnerabilities or isolating infected devices as soon as a threat is detected. This swift response minimizes downtime and potential damage.
The Future Of Cybersecurity: A Race
Malicious actors are constantly innovating, launching sophisticated attacks that can bypass traditional security methods. CISOs must remain vigilant and proactive in the face of these emerging challenges. This requires a strategic shift that involves leveraging machine learning to tackle complex threats.
However, it's important to remember that AI is not a silver bullet. CISOs must continuously adapt their strategies and embrace a multifaceted approach that combines AI with human expertise, threat intelligence and regular security audits. By embracing a proactive and comprehensive approach, organizations can harness the power of AI to build a truly resilient security posture that can withstand the ever-evolving threat landscape.
AI presents a powerful new weapon in the fight against cybercrime. By understanding the challenges and opportunities associated with AI adoption, CISOs can leverage this technology to build a stronger, more proactive security posture.

title: Council Post: AI: Who Is Really In Control, Business Leaders Or Technocrats?
text:
Dr. Jamil El-Imad is Senior Research Fellow at Imperial College, Institute of Biomedical Engineering.
Having led the design and deployment of numerous information technology systems for over four decades in multiple sectors, I have witnessed first-hand the transformative potential of technology in business. However, I have also seen the pitfalls of technology-driven initiatives that lack a strategic alignment with business goals.
The rapid advancement of AI technology has presented businesses with unprecedented opportunities for innovation, efficiency and competitive advantage. However, in the rush to adopt AI, many organizations risk allowing technocrats—those deeply entrenched in the technical aspects of AI—to drive its deployment without a clear business strategy. This approach can lead to misaligned priorities, wasted resources and, ultimately, a failure to achieve meaningful business outcomes. To avoid this, businesses must develop and adhere to a comprehensive AI strategy that aligns with their broader corporate goals.
The Three Key Components Of An AI Business Strategy
A robust business strategy serves as the foundation for any successful AI deployment. This strategy in my view should address three key areas.
1. Business Scope: This includes the choices pertaining to products and market offerings. A clear understanding of the business scope helps in identifying where AI can add the most value, whether through enhancing existing products, developing new offerings or entering new markets.
2. Distinctive Competencies: These are the unique strengths a business wishes to leverage, such as product pricing, quality of distribution channels or customer service excellence. AI can enhance these competencies by providing deeper insights, improving operational efficiencies or offering new capabilities.
3. Business Governance: This involves the structural choices of managing the business, including ethics, sustainability and other organizational principles. Effective AI deployment must align with these governance principles, ensuring that AI solutions are ethical, sustainable and supportive of the organization's long-term vision.
Linking AI Deployment To Corporate Goals
Once the business strategy is understood, the next challenge is ensuring that AI solutions are deployed in a manner that aligns with and supports corporate goals. This requires a coherent policy that integrates AI into the strategic framework of the organization. AI is a powerful productivity tool, capable of transforming business processes. However, if not aligned with corporate strategy, AI initiatives can lead to disjointed efforts that fail to deliver meaningful value.
In the AI era, IT plays a critical role not only in supporting business strengths and mitigating weaknesses but also in informing decisions related to external opportunities and threats. As such, effective AI deployment entails leaders from both the business side as well as the IT side to work closely to ensure that AI initiatives are aligned with strategic business goals. This collaboration is essential for identifying the most promising AI applications, setting priorities and ensuring that AI investments deliver the desired outcomes.
Having an explicit corporate strategy clearly defined and supported by policies and programs can shorten AI implementations and reduce the uncertainties in linking AI deployment to corporate goals. One of the challenges I face when designing knowledge systems and AI deployments is understanding the corporate strategy in companies where there isn’t an explicit strategy and gaining access to the top management is hard. In such an environment, my approach is to look first at the successful divisions in the company, as they tend to influence how the overall business is governed. Thereafter, I identify ways that an AI deployment can help them increase productivity, improve profitability or deliver better value and experience to their customers.
It's important to note that such tools—if deployed ahead of the competition—can deliver a competitive advantage. However, if they're deployed when such solutions are widely available, their value is more defensive.
Conclusion
In conclusion, the deployment of AI in organizations must be guided by a clear and comprehensive business strategy. Without this strategic alignment, there's a risk that AI initiatives will be driven by technocrats with little regard for business value, leading to missed opportunities. By developing and adhering to a robust AI strategy that is aligned with the business strategy, organizations can help ensure that AI serves as a powerful tool for achieving corporate goals. In doing so, they can avoid the pitfalls of allowing the AI tail to wag the organization’s dog and instead harness the full potential of AI to drive business success.
