title: Forget The Past No Longer: Generational Amnesia Getting Overridden Via Advent Of Generative AI
text:
In today’s column, I’ll be doing a deep dive into a fascinating topic known as generational amnesia. The topic is quite worthy of special attention in an era of rapidly advancing generative AI. You will soon see how the two vital considerations are inevitably intertwined, doing so for the good of humanity and yet possibly having some sobering downsides too.
Turns out that besides a generally interesting topic, there are decidedly mental health ramifications associated with these matters too. For those of you generally interested in AI and mental health, I have been extensively analyzing and covering generative AI and mental health, see my comprehensive overview at the link here. You might also find of notable interest a CBS 60 Minutes episode that recently examined crucial facets of this evolving topic, see the link here (I am honored and pleased to indicate that I was featured in the episode, see the link here).
Time to unpack a little-known construct known as generational amnesia.
Let’s get underway here with an all-time classic quote:
- “Those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat it” (George Santayana in his 1905 book “The Life of Reason, or The Phases of Human Progress”).
If we are to take that insight as a truism, we ought to feel compelled to make sure that we remember the past. Not just remember it, but also actively leverage the past. Continually and forcefully taking into consideration what has happened and how that can be avidly used to shape what will happen next.
A big problem with trying to abide by this credo is that we have only finite lives. Sorry to break the news on that notion that we do not live forever. Because we live just a finite period of time, whatever might be in our noggins is essentially lost to the ages. We can leave behind written records, artifacts, and all manner of leftover physical manifestations. For the foreseeable future, we are unable to leave behind the complete store of knowledge in our brains (some stretch-goal neuroscience and AI researchers aim to change this and allow humans to do a kind of mind-dump into AI, see my coverage at the link here).
I dare say that parents try their best to pass along their knowledge to their offspring. Again, this is only going to be a partial transmission. You can talk to your kids until you are blue in the face and yet the full depth of your knowledge is likely still only shared in a relatively miniscule way. Furthermore, a parent had the same done to them, such that they are passing along just a scrap of what was passed to them by their parents.
Making Memorable Points About Generational Amnesia
Here's where I am taking you.
Society has forever faced a dilemma that we can anoint with a handy moniker of saying that we confront or are immersed in generational amnesia.
Each generation gets passed to it some fractional amount of prior knowledge by the most immediate and alive generations, plus, a bit more via the no longer existent generations that have by design or happenstance left their presence in other recorded means. This is like doing one of those fire drills where you hand a bucket of water from one person to the next, each time slopping some of the water out of the bucket. When the bucket gets to the end of the line, there might only be a fraction remaining.
This intergenerational transmission presents a problem since the way that we do it now is wholly imperfect. In a sense, stuff is being forgotten due to not passing along each and every morsel of what was known in a prior generation. It is a loss of memory. Said to be amnesia on a generational scale.
Think of it another way.
Toddlers today are being showered with knowledge from the oldest living generation, The Silent Generation, along with Baby Boomers, Gen X, Gen Y, and their peers in Gen Z. How much of that knowledge will those Gen Z kids retain and actively use as they become adults, gradually age, and otherwise carry out the fullness of their lives?
Will they be able to avoid repeating the mistakes of the past by leaning into what they have garnered from the existent living generations, despite the fractional or amnesia losses of knowledge that have occurred?
Of course, this is all a sliding scale such that soon enough the Gen Z will find themselves passing along their wisdom to the generation that comes forth behind them. Regrettably, the next new generation is unlikely to glean much directly from The Silent Generation at that point since those people will no longer be around.
And, so on, things roll along.
It is the circle of life.
You might be protesting that recorded history makes up for those living generation-to-generation sharing processes that are fractional. Not really. Recorded history is another fractional distillation of the past. It is fragmented. It can readily be lost or misplaced. It can be extremely hard to access and find. How many ancient cave wall etchings do we still have available? Even paper-based books have been lost to the ages.
A Big Surprise Pops Out Of The AI Box
Is there any means to potentially overrie the generational amnesia and boost intergenerational transmission?
Hold your breath and sit down because I have an out-of-the-box suggestion for you to contemplate.
The solution to the problem could be in the hands of modern-day generative AI. Generative AI might very well be the fixer when it comes to overcoming or overriding generational amnesia. We could use generative AI as our intergenerational transmission mechanism.
The idea that anyone could ever again forget the past, and thus be condemned to repeat it, would be a foreign concept that would make people scratch their heads in wonderment. Are you saying, they would ask sheepishly, that people didn’t have generative AI that aided them in remembering everything about the past?
Sounds archaic, they would sardonically comment.
The generative AI that you are using these days to playfully write essays or engage in idle conversations could end up being a grand-scale generational retainer, nixing forever the woes of generational amnesia.
Boom, drop the mic.
Admittedly, it’s not AI alone that comes to the rescue.
The digital world all told is improving the odds of mitigating generational amnesia. We are capturing a lot of our current times by putting content into digital formats. Issues do exist. Digital content is often scattered, such as floating somewhere on the Internet. There are a lot of abysmal flotsams there too. Being digital is a crucial ingredient but is insufficient to take a big leap toward solving generational amnesia.
That’s where AI and particularly generative AI come into view.
Research On Generational Amnesia Is Unforgettable
Before exploring the role of generative AI in this generational knowledge-sharing divide-and-conquer, I’d like to share with you some key research on generational amnesia. We will do a fast-paced tour.
In a research study entitled “Daughters’ Stories: Family Memory and Generational Amnesia” by Daniela Koleva, The Oral History Review, December 2019, these major points were made (excerpts):
- “Here I explore how the women of three generations from the same family reinvent their identities in their life stories.”
- “Drawing on this particular case, I suggest an approach to the question of the interplay of individual and collective memory.”
- “I focus on family and generation as different types of collectivities influencing individual memories and self-actualizations.”
I brought up this research study to highlight that one of the most common approaches taken to dealing with generational amnesia consists of within-family efforts to hand down prior knowledge from generation to generation. The study focused on women in the same family tree who sought to share their respective knowledge across three generations.
That’s a rather conventional generational transmission effort. It is typically locally based and sporadically undertaken. Inconsistency, fractional pass-along, and other drawbacks are aplenty. Laudable but not moving the needle on any grand scale per se.
Shifting from a family unit focus, the next research study that I selected opted to examine generational transmission on a larger scale. In this case, there is often generational amnesia on monumental population-wide issues such as vaccines. Let’s see what they had to say.
A research study entitled “The Regulatory Shifting Baseline Syndrome: Vaccines, Generational Amnesia, and the Shifting Perception of Risk in Public Law Regimes” by Robin Craig, Yale Journal of Health Policy, Law, and Ethics, July 2022, made these salient points (excerpts):
- “In 1995, Dr. Daniel Pauly described the “shifting baseline syndrome” and its problems for fisheries management. Pauly posited that each generation forgets what the ocean and its fisheries used to be and that this generational amnesia allows successive generations to accept the current impoverished state of marine fisheries as normal.”
- “This Article brings the shifting baseline concept into public law, identifying for the first time a regulatory shifting baseline syndrome that can undermine the law’s ability to protect society at large.”
- “This syndrome arises when a public legal regime, like a school vaccination mandate, so successfully eliminates a societal problem, like dread diseases, that citizens, politicians, and lawmakers forget that the regime is in fact still working to keep that problem at bay.”
- “This generational amnesia, in turn, can lead to changes in law and policy allowing the prior problem to re-emerge in society, as occurred with measles outbreaks.”
An important concept is noted in the study, referred to as the shifting baseline syndrome.
Here’s how that works.
A new generation arises and tends to accept that the existing ways of the world must be the norm. They have not experienced directly what came before them. You could assert that the generation crafts a baseline based on what they know at the time of their generation. The thing is, they might not readily discern whether things are worse or better than before, and they cannot necessarily grasp the trajectory of what direction things are going.
The generation establishes a baseline predicated on their generational knowledge at the time of their generation.
The generation that comes after them will do the same. Once again, they won’t especially comprehend what took place before their generation. Thus, the baseline is constantly shifting and becomes a new baseline. This happens generation upon generation.
Seems okay, maybe, but not if the currently devised baseline hides potential gotchas of a historical nature. Consider a rough analogy. There is a classic tale of a frog that is placed into a pot of water at room temperature on a stove. A tiny degree at a time, the water is getting hotter and hotter, heading toward a boiling point. The frog is complacent and unable to discern that doom is where they are headed.
The same might be said of humans who take as a given that their standing during their generation is the way things are. Vaccines are a prime example of this. One generation gets decimated by a disease that a discovered vaccine can aid in undercutting or curing. They manage to get the vaccine widely distributed.
Later, a generation is born that has no direct awareness of the disease and assumes that there isn’t any danger afoot. They proceed to undervalue taking the vaccine. Lack of generational awareness draws them into complacency. It is conceivable they are priming themselves for a repeat of the ravaging disease. Lamentedly, they could have avoided the calamity if they knew of and fully comprehended what prior generations endured.
Voila, as per the famous quote, those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat it.
A research study examined whether the efforts of humankind to retain heritages provide a capability to contend with generational amnesia. In the article entitled “The Shifting Baseline Syndrome and Generational Amnesia In Heritage Studies” by Dirk H. R. Spennemann, Heritage, August 2022, these points were noted (excerpts):
- “It must be remembered that intergenerational transmission is selective.”
- “Humanity’s heritage is comprised of a range of tangible and intangible manifestations of people’s cultural, spiritual, and economic lives, and their interactions with their natural environment.”
- “The more distant the past, the more the minutiae of lived experience fade, with memories reduced to major personally, culturally, or environmentally catastrophic events. This change in granularity of memory has major implications on the shifting baseline concept.”
- “Thus, shifting baselines based on memory recall have a finite depth, unless specific events are canonically encoded in communal cultural memory.”
That research reinforces my earlier point that the communal cultural memory as exhibited in museums and other means of collecting the past is just not sufficient to override generational amnesia. It is a vaunted way to try. But it is only a drop in the bucket.
One area of generational amnesia that has garnered devout attention consists of the use case involving the ecosystem and the environment. Coined as “environmental generational amnesia”, the focus is akin to the vaccine's example about shifting baselines, though this is about generational baselines associated with the environment.
In a research paper entitled “Children’s Affiliations With Nature: Structure, Development, And The Problem Of Environmental Generational Amnesia” by Peter Kahn, Jr., in Peter Kahn, Jr. and S. R. Kellert (Eds.), Children and Nature: Psychological, Sociocultural, And Evolutionary Investigations, MIT Press, 2002, these vital points were made (excerpts):
- “In these studies, children were interviewed in diverse locations about their environmental moral conceptions and values.”
- “The author also seeks to explicate two ideas that frame his theoretical approach to investigating children's affiliations with nature-structure and development.”
- “Finally, the author builds on the structural-developmental framework and his research findings to articulate what may be one of the most pressing and unrecognized problems of the current age—the problem of environmental generational amnesia.”
The researcher interviewed children to discern their perception of the environment and environmental conditions. The idea was to see what baseline about the environment is currently taking hold.
In a similar study that was undertaken nearly fifteen years later, baselines were further identified, as noted in a paper entitled “The Importance Of Children Interacting With Big Nature” by Peter H. Kahn, Jr. and Thea Weiss, Natural Spaces and Development, 2017.
- “The problem of environmental generational amnesia is that nature gets increasingly diminished and degraded, but children of each generation perceive the environment into which they are born as normal.”
- “Thus, across generations, the baseline shifts downward for what counts as healthy nature.”
- “One solution is to broaden and deepen children’s interactions with nature, and whenever possible, with big nature.”
A proposition is that a new generation might perceive that the environment is what it is. If the environment is getting worse, there is a chance they won’t fully comprehend the worsening status because the prior status is not as immersive in their minds. Their collective effort to perhaps stop the environment from getting worse is muted to some degree. Again, this is akin to the tale of the frog.
An interesting twist on that same theme was done by examining how immersive technology that portrays nature could make matters worse rather than better. In a research study entitled “The Human Relation With Nature and Technological Nature” by Peter H. Kahn, Jr., Rachel Severson, and Jolina H. Ruckert, Current Directions In Psychological Science, February 2009, these points were noted (excerpts):
- “Two world trends are powerfully reshaping human existence: the degradation, if not destruction, of large parts of the natural world, and unprecedented technological development.”
- “Current examples of technological nature include videos and live webcams of nature, robot animals, and immersive virtual environments.”
- “Does it matter for the physical and psychological well-being of the human species that actual nature is being replaced with technological nature? As the basis for our provisional answer (it is “yes”), we draw on evolutionary and cross-cultural developmental accounts of the human relation with nature and some recent psychological research on the effects of technological nature.”
- “We discuss the issue — and area for future research — of “environmental generational amnesia.” The concern is that, by adapting gradually to the loss of actual nature and the increase of technological nature, humans will lower the baseline across generations for what counts as a full measure of the human experience and human flourishing.”
That study serves as a wake-up call.
The upshot is that technology can be a blessing or a curse when it comes to generational amnesia. In this instance, the research seemed to suggest that technology was distancing the generation from the environment. This further exacerbated the issue of generational amnesia.
It could be that technology might instead help. Suppose that similar technology immersed them in nature as it was before their generation arose. This might aid them in more clearly seeing what was happening before and enable them to make a more balanced comparison to where they are today. You could suggest that the baseline that otherwise existed by default could be reshaped by tapping into the knowledge and memories of the past.
That’s a great segue into the role of generative AI for dealing with generational amnesia.
Generative AI As Promise And Future
I’d like to lay out the fundamentals of generative AI and large language models (LLMs) so that we are all on the same page on what this type of AI consists of.
Perhaps you’ve at least heard about various generative AI apps, such as the popular ones of ChatGPT, GPT-4o, Gemini, Bard, Claude, etc. The crux is that generative AI can take input from your text-entered prompts and produce or generate a response that seems quite fluent. This is a vast overturning of the old-time natural language processing (NLP) that used to be stilted and awkward to use, which has been shifted into a new version of NLP fluency of an at times startling or amazing caliber.
The customary means of achieving modern generative AI involves using a large language model or LLM as the key underpinning.
In brief, a computer-based model of human language is established that in the large has a large-scale data structure and does massive-scale pattern-matching via a large volume of data used for initial data training. The data is typically found by extensively scanning the Internet for lots and lots of essays, blogs, poems, narratives, and the like. The mathematical and computational pattern-matching homes in on how humans write, and then henceforth generates responses to posed questions by leveraging those identified patterns. It is said to be mimicking the writing of humans.
I think that is sufficient for the moment as a quickie backgrounder. Take a look at my extensive coverage of the technical underpinnings of generative AI and LLMs at the link here and the link here, just to name a few.
Back to the crux of things.
When you make use of generative AI, you are essentially tapping into the past and potentially the present.
The data training of the generative AI encompasses whatever historical records and content happened to be used when doing the initial build of the AI. You could say that the collective memory or knowledge was being encapsulated into the AI system. If the generative AI is actively connected to the Internet, present data might also be feeding into the AI.
That sounds better than it actually is.
First, generative AI is a form of compression of the data that was used for data training. This means that you are getting a reduced version or variation of what was actually in the data. The resultant data that you get as output when asking questions is not necessarily an accurate reflection of that input data. As I’ve covered extensively, the mathematical and computational act of compression and transformation can contain and infuse all manner of biases, errors, and other unsettling issues, see the link here.
Second, the data that was chosen for the data training is yet another form of bias. If a generative AI app is fed data from the Internet that is say exclusively of the bent that the moon is made of cheese, there isn’t any other grounding or semblance of common sense that would correct that data training. A person using the generative AI might ask a question about the moon and get an answer that the moon is full of cheese. This seems zany to us but is merely a “factual” output based on what the AI was data trained on.
Third, generative AI is subject to so-called AI hallucinations, see my coverage at the link here and the link here. I disfavor the terminology since it is unduly anthropomorphizing AI. Nonetheless, it is vocabulary that has taken hold.
The meaning is that generative AI can produce an output that seems to be factual, but it is instead quite fictitious. Due to the use of probabilities, words have been strung together that say something of a made-up nature. You might have heard about the two lawyers who relied on generative AI to aid in writing their court-submitted legal brief, which contained AI hallucinations, and the lawyers got themselves into legal trouble, accordingly, see the link here.
I note these kinds of limitations and qualms about generative AI to emphasize that at least right now, our current times generative AI is not the silver bullet for generational amnesia. Data training is only a smidgeon of the sum total of human knowledge. Data that is being used might be skewed as to what data is available. Data itself can contain plentiful falsehoods, biases, and the like.
It is a severely flawed memory retainer at this time.
Gradually, it is conceivable that these weaknesses will be lessened. As I’ve stated, we are heading toward full-on multi-modal generative AI, see my discussion at the link here. Out of reach right now but something of great promise would be the connecting of AI with the human brain such as via BMI (brain-machine interfaces), see my analysis at the link here.
Step by step, advances in generative AI could demonstrably improve the odds of eroding generational amnesia. Not all at once. Not in a Big Bang way. However, some claim we are going to arrive at Artificial Superintelligence (ASI) that presumably might occur in a grand singularity of an intelligence explosion, as I cover at the link here. Would ASI encompass all of human knowledge? Seems a stretch, but that is part and parcel of those outlier theories.
Using ChatGPT To Explore The Generational Amnesia Issue
I will next proceed to lean into generative AI to see what else we can do about the use of generative AI to combat generational amnesia.
This will consist of a series of dialogues with ChatGPT. ChatGPT is a logical choice in this case due to its immense popularity as a generative AI app. An estimated one hundred million weekly active users are said to be utilizing ChatGPT. That’s a lot of people and a lot of generative AI usage underway.
A few quick comments before we launch into using ChatGPT.
If you are going to try to do the same prompts that I show here, realize that the probabilistic and statistical properties will likely produce slightly different results than what I show here. That’s the nature of generative AI and how it is devised.
You also should expect that different generative AI apps will respond in different ways. Not all generative AI apps are the same. The key is that sometimes a particular prompt will work in one generative AI app and not another. Nonetheless, the odds are relatively high that you will get roughly similar responses from all the major generative AI apps such as GPT-4, Gemini, Bard, Claude, etc.
There is also a timing factor to be considered. A prompt that worked today might not work the same way tomorrow. Most of the generative AI apps are continually being updated. The updates might alter internal mechanisms that could change how the generative AI reacts to your prompting.
We are ready to get underway with ChatGPT.
I opted to start by asking ChatGPT what generational amnesia is.
As an aside, whenever you are starting a conversation with generative AI, I recommend as a prompt engineering technique to begin by asking a question that will establish if the AI has been data-trained on the topic at hand. A generated response that is vacuous will give you a heads-up that you might be barking up the wrong tree with that generative AI app.
Here we go.
- My entered prompt: “What is generational amnesia?”
- ChatGPT generated response: “Generational amnesia refers to the phenomenon where each generation tends to forget or become unaware of the previous generations' conditions, social norms, or cultural practices. This concept is often discussed in the context of environmental degradation and climate change, where the baseline for what is considered ‘normal’ shifts with each generation, leading to a diminished awareness of gradual changes over time. Overall, generational amnesia implies that each successive generation has gaps in their understanding and must relearn or rediscover certain knowledge, skills, or practices that were known to previous generations.”
That reply is handy.
The response provides a useful and on-target definition. I trust you found that beneficial.
Plus, it is a nice relief that ChatGPT was able to provide such a suitable reply. You see, if ChatGPT had not had any data training associated with the topic, the answer could have been empty or might have been a big whopper. Those times that generative AI makes up facts or relates fictitious content as though it is true are customarily referred to as AI hallucinations, see my coverage at the link here. Those can be insidious and are to be diligently watched out for.
Let’s next see if ChatGPT can answer pointed questions on the matter.
Here we go.
- My entered prompt: “What are some major downsides of generational amnesia? Are there any upsides to generational amnesia?”
- ChatGPT generated response:
“Some upsides and downsides of generational amnesia include these points.”
“Reinvention of the Wheel: Without sufficient transmission of knowledge, each generation may waste time and resources rediscovering solutions to problems that were already solved by their predecessors.”
“Innovation and Adaptation: On the positive side, generational amnesia can also lead to fresh perspectives and innovation, as new generations approach problems without preconceived notions or limitations.”
“Loss of Expertise: Valuable skills and knowledge that are not passed down can lead to a loss of expertise in certain fields, impacting cultural heritage and technological advancement.
“Cultural and Historical Disconnect: A lack of understanding and appreciation for historical contexts and cultural practices can create a disconnect between generations, leading to a weakened sense of identity and continuity.”
“Understanding generational amnesia in this broader sense highlights the importance of effective communication and education across generations to preserve knowledge, culture, and progress while also embracing new ideas and advancements.”
End of ChatGPT response
Note that we didn’t get many upsides listed in that response by ChatGPT.
I could have done a follow-up to push ChatGPT to be more forthcoming, but I decided to leave things the way they were stated.
One of the biggest upsides as mentioned in the reply is that perhaps a new generation will feel unencumbered by the past. Ergo, rather than being mired in what had been, the latest generation might take a fresh look and come up with new ways of doing things. They are freed of the mental boundaries and confinement otherwise muddied by the past.
We now can get to the big question, namely whether generative AI could be a means of solving the inherent issues underlying generational amnesia.
Get a glass of fine wine and be ready for the response by ChatGPT to this telling consideration.
- My entered prompt: “I want you to consider how the advent of generative AI will potentially impact generational amnesia. On the one hand, pervasive and large-scale generative AI could allow greater intergenerational transmission of knowledge from one generation to the next. This would have advantages. There are potential downsides too. Comment on this.”
- ChatGPT generated response:
“The advent of generative AI has the potential to significantly impact generational amnesia in both positive and negative ways.”
“Positive Impacts.”
“Digitization and Archiving: Generative AI can assist in digitizing and archiving vast amounts of knowledge, including books, oral histories, cultural practices, and scientific research. This ensures that information is preserved and easily accessible for future generations.”
“Language Translation: AI can translate historical documents and oral histories into various languages, making previously inaccessible knowledge available to a broader audience.”
“Virtual Assistants and Mentors: AI can act as virtual mentors, providing guidance and expertise based on accumulated knowledge from previous generations. This can facilitate the transmission of skills and wisdom that might otherwise be lost.”
“Storytelling and Simulation: Generative AI can recreate historical events, cultural practices, and traditional stories through immersive simulations, helping to keep cultural heritage alive and relevant.”
“Negative Impacts.”
“Decreased Critical Thinking: If individuals become too reliant on AI for information retrieval and problem-solving, there might be a decline in critical thinking and problem-solving skills. This can lead to a superficial understanding of knowledge rather than deep, experiential learning.”
“Skill Atrophy: Skills that are essential but underused due to AI automation might atrophy. For example, manual calculation or navigation skills could diminish if AI takes over these tasks completely.”
“Algorithmic Bias: AI systems can perpetuate and amplify existing biases present in the data they are trained on. This can result in the transmission of biased or skewed knowledge, leading to a distorted understanding of history and culture.”
“Reduced Human Mentorship: The reliance on AI for knowledge transmission might reduce the role of human mentors and elders in teaching and guiding younger generations. This can weaken the personal connections and cultural continuity that come from direct intergenerational interaction.”
End of ChatGPT response
I especially liked the balance between the positive and negative impacts.
The reason I highlight that aspect is that you will find that the world seems to be composed of two radically opposing views on what generative AI will do when it comes to generational amnesia. There is one camp that says generative AI is the best thing since sliced bread and that generational amnesia is a goner. Once generative AI becomes more advanced and ubiquitous, we are on a free trajectory toward overcoming generational amnesia.
That’s one of the two views.
The other view says that the first view is pure hogwash. Generative AI is not going to substantively help deal with generational amnesia. Anyone thinking that it will is delusional or having the wool pulled over their eyes. Going further, this camp proclaims that generative AI is going to actively worsen generational amnesia by confounding new generations with a gaggle of AI hallucinations, data issues, and the like.
Wow, takes your breath away.
Which camp are you leaning toward?
I opted to see what ChatGPT has to say.
- My entered prompt: “On a bottom-line basis, will generative AI play a substantial role in overcoming or overriding generational amnesia?”
- ChatGPT generated response: “Overall, while it may be overly optimistic to expect that generative AI will entirely eliminate generational amnesia, it can certainly play a significant role in enhancing knowledge transmission. By addressing the challenges and harnessing the potential of AI, we can make meaningful strides towards preserving and sharing knowledge across generations.”
That answer is a seemingly proverbial politically correct response that tries to appease both camps. The thing is that polarized camps often don’t like the middle ground. In that sense, both camps would likely find that answer to be detestable.
Poor ChatGPT, darned if it does, darned if it doesn’t.
Conclusion
A few final comments for now.
Confucius famously said, “Study the past, if you would divine the future.” This is a handy reminder that besides overcoming generational amnesia to aid the present, doing so would presumably provide a leg up on what the future will be. It is a twofer.
The last word goes to Albert Einstein: “The distinction between the past, present, and future is only a stubbornly persistent illusion.”
Wait for a second, does that mean that there isn’t any such generational amnesia and that everything is always everywhere, and with us at all times? I’ll ask generative AI about this mind-bending notion and get back to you.

title: Council Post: Overcoming Challenges Associated With Predictive Testing For QA
text:
Maneesh Sharma is the COO of LambdaTest, an AI-powered unified enterprise test execution cloud platform.
Traditional testing, though valuable, is often reactive and identifies quality issues only after they have occurred. This can lead to project delays and financial and reputational losses. In fact, according to CISQ, the cost of poor software quality in the U.S. has grown to $2.41 trillion.
I've found that adopting a predictive testing approach with AI can help you identify and mitigate these issues earlier in the software development lifecycle.
As a leader in this space, I have seen how earlier detection can help lower costs, ensure a faster time to market and enhance software quality; however, implementing this technology requires overcoming certain challenges.
The Potential Benefits Of Predictive Testing
By leveraging AI/ML algorithms, predictive testing can analyze vast data sets, including past test results, code structures and user behavior patterns. By identifying trends and correlations, these algorithms can help predict potential issues.
According to IBM, AI-based testing can reduce software defects by up to 30%. AI can further anticipate the specific functionality that might crash under heavy load by analyzing millions of lines of code and user interactions.
Predictive testing can also help uncover edge cases, leading to more comprehensive testing. Further, by analyzing the historical test execution data for patterns and unusual behavior, predictive testing can identify and flag flaky tests.
As a part of this, you can also measure your flaky test debt, allowing developers and quality analysts to refine the user interface and user flow before real users stumble, leading to a more intuitive and enjoyable experience.
Solving The Challenges Associated With Predictive Testing
While there are many benefits promised by predictive testing, it is important to understand some of the challenges you can encounter while integrating it into real-world workflows. Here are some of these challenges and the ways I recommend solving them.
Dealing With Fragmented Test Data
The biggest challenge with modern-day quality engineering is consolidating test data from multiple sources. A simple checkout flow would involve multiple applications programming interfaces (APIs), both internal and external to complete the test build. Debugging test failures with fragmented test data becomes nightmarish in complex workflows, making it difficult to pinpoint what led to test failure and where.
To streamline the process, start by implementing robust data governance practices and centralizing the data aggregation process. Toward this, having a unified test execution platform can help. Make sure the platform supports all operating systems for desktop and mobile and can help you create a just-in-time orchestration (JITO) environment to run tests with any framework, language or API on any device.
Gather data from multiple sources and highlight test execution data in one place. I find that this enhances test observability by grouping and classifying errors, highlighting error trends and identifying flaky test percentages in your overall test build.
Additionally, ensure your tool integrates seamlessly with third-party CI/CD systems, project management tools and team communication platforms to accelerate feedback and enhance efficiency.
Overcoming Resource Resistance And Skill Gap
According to my company's Future of Quality Assurance Survey, 54.4% of organizations say there is a lack of skilled professionals in the field of AI. Furthermore, resistance to AI remains high with 26.4% of mid-sized companies hesitant to adopt AI-based testing due to factors like potential job losses and complexities.
To overcome the skill gap, leaders should encourage knowledge transfer through regular senior-led training and build collaboration with joint Dev/QA code review sessions. They can also ensure that their testing platform includes methods to add comprehensive documentation, tutorials and community forums. Lastly, consider certification programs to formally validate skills and ensure a consistent level of expertise across your team.
To overcome resource resistance to AI, I recommend that you showcase initial AI success on smaller projects to demonstrate its perks—be it in the form of cost reduction or efficiency gains. Once the gains are evident, resources should feel more aligned to incorporate and expand AI in existing testing workflows.
Role Of Predictive Testing Across Industries
To illustrate and help generate strategies in tackling predictive testing, I think it can be helpful to see some use cases across industries.
• E-commerce: In the e-commerce sector, I often see predictive testing helping to identify possible pain points in the checkout process as well as optimizing the web layouts for better user experience.
• Streaming services: Online streaming platforms use predictive testing to anticipate user behavior and enhance their content delivery network. Further, predictive testing can also help understand when to expect high viewership periods and, therefore, optimize server capacity to prevent buffering issues.
• Fintech applications: Predictive testing can identify anomalous transactions that may trigger fraudulent activity, thus preventing such transactions in real time. Within fintech apps, it can be used to simulate potential cyberattacks and identify vulnerabilities so developers can fix these issues in the architecture before attackers can exploit them.
What’s Next?
Overall, I see software testing is moving from a reactive approach to a predictive approach. With the help of machine learning and vast amounts of testing data, I foresee QA teams becoming more like strategic advisors instead of just fixing bugs.
Predictive software testing is all about leveraging data insights to build more sophisticated software that avoids failures and is released faster. As a leader of an AI-powered testing platform, I have witnessed how AI can streamline the QA process and boost output.

title: Karen Hao Empowers Journalists To Unravel AI’s Complexities And Impacts
text:
I awoke at the early hours of 4:00 am EDT to attend the first, in the series of online courses for AI Spotlight series which was hosted by Karen Hao, contributor for The Atlantic, and former foreign correspondent at The Wall Street Journal. Hao is known for her tremendous writing on AI, most notably, Artificial Intelligence is Creating a New Colonial World Order. My interest, along with other journalists who participated in the call, was to gather a crucial understanding of AI, not as just a technological advancement but as a force, as per Hao, “reshaping the power dynamics and societal structures.”
We've all been witness to the journey of AI, and unlike its predecessors that have shaped innovation from the steam engine, to the printing press, to the motor vehicle, society and law are unable to keep pace with AI’s rapid advancements to bring safety and accountability to this technology. This has benefited Big Tech, which makes billions of dollars, and for many years experimented under the radar, with little to no consequence, while wreaking havoc in its wake.
As a writer, I have covered stories about intersectionality and systems of oppression that have shaped technology; I have called out the increasing centralization of authority as Big Tech concentration strengthens at the expense of emerging innovation; I have written about Sam Altman, and the privilege he’s been afforded by Microsoft after he was effectively fired from OpenAI; I have written on the counter-narrative to the dystopian view of AI; I have written about organizations like Proton who continue to combat Big Tech Goliath, and who admonish legislation that increases surveillance across society; I have written about women in AI and the war to quiet the DEI movement in tech and in venture capital; I have written about wealthy investors like Elon Musk who have reshaped social media platforms like X/Twitter to use their power to enable freedom of speech “without fear of retaliation, censorship or legal sanction.” I’ve also written extensively on data privacy, the disrupted alternatives in verifiable credentials, and organizations that are innovating towards compliance.
These are just a sample of the breadcrumbs that have come to shape what society has become today. The emergence of generative AI, how it has inherited and amplified systemic bias, how it’s used to further widen political disparities, and manipulate and spread misinformation seems to be par for the course.
The AI Spotlight Series promises to bring perspective to the journalist to effectively unpack the complexities of artificial intelligence, to scrutinize the underlying technology, the data sources, the unintended consequences, the real impacts and implications to society and business. Never before has it been necessary for journalists to avoid drinking the Kool-Aid when it comes to artificial intelligence, to ensure the public receives, as Hao put it, “accurate, nuanced, and impactful reporting” on this transformative technology.
The AI Reporting Dilemma: Hype Vs. Reality
Artificial intelligence has become one of the most talked-about and hyped technologies in the world. From chatbots that can engage in human-like conversations to image generators that can create art from text prompts, AI seems to be everywhere. However, this rapid advancement and widespread adoption of AI technologies has created a significant challenge for journalists tasked with reporting on these developments.
Hao, a former senior editor at MIT Technology Review, identifies the problem as two-fold. First, there's the complexity of the technology itself. AI encompasses a wide range of techniques and approaches, from simple machine learning algorithms to complex deep neural networks. Understanding these technologies well enough to report on them accurately requires a level of technical knowledge that many journalists may not possess.
Second, there's the issue of separating fact from fiction, hype from reality. As Hao points out, "AI is sort of this big tent term that refers to all of these many different technologies. And Marvin Minsky, another founding father of AI... calls AI a suitcase word. So, you can shove whatever meaning you want into the suitcase and suddenly it becomes AI."
In 2018, Hao wrote, “Some experts believe that machine learning and deep learning will eventually get us to AGI with enough data, but most would agree there are big missing pieces and it’s still a long way off. AI may have mastered Go, but in other ways it is still much dumber than a toddler.”
Today, the pursuit of Artificial General Intelligence (AGI), popularized as the new term for achieving human-level AI capabilities, remains deeply rooted in the original goal of recreating human intelligence.
This ambiguity on the definition of AI, combined with the often-exaggerated claims made by companies and researchers in the field, makes it challenging for journalists to provide accurate, balanced, and critical coverage of AI developments. As per Hao, when large language models (LLMs) emerged, there was less transparency from AI companies about the details of their systems, including the amount of compute used as well as the contents of their training data. Over time, we’ve witnessed the fallout from the pervasive data scraping of these large language models including responses to poison the LLMs because of artist copyright infringements, as well as the exacerbation of online sexual exploitation.
AI Journalism Training: The AI Spotlight Series
Recognizing these challenges, Hao led this initiative to equip reporters with the knowledge and tools they need to cover AI effectively and responsibly.
The first track I attended was an introductory to AI reporting. The second track, in the series is a six-hour interactive program that delves into the questions journalists should be asking, and addressing things like misinformation, differing techniques employed to mitigate data risks, and insider sourcing methods within companies or government.
This 360-degree view is aimed to help journalists understand the technology's capabilities and limitations and enable them to engage in stories with more critical thought to cut through the hype and ask the right questions.
Hao identified several common pitfalls that reporters often encounter when covering artificial intelligence. These missteps can lead to inaccurate or misleading reporting, potentially shaping public perception of AI in ways that don't align with reality. One of the primary issues she highlights is the tendency to accept AI at face value without questioning its underlying premises. This can lead to reporting that reinforces problematic narratives or fails to critically examine the motivations behind AI development.
Additionally, Hao raises the reliance on potentially biased sources. She cautions against quoting business leaders or others with financial ties to the AI industry as impartial experts without acknowledging these connections. This practice can skew the narrative and present a one-sided view of AI's impact and potential.
What is clear is the pervasive anthropomorphizing of AI, describing these systems in human-like terms. This can create unrealistic expectations and when people attribute human-like characteristics to AI, they may assume that these systems possess human thought processes, emotions, and decision-making abilities. In reality, AI operates based on algorithms and data sets, lacking any form of consciousness or emotional capacity.
Finally, Hao emphasizes the importance of remembering the human element in AI stories, stating, "It would be a shame to forget that the story is about people." Behind every AI development or application, there are people affected, so focus on how AI systems impact individuals, communities, and society at large, rather than just discussing the technology in abstract terms. Also, consider the human developers, designers, and decision-makers. Reporting should also shed light on the people responsible for creating and implementing these technologies, including their motivations, biases, and ethical considerations.
Avoiding these pitfalls will help minimize the hype in the system’s AI capabilities and provide relatable narratives that readers will more likely trust.
Some key considerations to keep in mind, however, as Hao outlined the AI development pipeline and presented a framework that breaks down the AI development into stages: data, compute, models and applications. Journalists should be aware of the set of issues that each stage brings. As well, recognizing the limitations of generative AI is important, as Hao states:
"These systems are massive data systems. They're trained on vast swathes of the internet, and because they're so big... no one actually knows what's in the datasets that they're trained on. This can lead to biases, errors, and hallucinations in AI outputs.”
At this juncture of AI advancement, the development of AI systems means we also need to question the motives. As Hao points out, "The dominant vision of AI has really shifted from rule-based systems to increasingly big data and big compute-based systems... it really comes down to who is developing and who is funding AI."
Probing Deeper: Essential Questions for AI Reporting
To dig deeper into AI stories journalists should ask probing questions at each stage of the AI development pipeline. Here are some examples based on Hao's framework:
Data
- Where did the data come from? Was scraped or was it collected ethically, with permission?
- Who is amassing the data, and from what sources?
- How might the scramble for data lead to privacy issues or surveillance concerns? Have consent mechanisms been employed in their collection?
Compute
- What are the environmental impacts of the data centers used to train AI models?
- Who has access to the necessary computational resources, and what does this mean for AI development?
Models
- How was the model trained?
- What biases might be present in the training data?
- How transparent is the model?
- Can its decision-making process be explained?
Applications
- What are the expected outputs?
- What are the real-world impacts of this AI system?
- Who benefits from this AI application?
- What are the unintended consequences and who might be harmed?
Hao underscores the importance of these questions: "If you were to cover the $100 billion supercomputer story and state as fact that future AI systems could need this amount of compute, that would be entrenching this vision and making people feel like this is just inevitable. I think a more accurate statement would be 'OpenAI's vision of AI demands this amount of compute.’"
Beyond the Hype: Uncovering the Real AI Stories
Hao provides several examples of compelling stories that go beyond the surface-level AI hype.
Open AI’s Content Moderation Project in Kenya
Hao's own reporting uncovered the hidden labor behind AI and the story of Kenyan workers contracted by OpenAI to label violent and sexual content, leading to severe PTSD that persisted two years after the project ended. These workers were exposed to high volumes of violent and sexual content without adequate mental health support. One worker, Mofat, a 28-year-old, experienced significant personality changes, causing anxiety and withdrawal.
Hao emphasizes, "When we're thinking about AI accountability, we really need to be thinking about the entire pipeline of how AI is created."
AI-Powered Detection of Bomb Craters in Gaza
A Pulitzer Prize-winning investigation by the NYTimes used computer vision AI to detect bomb craters in Gaza, demonstrating how AI can be a powerful tool for journalism when used responsibly. The investigation used AI to analyze satellite imagery and identify hundreds of 2000-pound bomb craters in civilian areas. Every crater identified by the AI was manually verified before publication. This approach allowed for a comprehensive analysis that would have been impossible through manual methods alone.
This case demonstrates how AI can be used as a tool to augment journalistic investigations, while also highlighting the importance of human verification and oversight. As Hao points out, "There are ways to use AI in journalism that are not generative AI... Computer vision is a really powerful tool for doing investigative work."
Environmental impacts of Data Centers are a Growing Concern
Hao mentions the story where “The Oregonian, which had been covering issues about Big Tech and data centers, and ended up suing the water department of Oregon State for not disclosing Google’s water use. After a year-long legal battle, Google finally conceded and the released data showed the tech giant had consumed 25% of the city’s water, “tripling its usage in just a few years”. This reporting led to increased transparency about water usage and prompted government action to limit consumption.
As Hao contends, the environmental impact extends beyond water use. Data centers often rely on fossil fuels, contributing to climate change. She notes, Microsoft recently released its sustainability report, revealing a nearly 30% increase in carbon emissions for fiscal year 2023, largely due to rapid data center expansion. This increase occurred despite the company's previous commitments to reduce emissions.
This story highlights the tension between technological advancement and environmental sustainability, offering various angles for in-depth reporting.
AI’s Amplification of Systemic Bias
Hao also alluded to a Bloomberg’s investigation that found Stable Diffusion amplifies stereotypes about race and gender." As these systems become more powerful, the movement to increase representation across socio-economic policy, tech, and culture to remediate the biases inherited from these systems becomes an increasingly relevant topic.
The Path Forward: Empowering Journalists As AI Pervades
As AI continues to evolve and permeate various aspects of society, the role of journalists in providing accurate, critical, and insightful coverage becomes increasingly crucial.
Hao emphasizes the ongoing nature of this learning process: "It does take time and exposure, just simple exposure to actually start getting used to this. And if you already know this, then just use it to clarify your understanding."
She also encourages journalists to think creatively about finding AI stories: "Sometimes it's about casting a wide net and pushing on all of the different yarns, and then going with the easiest path because there are so many different ways to identify harms of these systems."
Journalists must adapt and steer clear of the AI Kool-Aid. This technology is infiltrating all aspects of society, our work, our personal identities, our homes, where we go, what we buy and how we live. As AI technologies continue to advance and their impact on society grows, the need for informed, critical journalism in this area has never been greater. By understanding the fundamentals of AI, recognizing common pitfalls in AI reporting, and asking probing questions, journalists can play a crucial role in demystifying AI for the public.
The Spotlight on AI is just the beginning. However, as Hao asserts, this is an ongoing process of learning and adaptation. As AI evolves, so must the approaches to reporting on it.
Ultimately, the goal is to move beyond surface-level reporting on AI breakthroughs and to dig deeper into the real-world impacts, ethical considerations, and societal implications of these technologies. It is Hao’s hope that that the public discourse around AI is grounded in reality, rather than hype, and that it considers the full range of stakeholders affected by these powerful technologies. Informed and critical journalism is not just valuable – it's essential. As Hao puts it, "If you can really tell the human stories behind it, it can help connect to your readership a lot more."

title: AI Energizes Your Career Path & Charts Your Professional Growth Plan
text:
In today’s rapidly evolving job market, staying ahead of the curve is more critical than ever. AI has emerged as a pivotal tool in shaping careers, offering innovative ways to learn, improve, and excel in various professions. From personalized learning paths to advanced career forecasting, AI is not just changing how we work; it's transforming how we plan and develop in our careers.
Personalized Learning and Skill Development
One of AI’s most significant impacts is in personalized education and skill development, tailoring learning experiences to individual needs, goals, and learning styles. AI platforms like Coursera and Udemy use machine learning algorithms to offer personalized course recommendations based on users' interests, previous courses, and job market trends. These platforms adapt to individual learning paces, providing resources that cater to specific skill gaps or career aspirations.
Virtual Mentors and Coaching
AI virtual mentors, like those offered by platforms like BetterUp or Sana Labs, provide personalized coaching and career advice. These AI mentors analyze users' performance, offer feedback, and set goals, ensuring that professional development is both targeted and effective.
AI in Recruitment
Platforms like LinkedIn use AI to match job seekers with relevant opportunities. By analyzing user profiles and job descriptions, AI algorithms can identify and recommend positions that align with a candidate’s skills, experience, and career goals. Likewise, companies are turning to AI tools like Fama to conduct background checks and improve the work style and corporate cultural fits of job candidates.
Networking Opportunities
AI networking tools help professionals connect with peers, mentors, and industry leaders. AI algorithms analyze professional interests, industry trends, and individual career paths to suggest relevant networking opportunities and professional groups. This also enables more sophisticated career forecasting and pathway planning, helping individuals make informed decisions about their professional trajectories by matching them with best-fit mentors. In conjunction, AI systems use predictive analytics to forecast industry trends, job market demands, and potential career trajectories. For instance, IBM’s Watson Career Coach uses AI to help employees identify potential career paths and the skills needed to achieve them. This then facilitates optimized networking opportunities and recommended people for career connections.
Role and Skill Gap Analysis
AI tools can analyze current job roles and identify emerging skills gaps. Platforms like Gloat and Eightfold.ai provide insights into evolving industry requirements, guiding professionals to acquire skills that keep them competitive and relevant. Recognizing these skills gaps allows people to select appropriate training to bridge the gap and accelerate their career progress. In conjunction, companies are identifying skill needs within their companies and offering training to improve their job candidate pool. For instance, Google offers AI-designed career certificates that help learners gain job-ready skills in high-demand fields like data analytics, project management, and UX design. These programs use AI to update content regularly, ensuring that learners acquire the most current and market-relevant skills. Likewise, IBM’s Watson Career Coach is an AI platform that assists employees in navigating their career paths within an organization. It provides personalized advice and insights, helping users understand where their skills are most needed and how they can grow within the company.
Ethical Considerations and Challenges
While AI offers numerous benefits in career development, it also presents ethical considerations and challenges that need addressing. First and foremost is data privacy and security. The use of AI in career development often involves processing large amounts of personal data. Ensuring the privacy and security of this data is crucial, requiring robust data protection measures and clear user consent protocols. Second is bias and fairness. AI algorithms can perpetuate biases if not carefully designed and monitored. Already, companies like Amazon have inadvertently perpetuated stereotypes in their hiring process. Ensuring AI systems in career development are fair and unbiased is essential to prevent discrimination and ensure equal opportunities for all users. Third, enterprises need to determine the best balance between AI and human judgment. While AI can provide valuable insights and recommendations, it's important to balance these with human judgment and personal intuition. Career decisions should be informed by AI but ultimately driven by individual aspirations and values.
The Future of AI in Career Development
Looking ahead, the role of AI in career development is set to expand, offering even more personalized and sophisticated assistance. Already, there is explosive growth in tools for continuous learning and upskilling. As job roles evolve, continuous learning and upskilling become crucial. AI will play a key role in identifying emerging skills and providing tailored learning opportunities, ensuring professionals remain adaptable and competitive. In addition, enterprises will continue their rapid integration of AI with human resources. This will optimize and increase human resource management systems to supercharge talent development, succession planning, and workforce optimization. Moreover, this integration will help align individual career goals with organizational needs. Finally, AI is expanding access to job opportunities. AI has the potential to democratize access to career opportunities, breaking down geographical and socioeconomic barriers. By providing personalized learning and job recommendations, AI can help individuals from diverse backgrounds access the resources and opportunities they need to succeed.
Ultimately, AI is a powerful ally in navigating the complexities of modern career development. It offers personalized learning, efficient job searching, insightful career forecasting, and much more. However, harnessing AI’s potential in career development requires a careful balance of technological innovation, ethical considerations, and personal judgment. As we embrace AI in our professional journeys, it's important to remain cognizant of its limitations and biases, ensuring that our career decisions are not only data-driven but also align with our personal aspirations and values. In the ever-changing landscape of work, AI stands as a dynamic tool, guiding us towards fulfilling and successful careers.

title: Facing Up To The Threat Of AI
text:
In 1983, the singer-songwriter Rockwell released a funky pop song with the lyric, “I always feel like somebody’s watching me, and I have no privacy.”
It was a goofy send-up of paranoia, glittered on top of an infectious beat. But these days, the song is more tedious than funny.
We are all being watched and videotaped almost nonstop. Security cameras are everywhere: malls, convenience stores, sandwich shops, parking lots, protests, marches, hospitals, airports, toll booths, ports, and front porches.
In some ways, we love it. Good luck finding a reality crime show that does not have a starring role for closed circuit cameras. Advanced camera systems used by law enforcement have either facial recognition or license plate recognition algorithms.
As a result, the mashup of cameras and artificial intelligence algorithms has quietly become a pervasive factor in our social, political, and economic lives, for better or worse.
The market for this technology is growing at an astounding 22 percent per year, according to some estimates.
Are We Ready for Our Close-Up?
That’s why I find the career and work of Joy Buolamwini so fascinating. She’s the author of Unmasking AI, founder of The Algorithmic Justice League and AI researcher at MIT Media Lab.
She stands at the center of a growing debate about how these technologies affect our lives and how that is changing in worrisome ways.
Her a-ha moment was a 2016 study that estimated one of every two adults in America already has their face registered in a facial recognition database of some kind—databases that are often not vetted for biases.
“This is when I realized the issues I was dealing with with facial analysis systems were not just research and development questions. These systems were getting into the real word in high stakes domains like law enforcement,” she said.
Buolamwini is not reflexively antagonistic toward advanced information technology.
She has seen firsthand how it can be used, for example, to help stem tropical diseases in Ethiopia or improve women’s rights in Zambia. She is cheered by the life-saving pharmaceuticals that may emerge from AI projects such as Alpha Fold.
Killer Robots and Mistaken Handcuffing
In the social and economic sphere, however, she worries about “digital dehumanization.”
In military arena, there are robust debates about the ethical and strategic implications of “killer robots”: aerial, land, and marine drones that can be programmed to attack without human intervention.
“Beyond that, AI can harm people significantly over time through perpetuating structural violence, exhibiting bias and lacking accountability in decision-making processes” Buolamwini said. “AI systems can perpetuate structural violence by denying individuals access to essential services like healthcare, housing, and employment. This denial of fundamental needs can cause irreparable harm to individuals for generations to come.”
She cites cases that would shock Russian novelists such as Dostoevsky and Kafka.
In February 2023, Detroit woman Porcha Woodruff was arrested, handcuffed in front of her two crying daughters, and wrongfully accused of robbery and carjacking on the basis of facial recognition technology. She was eight months pregnant at the time, held for 11 hours in detention and began having contractions while in jail.
Similar cases have occurred in Louisiana and Texas. A preponderance of these cases have involved minorities because image algorithms have more difficulty accurately processing darker skin tones.
In March, Buolamwini provided testimony to the U.S. Commission on Civil Rights, noting how far ahead this technology is racing ahead of regulation.
She underscored the troubling role of the technology within the Department of Justice, Department of Homeland Security, and Department of Housing and Urban Development.
Who’s Zooming Who?
The risk is far from contained to government agencies, however, she argued.
“Our faces are unique. If our face data is leaked, a risk that has become a reality specifically in the context of federal contractor’s data practices, there is little chance to get it back,” she wrote.
“We have seen voice clones and deepfakes used for scams; but when our face data is put at risk, anything from our bank accounts to our benefits could be at risk,” she wrote.
“Even if the image capture date is deleted within minutes, hours, days, or months, we need to know whether and how the government or third-party vendors hold faceprints also known as face template data.”
Facing Up To Problems Through Soft Power
My conversation with Buolamwini focused on how soft power—the changing of conventions, norms, customs, mores, and habits—might be used to address some of these threats.
She talked about how her own behavior has changed. “I am more careful about my biometric rights. When I do recordings and interviews, where possible I generally have a clause that states that the organization cannot use my biometric information—that is my face, my voice, and so forth—to train current or future AI systems,” she said.
“Algorithmic literacy” and “algorithmic hygiene” should become part of the fabric of our social and personal well-being and careers, she said.
“You won’t floss once a year and think you will have good dental health. Likewise we need to continuously be checking the design development and deployment of AI systems,” she said. “We have to think about what we do when something goes wrong for the people I call the excoded, or in other words, those harmed by AI systems. We need to have pathways for redress and design with redress in mind.”
I am by nature an optimist. However, after spending a few hours reflecting on her research and the trend lines of this area of technology and regulation, it’s hard to escape the gnawing feeling that we have yet to witness the worst.
We will need more than harrowing anecdotes, new data, or ethical debates to get a handle on this new era. We will need creativity and a re-conception of the boundary of our public and private lives.
Buolamwini, a graduate of both MIT and Oxford University who has been described as the “conscience of the AI revolution,” recognizes this.
She has turned to a wide array of inspirational platforms ranging from poetry, nonfiction, film, and social media to ring the alarm bell.
She recognizes that we should not need to wait for another miscarriage of justice or public policy catastrophe before we take action. We have enough evidence to act.
Just look around. If you always feel like somebody’s always watching you, you are right. And it’s time we stop thinking this is just another funny, funky thing about the artificial intelligence revolution.

title: Generation AI: How Students Feel About AI In College Admissions
text:
2023 was the worst year in the history of Student Search yet, and 2024 is shaping up to be even more disastrous. As we stand on the precipice of the Search Cliff, one thing is clear: the traditional methods of student recruitment are not just failing—they're in free fall. But there's a beacon of hope on the horizon: AI is poised to revolutionize college admissions and potentially save institutions from the looming recruitment crisis.
Fewer names are available, and those that are don’t want to hear from you
The Search Cliff is coming, promising a 40-80% drop in name availability due to the shift to digital exams. By 2027, there will be 2 million fewer names in Search and 840,000 fewer 12th-grade names. This effect is further exacerbated by the upcoming demographic cliff as the nation ages and fewer and fewer students see higher education as a viable option post-graduation. In 2024, confidence in US higher education was at an all-time low for the past decade of survey data.
Not only are fewer names available — Search on average is performing worse per name. Last year, we found that student Search conversion dropped 67% between 2018 and 2023. In concrete terms, 100,000 purchased names turned into a mere 43 enrollments in 2023, down from 131 in 2018. A decade ago, those same 100,000 names would have yielded 300-400 enrollments. Today? It's less than a tenth of that.
Why is this happening? The median student is bombarded with 1,300 emails and mailings from colleges annually, but only 13.6% say this outreach motivates them to apply. Even worse, 68% of students view these emails as spam, actively discounting universities that repeatedly send them generic outreach with no response.
And despite this constant outreach, 46% of students say they haven't spoken to an admissions officer in the last year.
If you think the performance metrics are bad, wait until you see the financials. The direct cost per enrollment from Search has tripled since 2018, now standing at a staggering $1,260. Factor in all the associated costs, and you're looking at over $4,000 per enrolled student via Search. In a few years, it could balloon to $6,000 or even $7,000 per enrollment.
In an era where fewer and fewer students want to attend college, schools cannot afford to make mistakes when it comes to their recruitment strategy. Personalized communication and a return to 1-on-1 recruiting is crucial for the survival of institutions.
The modern-day student and what they expect:
While traditional methods falter, a new generation of students is emerging — one that's primed for a different approach. Let's look at the numbers. According to a 2024 report from the Pew Research Center:
- 95% of teens have smartphone access
- 47% report being online "almost constantly"
- Students spend an average of 7 hours and 22 minutes daily on screen media
- 87.5% of these students have used AI in the past year
This is Generation AI, and they're not just tech-savvy—they're tech-immersed. They expect personalized, instant, and relevant interactions. It’s no wonder that generic mass emails have little resonance with this generation: their everyday shopping experiences feel more personal than their experience in deciding to invest hundreds of thousands of dollars into college.
This is where AI steps in, not just as a tool, but as a lifeline for admissions offices drowning in ineffective strategies. Imagine an AI recruiter that can provide personalized, 24/7 support across multiple channels—email, SMS, even phone calls. This isn't a far-off possibility; it's happening now.
With 58.2% of students willing to endorse AI use in admissions, we're seeing a clear signal: Generation AI is ready for a more sophisticated approach to college recruitment. And it's not just about meeting student expectations—it's about dramatically improving the economics of recruitment.
AI will unlock prospective student engagment
AI can analyze vast amounts of data to create hyper-personalized interactions, potentially reversing the dire conversion rates we're seeing in traditional Search. No more generic "Dear Student" emails—instead, communications that speak directly to a student's interests, goals, and concerns.
For admissions teams, this means maintaining large prospect funnels without the ballooning costs we're seeing in traditional methods. It's like having a thousand well-trained admissions officers working around the clock, at a fraction of the cost.
Consider this: 75% of students say they would ask more questions if they could do so anonymously. AI provides that safe space for exploration and inquiry, potentially boosting inquiry-to-application rates that have dropped 15% since 2018.
Moreover, AI can break down language barriers, offering support in multiple languages—a game-changer for diverse student populations and their families.
As we hurtle towards the Search Cliff, the question for colleges isn't whether to adopt AI in admissions, but how quickly they can implement it. The institutions that embrace this technology won't just set new standards for student engagement—they'll be the ones that survive and thrive in this new landscape.
Remember, this isn't about replacing human interaction—it's about enhancing it and making it economically viable. By leveraging AI, colleges can create more meaningful connections with students, reverse the trend of plummeting conversion rates, and do it all at a fraction of the cost of traditional methods.
The AI revolution in college admissions isn't just an opportunity—it's a necessity. Will your institution lead the charge, or be left behind as the Search Cliff claims its victims?

title: The lower the AI exposure, the bigger the problem for Europe's chip firms - ET Telecom

The lower the AI exposure, the bigger the problem for Europe's chip firms
But even they aren't immune to a "correction" in stock valuations after strong rallies this year, coupled with worries around the impact of trade spats involving China, the U.S. and Europe, Hesselink added.
By Olivier Sorgho and Nathan Vifflin
Shares in European semiconductor firms less exposed to AI chips slumped on Thursday as falling demand from their key automotive and industrial clients hit business prospects, on top of a wider sector correction.
Chip component suppliers like ASML and ASM International are more exposed to the booming AI chip market and demand from high-end tech clients like Nvidia, TSMC, and Intel.
"The more high-end applications, linked to AI, those are doing much better," said ING analyst Marc Hesselink.
But even they aren't immune to a "correction" in stock valuations after strong rallies this year, coupled with worries around the impact of trade spats involving China, the U.S. and Europe, Hesselink added.
Shares in both ASML and ASMI were down about 3% in early afternoon trading.
Companies with less AI exposure meanwhile were hit harder by industrial clients and automakers cutting orders. Demand for electric vehicles has slowed sharply in Europe.
STMicroelectronics, which supplies Tesla, tumbled 14% after it cut 2024 sales and margin targets for a second time this year, as orders from industrial customers did not improve and automotive demand fell.
Germany's Infineon, a top automotive chip supplier, fell 6%.
Dutch company NXP Semiconductors earlier this week reported its worst decline in quarterly revenue in four years on weak demand from automotive customers, dragging down some U.S peers with auto exposure.
And while German chip materials supplier Siltronic raised its guidance, that was mostly due to the AI market which it said would grow this year.
BE Semiconductor Industries slumped 13% after forecasting flat third-quarter sales, hit by weak growth in mainstream assembly markets, particularly in China, even as orders for its systems used in AI grew.
Europe's STOXX 600 Technology index was down 2.8%, largely dragged by semiconductor stocks including ams OSRAM that fell 7% ahead of results on Friday, STMicro peer Melexis falling 4%, and Technoprobe, Soitec and Nordic Semiconductor also down.
The sector's fundamentals remain strong, Hesselink said. Companies still hope that EV demand will be robust in the longer term.
Chip components related to EVs, particularly silicon carbide, will be a growth driver in the second half of the year, STMicro's CEO Jean-Marc Chery said in a conference call.
