title: FCC pursues new rules for AI in political ads, but changes may not take effect before the election
text:
FCC pursues new rules for AI in political ads, but changes may not take effect before the election
The Federal Communications Commission has advanced a proposal that would require political advertisers to disclose their use of artificial intelligence in broadcast television and radio ads
NEW YORK -- The Federal Communications Commission has advanced a proposal that would require political advertisers to disclose their use of artificial intelligence in broadcast television and radio ads, though it is unclear whether new regulations may be in place before the November presidential election.
The proposed rules announced Thursday could add a layer of transparency in political campaigning that some tech watchdogs have called for to help inform voters about lifelike and misleading AI-generated media in ads.
“There’s too much potential for AI to manipulate voices and images in political advertising to do nothing,” the agency's chairwoman, Democrat Jessica Rosenworcel, said Thursday in a news release. “If a candidate or issue campaign used AI to create an ad, the public has a right to know.”
But the FCC’s action is part of a federal turf war over the regulation of AI in politics. The move has faced pushback from the chairman of the Federal Election Commission, who previously accused the FCC of stepping on his own agency’s authority and has warned of a possible legal challenge.
Political candidates and parties in the United States and around the world already have experimented with rapidly advancing generative AI tools, though some have voluntarily disclosed their use of the technology. Others have weaponized the technology to mislead voters.
The FCC is proposing requiring broadcasters to ask political advertisers whether their content was created using AI tools, such as text-to-image creators or voice-cloning software. The agency also aims to require broadcasters to make an on-air announcement when AI-generated content is used in a political ad and include a notice disclosing the use of AI in their online political files.
The commission acknowledges it would not have authority over streaming, leaving the growing political advertising industry on digital and streaming platforms unregulated at the federal level.
After the commission's 3-2 vote, the proposal will move into a 30-day public comment period, followed by a 15-day reply period. Commissioners are then expected to finalize and pass a rule. It is unclear whether there is time for it to go into effect before a presidential election that is just over three months away.
Jonathan Uriarte, a spokesperson for Rosenworcel, said the chairwoman “intends to follow the regulatory process but she has been clear that the time to act is now.”
After Rosenworcel announced her proposed rule in May, FEC Chairman Sean Cooksey, a Republican, sent her a letter cautioning her against the move.
“I am concerned that parts of your proposal would fall within the exclusive jurisdiction" of the FEC and would "directly conflict with existing law and regulations, and sow chaos among political campaigns for the upcoming election," he wrote.
If the FCC moves forward, it could create “irreconcilable conflicts” between the agencies that may end up in federal court, he said in the letter.
A Republican commissioner at the FCC, Brendan Carr, agreed with Cooksey, saying on the social media platform X in June that the FCC’s “plan to impose new regulations on political speech in the run up to the election is as misguided as it is unlawful.”
But the FEC's vice chair, Democrat Ellen Weintraub, contradicted Cooksey in a separate letter to Rosenworcel, saying “no one agency currently has the jurisdiction or capacity to address every aspect of this large and complicated issue.”
The FCC maintains it has authority to regulate on the issue under the 1934 Communications Act and the Bipartisan Campaign Reform Act.
Congress has not passed laws directing the agencies on how they should regulate AI in politics. Some Republican senators have circulated legislation intending to block the Democratic-led FCC from issuing its new rules. Meanwhile, the FEC is considering its own petition on regulating deepfakes in political ads.
In the absence of federal action, more than one-third of states have created their own laws regulating the use of AI in campaigns and elections, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures.
In February, the FCC ruled that robocalls containing AI-generated voices are illegal, a step that empowered the commission to fine companies that use AI voices in their calls or block the service providers that carry them.

title: How To Use AI To Make Money
text:
Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming the investing landscape with new tools and applications that improve the strategies, knowledge and decision-making abilities of investors. AI now empowers investors through near-instantaneous analysis of vast quantities of data, market predictions and even automation of portfolio management. As investors are deluged with information and rapidly changing markets, AI can provide clarity and the competitive advantage needed to succeed in financial markets.
Understanding AI In Investing
AI in investing refers to the application of algorithms and machine learning for financial purposes including analyzing data, recognizing patterns, and providing recommendations to make investing decisions. AI technologies can assist investors in acquiring insights, assessing risk, and gauging sentiment to make informed investments. These technologies can also be utilized to make trades based on pre-set conditions and manage portfolios using guidelines and rules set by an investor.
While AI technology has a learning curve, even for seasoned investors, it offers the potential for enhanced strategies, quicker decision making, and ultimately better returns.
6 Ways To Use AI When Investing
Investors can use AI to enhance their investment strategies through analysis of stocks, data, sentiment and potential risks to identify opportunities and threats to their portfolio. AI can also be used to proactively execute trades with algorithmic trading as well as through portfolio management to oversee diversification and allocation. This section will explain the 6 key ways to fully leverage AI in your investing strategy.
Stock Analysis And Picking
AI stock screeners can be used to identify new investment opportunities based on criteria you set, the model used by the screener and applied datasets. Investors can use these stock screeners to find the best stocks to trade or identify patterns in various markets. These screeners can help investors to more quickly analyze and act on opportunities.
Risk Evaluation
AI can be used to assess and manage potential investment risk by analyzing data to identify or predict volatility, threats and opportunities. Real-time insights from AI based on political events, company news or economic factors can help you adjust your portfolio by quickly offloading positions at risk. AI-powered risk evaluation can help boost your portfolio returns efficiently and quickly all while reducing costs by automating analysis.
Algorithmic Trading With Robo-Advisors
Robo-advisors are investing platforms that automate portfolio management by rebalancing and harvesting tax losses. They are usually personalized based on the age, time horizon or goals of an investor. Algorithmic trading uses AI to trade based on conditions set by the user and data. These strategies can be complementary if an investor utilizes a robo-advisor for a more conservative strategy while utilizing algorithmic trading with a smaller percentage of their portfolio to make high-risk, high-reward trades.
Portfolio Management
AI can assist with portfolio management to propose or execute changes to maintain asset allocation, diversification and rebalancing based on the potential for returns or to avoid risk. Portfolio management can be costly due to the need for human analysis but AI presents the opportunity to automate laborious tasks while matching or exceeding human efficacy.
Enhanced Data Analysis
By processing vast quantities of data, including market data, financial reports and news, AI can uncover insights that assist investor decision making. Through pattern recognition and trend analysis, AI helps investors to find new opportunities and make better investment decisions. By utilizing AI to conduct data analysis, investors can more quickly and efficiently take advantageous action.
Sentiment Analysis
AI can be used to gauge investor sentiment towards specific stocks, for example small-cap value stocks or markets to help you identify opportunities or upcoming changes to your positions. AI accomplishes this by assessing tone and sentiment from data sources like social media or articles to help predict stock, sector, or market movements.
How To Begin Incorporating AI Into Your Investing Process Research AI Tools
Before getting started with using AI to invest, you should explore different available AI tools and determine how they can fit your unique situation and needs. For example, seeking out an AI tool that can perform algorithmic trading on its own vs. a data analysis tool that would help you find stocks to trade. Another key component of your research should be on the accuracy and credibility of these tools. Learning more about the creators of the tool, their disclosures and data sources. Finally, it will be key to research the costs of AI tools to strike a balance between how much you’ll spend with the value you’ll receive.
Start Slowly
As you get started with your new AI toolset, take it slow to make sure you understand the tool’s capabilities and your comfort level with utilizing it. This is especially key to ensure you don’t commit too much money to an unproven strategy. As you gain confidence in using AI in your investing process, monitor outcomes and determine whether you have the right tools you need for investing success.
Closely Monitor Investments Over Time
As you incorporate AI into your investing strategy, gauge how effective recommendations or performance are against an industry benchmark. For example, if you’re using a robo-advisor, compare performance against the market as a whole. If you’re trading on AI insights, pay attention to news and stock screeners to be aware of new information which could affect your trading strategy.
Tips For Maximizing AI Benefits
When using AI to invest, there are a few key strategies you should employ to maximize the benefits of this technology and the returns for your portfolio.
Explore And Update Your Toolset
AI is a fast moving space with tools being updated and replaced seemingly on a monthly basis. Utilizing tools you’ve discovered to their full extent as well researching new tools to utilize will increase your AI investing odds. Your investing results will only be as good as your tools and the underlying data they use and the insights they provide.
Adjust Strategies Based On AI Insights
Be ready to change your investing strategies based on new insights provided by your AI tools but be aware of the limitations of these tools such as knowledge gaps or biases. AI is excellent at quick pattern and trend recognition with the right data sets so trust, but verify. With the right model and evaluated data, AI can identify upcoming market or stock moves which could require quick strategy changes.
Combine AI With Human Insights
AI can provide excellent analysis but human insight and oversight is essential to make the right investment decisions. Utilizing the human insight of experts on topics like this AI investing outlook as well as your own insight is key. By combining your unique experience and judgment with AI data analysis and evaluation, you can make informed decisions and maximize investment outcomes. AI is not yet omniscient and shouldn’t be treated as such.
Bottom Line
By adding AI to your toolkit, you can improve the speed and efficacy of your investing strategies. As covered, these powerful new algorithms, models and tools can assist with your stock picking, risk management, and portfolio returns. title: How A Harris Presidency Could Affect Big Tech
text:
As Joe Biden bowed out of the 2024 presidential race last weekend, he endorsed Vice President Kamala Harris to replace him.
We in Silicon Valley know Harris well, as she was a top prosecutor in San Francisco, California's attorney general, and U.S. Senator. In those roles, she often visited Silicon Valley to meet with its leaders and became a long-time friend of the tech industry.
Now that she is the leading Democratic candidate to replace President Biden, tech leaders are scrutinizing how a potential Harris presidency could affect them and the industry at large.
In addition to her deep relations with tech leaders, Harris has a solid grasp of technology and understands its role in the U.S. and around the world.
President Biden appointed Harris to lead his AI task force last year. In May 2023, she met with major tech CEOs about advancing responsible AI innovation.
AI has great potential but also serious downsides. This will perhaps be the most important tech, demanding many forms of regulation in the near future. Biden has already put in place an aggressive executive order on AI that, among other things, has a big emphasis on human rights and algorithmic fairness.
Since Harris helped craft this executive order, a potential Harris administration would adhere to its principles and push hard for congressional leaders to craft laws needed to keep AI on the right track and safe for all.
Besides AI, many tech issues are at stake, such as regulating companies in other segments of the industry, antitrust, privacy, protecting kids from predators, and more.
Silicon Valley leaders could benefit from having someone in the White House who understands technology and could be friendly with Big Tech in the coming years.
One big question about a potential Harris presidency is whether she would alter the current ongoing tech antitrust cases at the DOJ and FTC.
I would be surprised if she changed the current leadership of these agencies since, as Vice President, Harris has been close to these cases and has not shown any sign of opposing them.
I spent the last two days talking to senior executives of major tech companies about their views on a Harris presidency's potential impacts on the technology industry. Here is a summary of those discussions.
- Data privacy and consumer protection: Harris has strongly advocated data privacy. She might push for stricter regulations on how tech companies collect, use, and share user data, potentially similar to the E.U.'s GDPR.
- Antitrust enforcement: Harris has expressed concerns about the concentration of power among Big Tech companies. Her administration might pursue more aggressive antitrust actions, potentially leading to increased scrutiny of mergers and acquisitions in the tech sector.
- Artificial intelligence regulation: Harris has called for responsible AI development. Her administration might introduce guidelines or regulations to ensure AI systems are developed and deployed ethically, with a focus on preventing bias and protecting civil rights.
- Cybersecurity: Given her background as California's attorney general and her work in the Senate, Harris might prioritize strengthening national cybersecurity measures, which could impact tech companies' security practices and responsibilities.
- Broadband access: Harris has supported expanding broadband access, especially in rural and underserved areas. This could create opportunities for telecom and internet service providers.
- STEM education and workforce development: Harris has advocated for increased investment in STEM education and workforce development programs, which could benefit the tech industry by expanding the pool of skilled workers.
- Immigration reform: Harris has supported immigration reform that could make it easier for high-skilled tech workers to obtain visas, potentially addressing talent shortages in the industry.
- Climate tech: Given her focus on climate change, a Harris administration might provide incentives or support for clean energy and climate-related technologies.
- Section 230 reform: Harris has expressed interest in reforming Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act, which could have significant implications for social media and other internet platforms.
In 2022, the United States tech sector contributed nearly two trillion U.S. dollars to the country's overall gross domestic product (GDP), making up approximately 9.3 percent of total GDP.
Given that the U.S. tech industry drives nearly 10% of the total U.S. GDP, Silicon Valley will examine Harris and Trump closely to see if they are friends or foes.

title: Cohere AI’s $500 Million Series D, Musk’s Memphis Gigagactory, Cuts At Magic Leap, Meta Reality Labs
text:
With the Olympics starting in Paris tomorrow, Nexus Studios shared the trailer for BBC’s coverage of the 2024 Summer Olympic Games. Directed by Fx Goby and brought to life by Nexus Studios, the one minute trailer is a love letter to the games.
Embracing Paris' reputation as the City of Love, Fx artfully explores the romance between athletes and their sports. The exquisite 2D animation foregoes traditional outlines, instead using light and shadow to suggest volume, effectively recreating each illustration 25 frames per second. Take that, AI.
Meta’s got four major-ish items in the news roundup this week. They are so broadly diversified in social media, AI and XR, today, they are eating my entire beat. Meta is a social company and they like to talk about what they are doing. Interestingly, today’s column, by topic, goes, AI, AI, AI, Meta AI, Meta AI, Meta XR, Meta XR, followed by news from the Metaverse (which is thriving on Roblox and Fortnite).
Cohere Closes $500M Series D. Toronto-based enterprise AI startup Cohere has raised $500 million in a Series D funding round, bringing its valuation to $5.5 billion. The capital will advance Cohere's AI models, emphasizing data privacy, security, and multilingual accuracy. Cohere's large language modelshave shown competitive performance against rivals like ChatGPT-4 Turbo. Led by PSP Investments, the round included new investors like Cisco Systems, Fujitsu, AMD Ventures, Magnetar, and Export Development Canada, with returning support from Oracle, Salesforce Ventures, and Nvidia.
XAI Opens Massive Data Center in Memphis. Training has commenced at Elon Musk's “gigafactory of compute” supercomputer facility in Memphis, Tennessee. Musk says this supercluster, named Project Colossus, is the world's most powerful AI training cluster, housing 100,000 Nvidia H100 chips. This is the largest capital investment in the city's history, they were all pretty happy until the facts of new AI data center started to sink in: the gigafactory will use 50 megawatts of electricity, and will use 1.3 million gallons of water every day for cooling. That’s enough to power approximately 50,000 homes.
Former NFL quarterback Colin Kaepernick Raises $4 M, launches Lumi Story AI. This AI company helps creators to produce, distribute, and merchandise their work. Lumi provides AI tools to content creators to generate content, manage logistics, and maintain control over their projects. Founder and CEO Kaepernnick raised $4M for Lumi in a seed round led by VC Seven Seven Six. Lumi's platform will initially focus on comic books, later expanding to other formats. Kaepernick highlighted the platform's role in filling creators' skill gaps and democratizing storytelling. You can sign up for the waitlist on their website.
Meta Releases Llama 3.1 Open Source LLM. On Tuesday, Meta announced Llama 3.1, its latest open-source AI model, which comes in three versions, with the largest being the most advanced to date. Meta's making significant investments in AI to keep up with competitors like X, OpenAI and Google. A key partner in this endeavor is Nvidia, providing the GPUs essential for training the models. Unlike its competitors, Meta doesn’t plan to monetize Llama directly but partners with companies like AWS, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure to offer access via their platforms. The largest model, Llama 3.1 405B, has 405 billion parameters, enabling complex tasks. Smaller versions are also available for applications like chatbots and coding assistants.
Meta AI Gets New Image Generation Features. The AI assistant is now accessible on WhatsApp, Instagram, Messenger. The new features include "Imagine me" prompts, allowing users to create images based on their photos and prompts, and creative editing tools for modifying objects within images. The advanced Llama 405B model offers enhanced reasoning, particularly for math and coding queries, and is available on WhatsApp and meta.ai. An experimental AI upgrade to Meta’s RayBan audio smart glasses may be here as early as this fall.
Meta is making a strategic move to invest billions to acquire roughly 5% of EssilorLuxottica for $5B. Meta collaborated with the European eyewear gianton two generations of Ray-Ban smart glasses. This significant investment, confirmed by various sources, appears driven by Google's recent interest in integrating its Gemini AI assistant into future smart glasses from EssilorLuxottica. The partnership with EssilorLuxottica is crucial for Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg’s long-term metaverse vision, offering manufacturing expertise and style that Meta needs to produce glasses people want to wear. With the latest Meta Ray-Bans performing well in the market, this collaboration is essential for Meta to maintain its competitive edge and expand its AR glasses' acceptance.
Belt Tightening Comes to Reality Labs. Even with tens of billions of dollars in profits, Meta has to balance the massive funding needs of both XR and AI. The bright spot has been their audio smart glasses, which are getting smarter all the time. The third generation is expected in 2025. The Meta Quest 4 headset is slated for 2026, with two versions planned. Additionally, a new Quest Pro is scheduled for 2027 to compete with the Apple Vision Pro.

Despite early hype and significant investment, Magic Leap has struggled to meet performance targets and sales expectations, particularly with its Magic Leap 2 headset. The company's reliance on Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, structured around performance-based funding, has not yielded the expected results. With its optics technology still considered advanced, Magic Leap's future now hinges on its ability to reposition itself in the competitive AR market, while managing reduced revenue streams from military and healthcare contracts.

title: Council Post: 16 Ways To Create Personalized, Immersive Digital Marketing Experiences
text:
As customers juggle competing demands for their attention, brands are finding creative ways to offer personalized digital marketing experiences that help them stand out in a crowded market. Companies can draw customers into digital platforms through personal touches that address their audience's specific needs, making it easier for customers to browse and shop.
Below, members of Forbes Communications Council share strategies for creating digital journeys that resonate with your customers on a personal level. Follow their advice to craft individualized, immersive and personally relevant digital experiences for your target audience.
1. Train AI For Better Customer Conversations
Leverage AI and large language models to engage in deeper and more nuanced conversations with your customers. Then, turn the insights from those conversations into personalized recommendations, content and other materials that serve their specific needs. - Karina Kogan, Infinite Reality
2. Conduct Thorough Audience Research
Know your audience. Segment your target audience to understand each unique persona, specific titles, annual priorities, goals, ways they are measured, buying habits and the outlets they leverage to research solutions. Doing so will enable you to meet them where they are at with personalized and relevant messages for how your product can help them solve their challenges. - Megan Ruszkowski, CoreSite
3. Use Data To Understand Your Customers
Aim for data-driven proactivity. Use your data to understand customers' preferences and behaviors. Incorporate AI tools to anticipate customers' wants and demands, and always be proactive in providing those services. When a customer base feels you truly get them, the magic of a deep and engaging experience happens, and the connection solidifies that brand-client bond. - Daniela Martucci, DMH & Associates Communications
4. Use Virtual Reality To Draw Customers In
Virtual reality tours and augmented reality allow potential users to see how the products will look on them. Create immersive stories to differentiate your product and highlight how users feel while using them. While changes are constant in the market, the customer remains the king. Play on the power of emotions, engagement and experience while offering your services to your customers. - Namita Tiwari, Namita Tiwari
5. Put A Face To Your Brand
Connect with your audience on a more personal level by sharing the human side of your brand—give employees the spotlight. Do this by sharing their stories, conducting brand channel social media takeovers and encouraging them to create original content. - Bradley Keenan, DSMN8
6. Consider Your Customer's Motivations
Ask your customers questions, and don’t assume you know them better than they do. How did they get to know you? Why do they like you? Why do they trust you, and why do they do business with you? This will create your personalized strategy. - Salim Gheewalla, Calian IT & Cyber Solutions
Forbes Communications Council is an invitation-only community for executives in successful public relations, media strategy, creative and advertising agencies. Do I qualify?
7. Reach Out To Your Audience For Feedback
This may seem obvious, but not many marketing teams do it: Actually talk to customers. Go out and interview them. If you can't, seek other ways to learn what's on their minds. At our company, for example, we have a newsletter asking new subscribers to reply with the type of content they want to see most. You can use these insights, along with personalization tech, to drive cohesive buyer journeys. - Nate Roy, Constructor
8. Build Relationships Across Stakeholder Groups
Engage directly with your customers, staff and stakeholders to gather their valuable opinions. This approach ensures your strategy is tailored to their needs and preferences, fostering a deeper connection and enhancing the overall customer experience. It's not rocket science—it's about meaningful engagement. - Marie O'Riordan, The Vita Foundation
9. Focus On Behaviors
Marketers should ground personalization efforts in their customers’ behaviors, not their demographics. For example, to encourage free users to upgrade to a paid plan, identify free-plan customers whose behavior mirrors that of customers who upgraded recently—perhaps they tried to access a paid-only feature or their average session time has increased. Then target that cohort with in-app promotions. - Tifenn Dano Kwan, Amplitude
10. Create Continuity For Customers
Make sure to leverage your employees on social media, including those who work in support and customer success. Customers love it when they can engage digitally with people from your company whom they already engage with in real life. - Nataly Kelly, Zappi
11. Pair Customized Content With Automated Workflows
Automation and personalization are crucial for an effective digital marketing strategy. Implement automated workflows to deliver personalized content at the right time and through preferred channels. Utilize dynamic content elements to customize emails, website experiences and ads based on user data and behavior. This ensures tailored interactions, enhancing engagement and driving conversions. - Jawaher Al-Khuzaei, GWC
12. Showcase Content From Your Audience
Leverage user-generated content to not only engage your customers but to truly relate to them as well. Because the content comes from people within their peer group, customers are more likely to identify with it and feel like it is more personalized. - Roshni Wijayasinha, Prosh Marketing
13. Be Strategic With Calls To Action
Understand and respect where your customer is in their journey. Countless digital marketing campaigns end with a call to action (CTA) to request a demo. Most of the time, this CTA is used too soon. The creativity may be engaging and resonate with the target audience, and the messaging may be relevant and address the right pain points, but, if the CTA is wrong, it's a personalization fail. - Rekha Thomas, Path Forward Marketing LLC
14. Leverage Intent Data
Think beyond generic personalization. Utilizing first- and third-party intent data to target prospects opens up a whole new world of personalization and enables you to target those researching your product. With this data, you can use AI tools for personalized SDR outreach and chatbots that react based on user behavior. Even basic personalization with this data can enable significant efficiency gains. - Jeff Marcoux, Entry Point 1
15. Use AI For Quick Customer Responses
Meet customers where they are. This can be challenging for brands as today’s consumers expect fast, personalized responses from brands on channels like social media. AI-powered tools can help brands engage with customers at scale and provide prompt, personalized communication, making customers feel valued and creating a memorable experience in a crowded marketplace. - Scott Morris, Sprout Social
16. Use Your Customer's Name In Videos
Use hyper-personalized AI videos. Psychological research shows that hearing your name activates a part of the brain. So, an AI-generated video with the person’s name on screen and in the sound will make the target customer take pause and listen to your message. I believe hyper-personalized AI videos can transform all parts of the customer journey. - Ken Louie, MetroPlusHealth

title: Council Post: AI Applications In Farming: How Technology Can Help Solve Hunger
text:
Artificial intelligence is helping businesses in multiple industries streamline processes, make better decisions, boost productivity and more. But there’s no industry in which AI’s capabilities could have a bigger potential impact than the global agriculture sector. Experts are optimistic that revolutionary technologies powered by AI can help usher in an era of sustainable, high-yield farming to feed a growing worldwide population.
From developing robust new crops to ensuring fresh, healthy foods are delivered in a timely fashion, AI applications in farming may soon play a big role in solving global hunger crises. Below, members of Forbes Technology Council describe a few of the exciting new AI-powered developments that may soon be coming to the agriculture industry—developments that could genuinely help improve life for everyone on the planet.
1. Remote Crop Monitoring
One promising agricultural AI application that could help address global food scarcity is AI-driven remote crop monitoring using 5G technology. In Japan, where an aging population and shrinking workforce are challenges for the agriculture industry, 5G-powered AI can support farmers by providing real-time data and expert recommendations, optimizing crop production and efficiently managing resources. - Kazuhiro Gomi, NTT Research
2. Resilient Crop Development
AI-driven advancements in seed genetics and precision fertilizers hold immense potential to address global food scarcity. By enhancing crop resilience, improving yields and tailoring fertilizer use to specific soil conditions, AI can contribute to a more sustainable and productive agricultural future. However, addressing global food scarcity requires a multifaceted approach. - Amitkumar Shrivastava, Fujitsu
Forbes Technology Council is an invitation-only community for world-class CIOs, CTOs and technology executives. Do I qualify?
3. Real-Time Farming Guidance
We struggle to feed everyone on our planet, particularly in underserved regions. With the planet’s rapidly increasing population, this will only get worse. AI-powered mobile apps can provide real-time farming advice to smallholder farmers to help them optimize their yields and manage their resources more efficiently. This will significantly contribute to global food security and distribution. - Jo Webber, Pod
4. Transparent And Efficient Supply Chains
Integrating AI with blockchain technology can create transparent and efficient agricultural supply chains. AI can predict demand, optimize logistics and reduce waste, while blockchain ensures the traceability and authenticity of food products. This system can help reduce losses, ensure fair prices for farmers and provide consumers with access to safe and affordable food. - Cristian Randieri, Intellisystem Technologies
5. Pollination By Autonomous Drones
One unique application of AI in the agriculture industry is the development of autonomous drones for pollination. These AI-driven drones can help natural pollinators such as bees, which are declining in number due to environmental issues. By efficiently pollinating crops, drones can enhance crop yields and ensure food security, even in areas with limited natural pollinator populations. - Jabin Geevarghese George, Tata Consultancy Services
6. Soil Health Management
AI can revolutionize soil health management by analyzing data from soil sensors to optimize nutrient delivery and irrigation schedules. This targeted approach ensures crops receive the exact nutrients they need, reducing waste and improving yields. By maintaining optimal soil health, farmers can produce more food sustainably, addressing global food scarcity efficiently. - Jagadish Gokavarapu, Wissen Infotech
7. Intelligent Food Transit Systems
One area where I see big potential for AI to help with food scarcity is by using it to get food from farms to people’s plates in a smarter way. AI can crunch a ton of data on crop yields, weather patterns, shipping routes and demand forecasts to figure out the best paths to move food supplies efficiently. With fewer logistical errors comes less waste, which means more people get to eat. - Thomas Griffin, OptinMonster
8. Precision Irrigation
AI-driven irrigation systems will revolutionize the global agriculture industry. Currently, both overirrigation and underirrigation, based on generic or historical patterns, result in suboptimal global food production. With AI, irrigation systems will be able to use current data for microirrigation, which will adapt in real time and help address both global food scarcity and water conservation. - Rahul Mewawalla, Mawson Infrastructure Group
9. Crop Phenotyping
AI-powered crop phenotyping can help address global food scarcity. It uses advanced imaging and machine learning to study plant traits, finding the best and most resilient crops. This speeds up breeding new crop varieties that can grow well in different environments, leading to increased food production. - Margarita Simonova, ILoveMyQA
10. Weather Prediction
One promising application of AI in agriculture is predicting weather patterns. By analyzing historical weather data, AI can forecast conditions such as droughts, enabling farmers to proactively employ water-conservation techniques. This predictive capability helps optimize resource usage, ensuring sustainable farming practices and contributing to efforts to address global food scarcity. - Rohit Garg, Meta
11. Vertical Farming
AI-driven vertical farming is a promising solution to global food scarcity. By optimizing growth conditions, resource use and pest management, AI enhances crop yields and efficiency in vertically stacked, controlled environments. This sustainable approach significantly reduces water and nutrient consumption while increasing productivity. AI also automates labor-intensive tasks through data analysis. - Deepak Gupta, Cars24 Financial Services
12. GeoAI
The most important innovation in addressing global food scarcity is the combination of satellite data with AI. Multiple sources of hyperspectral and high-resolution thermal imagery are currently hitting the market, which for the first time ever allows the monitoring of crop-level conditions to be fully automated. Geospatial artificial intelligence is the most important available tool to counter the impact of climate change on crop yields. - Mike Flaxman, Heavy.AI
13. Livestock Monitoring
One impactful use of AI technology in farming is smart sensors that are ingested by farm animals. Imagine the advantages if a farmer can predict sickness within a herd and move to mitigate it before there are any widespread or long-lasting impacts. Working smarter with what you already have will always give you an advantage! - Bankim Chandra, DotSquares LLC

title: Video game performers will go on strike over artificial intelligence concerns
text:
Video game performers will go on strike over artificial intelligence concerns
Hollywood’s video game performers are going on strike, throwing part of the entertainment industry into another work stoppage after talks for a new contract with major game studios broke down over artificial intelligence protections
LOS ANGELES -- Hollywood's video game performers voted to go on strike Thursday, throwing part of the entertainment industry into another work stoppage after talks for a new contract with major game studios broke down over artificial intelligence protections.
The strike — the second for video game voice actors and motion capture performers under the Screen Actors Guild-American Federation of Television and Radio Artists — will begin at 12:01 a.m. Friday. The move comes after nearly two years of negotiations with gaming giants, including divisions of Activision, Warner Bros. and Walt Disney Co., over a new interactive media agreement.
SAG-AFTRA negotiators say gains have been made over wages and job safety in the video game contract, but that the studios will not make a deal over the regulation of generative AI. Without guardrails, game companies could train AI to replicate an actor’s voice, or create a digital replica of their likeness without consent or fair compensation, the union said.
Fran Drescher, the union's president, said in a prepared statement that members would not approve a contract that would allow companies to “abuse AI.”
"Enough is enough. When these companies get serious about offering an agreement our members can live — and work — with, we will be here, ready to negotiate," Drescher said.
A representative for the studios did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment.
The global video game industry generates well over $100 billion dollars in profit annually, according to game market forecaster Newzoo. The people who design and bring those games to life are the driving force behind that success, SAG-AFTRA said.
“Eighteen months of negotiations have shown us that our employers are not interested in fair, reasonable AI protections, but rather flagrant exploitation,” said Interactive Media Agreement Negotiating Committee Chair Sarah Elmaleh.
Last month, union negotiators told The Associated Press that the game studios refused to “provide an equal level of protection from the dangers of AI for all our members" — specifically, movement performers.
Members voted overwhelmingly last year to give leadership the authority to strike. Concerns about how movie studios will use AI helped fuel last year’s film and television strikes by the union, which lasted four months.
The last interactive contract, which expired November 2022, did not provide protections around AI but secured a bonus compensation structure for voice actors and performance capture artists after an 11-month strike that began October 2016. That work stoppage marked the first major labor action from SAG-AFTRA following the merger of Hollywood’s two largest actors unions in 2012.
The video game agreement covers more than 2,500 “off-camera (voiceover) performers, on-camera (motion capture, stunt) performers, stunt coordinators, singers, dancers, puppeteers, and background performers,” according to the union.
Amid the tense interactive negotiations, SAG-AFTRA created a separate contract in February that covered indie and lower-budget video game projects. The tiered-budget independent interactive media agreement contains some of the protections on AI that video game industry titans have rejected.

title: Video game actors are going on strike. Here's why
text:
Video game actors are going on strike. Here's why
More than 2,500 video game voice actors and motion capture performers are going on strike after negotiations with game industry giants that began nearly two years ago failed to result in an agreement
LOS ANGELES -- Hollywood's video game performers voted to go on strike Thursday after negotiations with game industry giants that began nearly two years ago came to a halt over artificial intelligence protections.
Leaders of the Screen Actors Guild-American Federation of Television and Radio Artists have billed the issues behind the labor dispute — and AI in particular — as an existential crisis for performers. Game voice actors and motion capture artists' likenesses, they say, could be replicated by AI and used without their consent and without fair compensation.
The union says the unregulated use of AI poses “an equal or even greater threat” to performers in the video game industry than it does in film and television because the capacity to cheaply and easily create convincing digital replicas of performers' voices is widely available.
“We’re not going to consent to a contract that allows companies to abuse AI to the detriment of our members. Enough is enough. When these companies get serious about offering an agreement our members can live — and work — with, we will be here, ready to negotiate,” SAG-AFTRA President Fran Drescher said in a statement Wednesday. "
Here are five things to know about the strike, which starts at 12:01 a.m. Friday:
The agreement covers more than 2,500 “off-camera voiceover performers, on-camera (motion capture, stunt) performers, stunt coordinators, singers, dancers, puppeteers, and background performers,” according to SAG-AFTRA.
The union had been negotiating with an industry bargaining group consisting of signatory video game companies, including divisions of Activision and Electronic Arts. Those companies are Activision Productions; Blindlight; Disney Character Voices; Electronic Arts; Productions Inc.; Formosa Interactive; Insomniac Games; Take 2 Productions; VoiceWorks Productions; ad WB Games.
The game companies have said that they were negotiating in good faith and had reached tentative agreements “on the vast majority of proposals.”
Wednesday's labor action marks the second time SAG-AFTRA's video game performers have gone on strike. Their first work stoppage, in October 2016, began after more than one year of negotiations failed. The union and video game companies reached a tentative deal 11 months later, in September 2017. At the time, the strike — which helped secure a bonus compensation structure for voice actors and performance capture artists — was the longest in the union's history, following the merger of Hollywood’s two largest actors unions in 2012.
SAG-AFTRA has said that some of the key issues include securing wages that keep up with inflation, protections around “exploitative uses” of artificial intelligence and safety precautions that account for the strain of physical performances as well as vocal stress. Union negotiators told The Associated Press that they had made gains in bargaining over wages and job safety, but that the game studios refused to “provide an equal level of protection from the dangers of AI for all our members.”
The signatory companies refused to extend AI protections to on-camera performers, the union said.
“They’re saying we’ll protect voiceover performers, but we won't protect anybody else,” Duncan Crabtree-Ireland, SAG-AFTRA’s executive director, said in an interview last month. “The bottom line is if you have performers working for you, helping create the content that’s in your game, whether it’s voice content, whether it’s stunt work, whether it’s motion work...all of those performers deserve to have their right to have informed consent and fair compensation for the use of their image, their likeness or voice, their performance. It’s that simple.”
Although the unchecked use of artificial intelligence has been a sticking point in talks, voice actors and members of the union negotiating committee have said they are not anti-AI. The performers are worried, however, that unchecked use of AI could provide game makers with a means to displace them — by training an AI to replicate an actor’s voice, or to create a digital replica of their likeness without consent.
Some also argue that AI could also strip less experienced actors of the chance to land smaller background roles, such as non-player characters, where they typically cut their teeth before landing larger roles. The unchecked use of AI, performers say, could also lead to ethical issues if their voices or likenesses are used create content that they do not morally agree with.
SAG-AFTRA created a separate contract in February that covered indie and lower-budget video game projects. The tiered-budget independent interactive media agreement contains some of the protections on AI that video game industry bargaining group rejected.
The union also announced a side deal with AI voice company Replica Studios in January that enables major studios to work with unionized actors to create and license a digital replica of their voice. It also sets terms that allow performers to opt out of having their voices used in perpetuity.

title: SAG-AFTRA Video Game Workers Strike Over Lack Of AI Protections
text:
Stop me if you’ve heard this before, say, all of last summer: SAG-AFTRA union members have called a strike against big media companies over concerns about the impacts of artificial intelligence on their profession and job security.
Except this year, it’s not the Writers Guild and SAG-AFTRA’s actors on strike. It’s SAG-AFTRA’s voice actors who bring characters to life in video games. They’re concerned about possible rampant use of AI-cloned voices replacing their jobs. And the strike takes effect tonight, at 12:01 AM.
The struck companies include some of the biggest in Hollywood and beyond: Walt Disney-owned Disney Character Voices Inc., Sony-owned Insomniac Games Inc., and Warner Bros. Discovery’s WB Games Inc. Others being struck are publishing giants Microsoft-owned Activision Productions,Take-Two Interactive (Take 2 Productions Inc.) and EA (Electronic Arts Productions Inc.), as well as Blindlight LLC, Formosa Interactive LLC, Llama Productions LLC, and VoiceWorks Productions Inc.
The lineup of struck companies may be somewhat different from last year’s six months of strikes that crippled Hollywood. But the sticking point remains a familiar and perhaps even trickier one, controlling how AI can be used, in this case to create voices for in-game characters. Given that voice actors can have their voices “cloned” by readily available AI tools, or generated wholesale without an actor’s involvement at all, the issue is seen as potentially devastating for the particular art of voice acting.
Actors and stunt performers also are widely used in motion-capture work to create the digital armatures for in-game characters.
The strike came after 19 months of negotiating, and months of leafletting and informational pickets by union members at industry events such as game awards and conferences. Union members authorized a strike last September after a year of negotiations, with 98.23% in favor, the union said.
“The video game industry generates billions of dollars in profit annually,” said SAG-AFTRA National Executive Director Duncan Crabtree-Ireland, once again the union’s lead negotiator. “The driving force behind that success is the creative people who design and create those games. That includes the SAG-AFTRA members who bring memorable and beloved game characters to life, and they deserve and demand the same fundamental protections as performers in film, television, streaming, and music: fair compensation and the right of informed consent for the A.I. use of their faces, voices, and bodies.”
SAG-AFTRA President Fran Drescher, a notable and strident voice in last year’s strike announcements, said “We’re not going to consent to a contract that allows companies to abuse A.I. to the detriment of our members. Enough is enough. When these companies get serious about offering an agreement our members can live — and work — with, we will be here, ready to negotiate,”
The global video game industry has generated north of $180 billion in annual revenues for the past few years, but also has seen many thousands of layoffs in the past year or so, in part as pandemic-era optimism about widespread uptake of gaming has tempered in the following return to normalcy.
The industry has been struggling to turn revenues into profits. The economics of premier AAA titles, which typically employ the biggest casts of voice and motion-capture actors, have shifted.
Now such games typically require years-long development cycles and production budgets that rival major Hollywood movies, with very high stakes if the games fail. One example is the recent WG Games Suicide Squad title, an expensive flop after last year’s huge success with the Harry Potter title Hogwarts Legacy.
The mobile game space, which generates a majority of industry revenues, employs far fewer voice actors typically, but is also struggling with its most popular business models, including free-to-play titles that depend on “whales,” hard-core players who buy lots of in-game resources, or ads whose rates have flatlined amid vast inventory.
As with last year’s studio deals, projects that want to use union-represented performers must sign one of three interim interactive-media agreements that include what the union calls “critical A.I. protections for members.”
Notable examples of AI voice cloning include a recent deal by Hall of Fame sports announcer Al Michaels, who partnered with NBC to create an AI-generated version of his voice to narrate custom-generated daily newsletters of Olympic sports footage that the network is shooting for this year’s Olympics.
Michaels told a CNBC live audience that he was “frightened and astonished at the same time” when shown the cloned version of his voice, but decided to do the deal because, “AI is here. Ready or not, here it comes. You can resist it or embrace it. I chose the latter.”
Two years ago, James Earl Jones, long the menacing voice of Darth Vader in the Star Wars films but now in his early 90s, was seeking to retire from the gig. He agreed with Disney to allow a cloned version of his Vader voice, created by another actor using an app called Respeecher, for his voice part in the Obi-Wan Kenobi series and other future projects.

title: Honeywell BrandVoice: The Secret To Mastering The Supply Chain Equation? Artificial Intelligence
text:
By Torsten Pilz, Senior Vice President and Chief Supply Chain Officer, Honeywell
For decades, the various components of the supply chain have ebbed and flowed as new technologies and innovations have come into play. No matter what the supply chain looks like, its goal is simple: to satisfy customer demand. The companies that can do this the best will win out, but what’s the secret? How do you make the right decisions early in the supply chain? And how do you plan to satisfy customer demand before you even know what specifically that demand will be for?
Consider the example of ordering a new pair of shoes online. Historically, planning and forecasting functions within a company would need to rely on a combination of previous data and intuition to anticipate and predict what a customer would need and want months ahead of time. For instance, sandals will be popular in the summer, but which styles will be trending? These calculations have always been a gamble, until now, thanks to the power of artificial intelligence (AI).
With AI, companies can leverage broad data sets to gain more granular detail on the customer level. If you read The Wall Street Journal and live in New York, you may prefer a certain style of sandals versus a reader of Vanity Fair in California, for example. AI takes a range of personalized factors into account that could never be tabulated manually and provides a more sophisticated way to anticipate what a potential customer may buy. The result is that a company can more accurately forecast expected output to set a supply chain up for success, even without knowing definitively where customer demand will come from.
Planning and forecasting are just the start. AI and other digital technologies can revolutionize nearly every aspect of the supply chain. From inventory and shipment management to customer service, there are hundreds of use cases that can transform the global supply chain’s efficiency, reliability and environmental impact.
While AI is revolutionary, it can also be overwhelming. The good news is it is relatively simple to integrate and inexpensive to implement. However, you need to have the right data infrastructure before you can do that. This is where most companies are struggling right now. To understand the opportunity AI holds, let’s explore some of the key use cases it offers and how they can correspond to a business’ long-term strategic objectives.
The Legacy Supply Chain: Transforming the Equation
Managing a global supply chain is the equivalent of a giant mathematical equation with many different variables. There are tens of thousands of customers, suppliers and employees, and millions of pathways that all need to meet at some point.
The ability of a supply chain to operate smoothly and successfully has always been reliant on the success (or failure) of individual siloed functions—procurement, planning, logistics, customer service, etc.—and their ability to serve each variable in the equation. But with AI, companies can more easily integrate these functionalities so data, insights and information flow between them in real-time to enhance operations.
AI has exponentially increased operational speed and efficiency for companies in many areas that have historically hamstrung supply chain operations. Consider just a few of the most common use cases:
- Inventory Retrieval: Distribution center teams have historically had to hand-pick and pack inventory. Now, automated storage and retrieval systems that use AI and machine learning algorithms can retrieve orders accurately, increasing fulfillment capabilities while augmenting our workforce with new opportunities for upskilling and reskilling.
- Shipment Management: With vision-based AI, companies can use technology to identify each item that comes into a warehouse and where it belongs. From there, a self-navigating autonomous mobile robot (AMR) can transport pallets or carts through distribution centers, vastly reducing the time it takes to move and manage shipments.
- Customer Service: When a customer calls about a problem with their order, AI now enables a support technician to immediately gain access to a wealth of data and insights on the customer, their current order and past purchases – this helps them reduce response time and deliver a tailored outcome.
As AI and autonomous technology-based use cases are combined across functions over time, a clearer picture of the impact across the supply chain emerges. It is no coincidence that when you look at some of the most successful e-commerce companies, many of them have found success by creating an AI-powered supply chain to improve efficiency and reliability, expediting delivery times and reducing costs.
The Opportunity: A Holistic Strategy, Not Just Hype
The transformative power AI holds for supply chains is undeniable, but it is not magic. Technologies like AI are only a part of the puzzle. Long-term success in AI implementation requires a thoughtful end-to-end strategy customized to your most important business objective, such as productivity, growth or resiliency. As you get started, here are some best practices to keep in mind:
- Simplify and focus your objective: It’s not enough to say you want to implement AI into your supply chain, you must put it in the context of your forward-looking objective: what do you need most from your supply chain? From there, ask yourself, what are the potential use cases with the greatest impact? And where does your supply chain currently have the biggest problem?
- Start small and expand: Select just one or two objectives at the start that AI can help solve. Over time, you can scale your supply chain from 1% AI-powered to 2% then 20%, creating a network of automated tasks and systems.
- Define and track success: Don’t forget to plan for how you will measure the ROI of AI implementation over time. By tracking success, you’ll be able to arm yourself with the data to back up the benefits of AI as you scale adoption.
- Focus on the long-term business opportunity: From the start, align your AI goals to long-term business objectives – this might include fewer product recalls or greater prediction accuracy.
- Involve your team from day one: A strong AI strategy must be paired with a skilled team. This means both committing to training your current team on new AI-based technologies, while also creating a map for hiring future team members with relevant skillsets in AI and automation.
The Urgency: It’s Now or Never
The reality is that companies that sit on the sidelines while others adopt AI will struggle to catch up. Doing nothing is catastrophic. Technology never sleeps, and there will very quickly be a divide between those companies that take advantage of an AI-powered supply chain and those that don’t.
Getting a late start on AI will have more dire consequences than any other technology before it. Just like we’ve seen with e-commerce, once a competitor pulls ahead, it is difficult for the rest to catch up. The benefits an AI-powered supply chain offers will forever tip the scale in your favor. It’s now or never.

title: 3 Reasons Why The Promised Gains From A.I. Are Still Faraway
text:
AI, we are told, is the future. It will transform every aspect of human life, fully justifying the hundreds of billions of dollars that big business is spending in pursuit of exponential gains in efficiency and productivity. The gold rush is in full swing and every company from Amazon to your local toy store is trying to implement AI in some way.
Yet three interlocking problems stand in the way of achieving major gains from A.I. in the near term.
1. A.I. Is Bad At Simple Math. Although A.I. can write poetry and detect patterns is large data sets, A.I. currently has trouble with simple math problems. As business runs on numbers, this is not a little issue: being bad at math is potentially a catastrophic flaw. Would you use a spreadsheet that systematically gave wrong answers? The flaw can be partially overcome if A.I is “trained” on a specific, consistent data set and focused on a significant operational issue. But this is far from the business-wide A.I. decision-making applications that are now endlessly hyped.
2. The Data In Most Big Firms Is Messy And Inconsistent: After years, or even decades, of quick fixes, multiple corporate acquisitions, and systemic neglect, the data in most big firms is messy and inconsistent and cannot be simply or quickly or inexpensively fixed. Until it is fixed, applying A.I. to such data is unlikely to succeed.
3. The Human Expertise Of Many Big Firms Is Siloed. The same organizational issues that have plagued digital transformations for decades also plague A.I. applications. Those staff how understand A.I. may not understand the business, and vice versa. In a siloed hierarchy, where horizontal collaboration is problematic, firms may be incapable of articulating the operational problems that A.I. systems might solve.
1. A.I.’s Catastrophic Math Problem
In this week’s article in the New York Times, technology reporter Steve Lohr revealed to a wider audience an embarrassing fact about A.I. that is well-known to A.I. insiders: A.I. is bad at simple math. “Chatbots like Open AI’s ChatGPT can write poetry, summarize books and answer questions, often with human-level fluency. These systems can do math, based on what they have learned, but the results can vary and be wrong. They are fine-tuned for determining probabilities, not doing rules-based calculations.”
A.I.’s math problem is not an accident. A.I. was designed to go beyond the limits of computer which were designed to crunch numbers following step-by-step rules and retrieve data from structured databases and perform pre-determined operations on that data. By contrast, A.I. learns by identifying patterns in vast amounts of data, and suggests probable conclusions, based on the information it has absorbed and the language patterns it has learned. “Likelihood is not accuracy, and language is more flexible, and forgiving, than math.”
When it comes to business data, like the price of a product, or the quantity of a delivery, or the amount of money in an account, or the timing of a decision, almost-right answers are not just bad. They are potentially calamitous. In such matters, the answer has to be exact.
“At times,” writes Lohr, “ A.I. chatbots have stumbled with simple arithmetic and math word problems that require multiple steps to reach a solution, something recently documented by some technology reviewers. The A.I.’s proficiency is getting better, but it remains a shortcoming.”
According to Lohr, the new version of ChatGPT “achieved nearly 64% accuracy on a public database of thousands of problems requiring visual perception and mathematical reasoning.” That compares to 58% in the previous version. But 64% accuracy for business data is unacceptably bad. Would you do business with a bank whose statements were only 64% accurate?
2. The Data In Most Large Organizations Is Messy And Inconsistent.
After years, or even decades, of multiple corporate acquisitions, haphazard quick fixes to solve urgent business issues, and siloed organizational structures, the data in most big firms is messy and inconsistent. Firms suffer from what is known as “technical debt”, a condition that cannot be simply or quickly or inexpensively fixed. Applying A.I. to such data is unlikely to succeed. According to technology expert, David Linthicum, “without good data, your generative AI system will be about as helpful as a warehouse fire.”
According to Linthicum, “until CIOs are ready to confront data that is siloed, redundant, or can’t be traced through the business process, generative AI will not pay off.” Often, the problem goes beyond the CIO, who is painfully aware of the mounting technical debt, but is unable to persuade the CEO to commit the substantial resources needed to fix the system from top to bottom. So the technical debt keeps compounding until there is a major collapse, as happened at Southwest Airlines in 2022.
“Until CIOs are ready to confront data that is siloed, redundant, or can’t be traced through the business process, generative AI will not pay off,” concludes Linthicum. “CIOs must fix their data before AI can provide any value This may be too expensive or too risky for many. The inability to adopt AI due to data issues could end up killing some businesses as their competitors embrace AI as a critical force multiplier of innovation. We’ll end up with the haves and the have-nots… If your data isn’t ready, you should avoid AI…My advice is that getting your data in a better state offers more benefits than just AI readiness, and it’s worth the time and money to do so.”
3. The Human Expertise Of Many Big Firms Is Also Siloed
The inherent flaws of generative A.I. can be partially overcome if A.is “trained” on a specific, consistent data set and focused on important operational issues. However, such training requires intense collaboration between those experts who understand the capabilities and limitations of A.I. and those experts who understand what business problems need to be solved. In a traditionally managed organization, those two sets of experts are likely to be located in different silos of the hierarchical structure, with only sporadic collaboration between them.
Even before A.I., horizontal collaboration was a fundamental constraint in getting benefits from digital transformation. Fims made massive investments in technology for digital transformation, and recruited the best experts. Yet the results were often often disappointing. “Many companies struggle to reap the benefits of investments in digital transformation, while others see enormous gains.” say Marco Iansiti and Satya Nadella in their article “Democratizing Transformation” in HBR (May-June 2022). “What do successful firms do differently?”
Digital transformation, the authors say, “requires that executives, managers, and front-line employees work together to rethink how every aspect of the business should operate.” This is not an easy message to digest or implement. This will be even more the case with A.I.
Change Is Possible: The Case Of Novartis
Yet the problem can be solved, as shown by the example of Novartis, the Swiss pharmaceutical giant. As Novartis moved its technology infrastructure to the cloud and invested in data platforms and data integration, it invested in staff. It “recruited AI specialists and data scientists to build machine-learning models and deploy them throughout the firm.” But it “did not have larger and more-diverse groups of employees—executives, managers, and front-line workers—coming together to rethink how every aspect of the business should operate.”
As a result, the authors report, “even as the technical teams grew, managers from across the business—sales, supply chain, HR, finance, and marketing—weren’t embracing the newly available information, nor were they thinking much about how data could enhance their teams’ work.” At the same time, the data scientists could not see into the business units and could not integrate data into day-to-day operations. As a result, the investments resulted in few successes.
It wasn’t a money problem. Novartis spent heavily on digital. It was a management mindset problem. It was only when Novartis began pairing data scientists and business staff that they began to see gains. If Novartis continues on this path, it will begin to function “more like software companies, developing comprehensive capabilities that enable product and program management and rapid experimentation.”
Conclusion
Thus, while a few big firms that have overcome these three constraints may make major gains from A.I., in the short run most other firms will not. The question is not whether the A.I. hype bubble will pop. The only question is when. Given the hundreds of billions of dollars being invested in A.I., and the limited benefits now being generated, the coming A.I. bust could make the Dot-com bust of 2000 look like a picnic.
Eventually, A.I. may get better at math and more firms may clean up their data and grasp the necessity of embracing 21st century management. When that happens, A.I. may climb back to a more practical, less hyped use.

The Management Paradigm Driving The World’s Most Valuable Firms

title: OpenAI enters Google-dominated search market with SearchGPT - ET BrandEquity
text:
- Digital
- 2 min read
OpenAI enters Google-dominated search market with SearchGPT
OpenAI said it has opened sign-ups for the new tool, which is currently in the prototype stage and is being tested with a small group of users and publishers. The company plans to integrate the best features from the search tool into ChatGPT in the future.
OpenAI is venturing into a territory long dominated by Google with the selective launch of SearchGPT, an artificial intelligence-powered search engine with real-time access to information from the internet.
The move, announced on Thursday, also places the AI giant in competition with its largest backer Microsoft's Bing search and emerging services such as Perplexity - a search-focused AI chatbot firm backed by Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and semiconductor giant Nvidia.
Shares of Google's parent company Alphabet ended 3% lower on Thursday after OpenAI's announcement.
OpenAI said it has opened sign-ups for the new tool, which is currently in the prototype stage and is being tested with a small group of users and publishers. The company plans to integrate the best features from the search tool into ChatGPT in the future.
"AI-powered search tools from OpenAI and Perplexity re-affirm search as a content engagement model but pressure Google to be better at its own game," Canaccord Genuity analyst Kingsley Crane said.
Google dominates the search engine market with a 91.1% share as of June, according to web analytics firm Statcounter.
SearchGPT will provide summarized search results with source links in response to user queries, OpenAI said in a blog post. Users will also be able to ask follow-up questions and receive contextual responses.
The company will give publishers access to tools for managing how their content appears in SearchGPT results. News Corp and The Atlantic are publishing partners for SearchGPT.
SearchGPT signals a closer collaboration between publishers and OpenAI, following content licensing agreements with major organizations like Associated Press, News Corp and Axel Springer.
"Newer AI-powered search providers could face challenges of their own, with Perplexity already facing pending legal action from publishers like Wired and Forbes, and Conde Nast," said Crane.
Major search engines have been trying to integrate AI into search since ChatGPT first launched in November 2022. Microsoft, through its early investment, adopted OpenAI technology for its Bing search engine, while Google rolled out AI-powered summaries for the wider public at its developer conference in May.
Google did not respond to a Reuters query on the potential impact of SearchGPT on its business.
Reuters had earlier reported on OpenAI's plans around AI search in May.

title: Musk to discuss $5 billion xAI investment with Tesla board - ET CIO
text:
- Artificial Intelligence
- 3 min read
Musk to discuss $5 billion xAI investment with Tesla board
The poll came shortly after Tesla said its second-quarter automotive gross margin and profit fell short of Wall Street estimates on Tuesday as the company cut prices and offered incentives to boost sales.
Tesla CEO Elon Musk said on Thursday he and the board of the electric vehicle company will discuss making a $5 billion investment in his artificial intelligence startup xAI, fueling concerns about a conflict of interest.
Musk, the world's richest person, launched xAI last year in a bid to compete with Microsoft-backed OpenAI. That sparked concerns he may allocate some resources of the automaker to the AI company.
Many Musk fans have supported the idea: On Tuesday, Musk launched a poll asking users on social media platform X whether Tesla should invest $5 billion in xAI. More than two-thirds of nearly 1 million respondents voted in favor. It is not clear how many are Tesla investors.
The poll came shortly after Tesla said its second-quarter automotive gross margin and profit fell short of Wall Street estimates on Tuesday as the company cut prices and offered incentives to boost sales.
continued below
During Tesla's earning conference call on Tuesday, Musk said xAI would be "helpful in advancing full self-driving and in building up the new Tesla data center," adding that there are opportunities to integrate xAI's chatbot, Grok, with Tesla's software.
Despite a frenzy of investment, most AI firms are still working out business models while spending heavily on technology.
"It's hard to make a claim that this is in the best interest of their Tesla shareholder," said Brent Goldfarb, a business school professor at the University of Maryland, who said it amounted to a transfer of Tesla wealth.
"In AI in general, nobody is quite sure where the money is going to be made and who is going to pay for it. AI right now has all the signs of a bubble," he said.
In 2018, Musk left OpenAI, which he co-founded because of a potential future conflict with Tesla, which is developing AI software for self-driving vehicles.
Musk said in April that xAI is hiring some engineers from Tesla to retain talent in the face of recruiting by Open AI.
Musk's xAI raised $6 billion in a series B funding in May, fetching a post-money valuation of $24 billion. Its investors include Andreessen Horowitz and Sequoia Capital.
Musk has previously said he plans for a quarter of xAI to be owned by investors in X, which he bought for $44 billion. The social media firm's value has plunged since then.
Musk previously has faced criticism over potential conflicts of interest among the many companies he owns and runs. Some Tesla shareholders alleged the 2016, $2.6 billion acquisition of struggling rooftop solar company, SolarCity, founded by Musk and his cousins, amounted to a bailout. Last year, however, the Delaware Supreme Court upheld a ruling that Musk did not push the electric carmaker to overpay for SolarCity.
(Reporting by Hyunjoo Jin in San Francisco and Akash Sriram in Bengaluru, Additional reporting by Paul Katie in New York; Editing by Shinjini Ganguli, Peter Henderson and Daniel Wallis)

title: The lower the AI exposure, the bigger the problem for Europe's chip firms - ET Auto
text:
- Auto Technology

The lower the AI exposure, the bigger the problem for Europe's chip firms
Companies with less AI exposure meanwhile were hit harder by industrial clients and automakers cutting orders. Demand for electric vehicles has slowed sharply in Europe.
Shares in European semiconductor firms less exposed to AI chips slumped on Thursday as falling demand from their key automotive and industrial clients hit business prospects, on top of a wider sector correction.
Chip component suppliers like ASML and ASM International are more exposed to the booming AI chip market and demand from high-end tech clients like Nvidia, TSMC, and Intel.
"The more high-end applications, linked to AI, those are doing much better," said ING analyst Marc Hesselink.
But even they aren't immune to a "correction" in stock valuations after strong rallies this year, coupled with worries around the impact of trade spats involving China, the U.S. and Europe, Hesselink added.
Shares in both ASML and ASMI were down about 3% in early afternoon trading.
Companies with less AI exposure meanwhile were hit harder by industrial clients and automakers cutting orders. Demand for electric vehicles has slowed sharply in Europe.
STMicroelectronics, which supplies Tesla, tumbled 14% after it cut 2024 sales and margin targets for a second time this year, as orders from industrial customers did not improve and automotive demand fell.
Germany's Infineon, a top automotive chip supplier, fell 6%.
Dutch company NXP Semiconductors earlier this week reported its worst decline in quarterly revenue in four years on weak demand from automotive customers, dragging down some U.S peers with auto exposure.
And while German chip materials supplier Siltronic raised its guidance, that was mostly due to the AI market which it said would grow this year.
BE Semiconductor Industries slumped 13% after forecasting flat third-quarter sales, hit by weak growth in mainstream assembly markets, particularly in China, even as orders for its systems used in AI grew.
Europe's STOXX 600 Technology index was down 2.8%, largely dragged by semiconductor stocks including ams OSRAM that fell 7% ahead of results on Friday, STMicro peer Melexis falling 4%, and Technoprobe, Soitec and Nordic Semiconductor also down.
The sector's fundamentals remain strong, Hesselink said. Companies still hope that EV demand will be robust in the longer term.
Chip components related to EVs, particularly silicon carbide, will be a growth driver in the second half of the year, STMicro's CEO Jean-Marc Chery said in a conference call.
