title: $1 trillion rout hits Nasdaq 100 over AI jitters in worst day since 2022 - ET Telecom
text:
- Internet
- 5 min read
$1 trillion rout hits Nasdaq 100 over AI jitters in worst day since 2022
The selloff was triggered by a middle-of-the-road earnings report from Alphabet Inc. late Tuesday that featured a bloated capital expense. The company’s stock sank more than 5% for its worst performance since January. Tesla Inc. plunged more than 12% after Chief Executive Officer Elon Musk offered scant details about his company’s self-driving vehicle initiative.
Investors soured on the promise of artificial intelligence Wednesday, sparking a $1 trillion rout in the Nasdaq 100 Index as questions swirled over just how long it will take for the substantial investments in the technology to pay off.
The Nasdaq indexes tumbled more than 3% for the worst days since October 2022. The list of laggards was a who’s-who of AI technology darlings, led by semiconductor companies such as Nvidia Corp., Broadcom Inc. and Arm Holdings Plc.
As a result, traders are now paying more to protect against swings in tech. Options volatility on Nvidia rose to the highest level since mid-March, and the premium for puts on Broadcom Inc. is at a three-month high.
The rout comes two weeks after a cooler-than-expected inflation reading set off a massive rotation from tech winners into companies that would benefit most from Federal Reserve rate cuts, primarily small capitalization stocks. For a fourth straight session — and the 10th time in 11 days — small caps’ performance exceeded that of their larger brethren on Wednesday. The Russell 2000 is up 0.5% this week compared with a loss of 1.5% in the S&P 500 and 2.6% in the Nasdaq 100.
Violent Selling
While the rotation from tech remains on display, the moves in tech were violent enough to suggest something else was at play. Specifically, investors appear to be listening to growing chatter in some Wall Street circles that the AI rally that fueled a bubble that added $9 trillion in value to the S&P 500 in the past year is bound to burst. While Wednesday may not mark the start of that, the magnitude of the drop raises alarms.
“In the short run, there may be a little AI fatigue, just because some of these investments that the Big Tech companies have made in AI may not be paying off in the time period that investors had in mind,” said Neville Javeri, portfolio manager at Allspring Global Investments.
The makers of hardware used in AI computing suffered some of the biggest drops on Wednesday after soaring this year. Super Micro Computer Inc. dropped 9.15%. Nvidia fell 6.8%, and Broadcom Inc. lost 7.6%. Megacaps also retreated, as Meta Platforms Inc. declined 5.6%, Microsoft Corp. slid 3.6%, and Apple Inc. dropped 2.9%.
Other traders, however, saw the moves as temporary.
“I don’t think you’re seeing anything other than some stocks that have done exceptionally well, have very solid year-to-date returns, seeing some profit taking in the face of not getting a giant beat and raise out of Google,” said Michael Sansoterra, chief investment officer at Silvant Capital Management.
The selloff sent a Bloomberg index of the so-called Magnificent Seven technology stocks down 5.9%, falling below its average price for the past 50 days for the first time since May. It remains up 33% since the start of the year.
AI Bubble Fears
Jim Covello, the head of equity research at Goldman Sachs Group Inc., is among a growing number of market professionals who are arguing that the commercial hopes for AI are overblown and questioning the vast expense required to build out infrastructure required for the computing to run and train large-language models.
Talk of a bubble in AI names was fanned by activity in derivatives markets, where investors piled into bullish options on indexes and individual stocks, especially Nvidia, that acted as rocket fuel during the rally. That sentiment shifted as the rotation from tech picked up speed, and potentially added to the downdraft Wednesday.
Last week, for example, demand for bearish puts in Nvidia outpaced calls by the most in five months. Tail-risk hedges that pay out in a stock crash – perhaps as much as a 30% downturn — were rising at the fastest pace since October. And the cost to protect against a retreat at around 10% or so was at the highest level since August 2023.
Tech stock valuations had moved into historically frothy territory. Two weeks ago, the S&P 500 information technology index’s price-to-estimated earnings ratio hit the highest since 2002. Many in the Big Tech group are still priced at nose-bleed levels despite the selloff. Nvidia is priced at 36 times profits projected over the next 12 months, compared with an average of 21 in the S&P 500. Apple and Microsoft are both priced at more than 30 times. That’s raised the stakes for earnings at an awkward time, with profit growth for the tech giants set to slow.
While Alphabet’s results dimmed hopes that AI would be a bigger contributor to financial results for megacaps, investors have yet to hear from the rest of the cohort. Microsoft Corp. is scheduled to report on July 30, followed by Meta Platforms Inc., Apple Inc. and Amazon.com Inc. later in the week. Nvidia, the biggest beneficiary of AI spending, will be the last to report on Aug. 28.
“We are still holding onto our large-cap, quality, growth view,” said Cayla Seder, macro multi-asset strategist at State Street. “Because even if there is trepidation around tech earnings, they are a more attractive option in terms of earnings growth and fundamental strength.”

Amazon racing to develop AI chips cheaper, faster than Nvidia's: Executives
Amazon is developing its own processors to limit its reliance on costly Nvidia chips - the so-called Nvidia tax - that power some of the artificial intelligence cloud business at its Amazon Web Services, the main growth driver.
Inside Amazon.com's chip lab in Austin, Texas, half a dozen engineers on a Friday afternoon put a closely guarded new server design through its paces.
The server was packed with Amazon's artificial intelligence chips that compete with those from market leader Nvidia, Amazon executive Rami Sinno said on Friday, during a visit to the lab.
Amazon is developing its own processors to limit its reliance on costly Nvidia chips - the so-called Nvidia tax - that power some of the artificial intelligence cloud business at its Amazon Web Services, the main growth driver.
Through its homegrown chips, Amazon wants to help customers compute complex calculations and process enormous amounts of data more cheaply.
Its rivals Microsoft and Alphabet are doing the same.
Sinno, the director of engineering for Amazon's Annapurna Labs that is a part of its cloud business AWS, said Amazon's customers were increasingly demanding cheaper alternatives to Nvidia.
Amazon bought Annapurna labs in 2015.
While the company's AI chip efforts are nascent, Amazon's workhorse chip Graviton that performs non-AI computing has been under development for nearly a decade and is on its fourth generation. The AI chips, Trainium and Inferentia, are newer designs.
"So the offering of up to 40%, 50% in some cases of improved price (and) performance - so it should be half as expensive as running that same model with Nvidia," David Brown, Vice President, Compute and Networking at AWS said on Tuesday.
Sales at AWS, which accounts for just under a fifth of Amazon's overall revenue, surged 17% to $25 billion in the January-March quarter, compared with a year earlier. AWS controls roughly a third of the cloud computing market, with Microsoft's Azure holding about 25%.
During its recent Prime Day, Amazon deployed a quarter million Graviton chips and 80,000 of its custom AI chips to handle the surge in activity across its platforms, the company said.

title: OpenAI takes aim at Google with limited roll out of SearchGPT - ET Telecom
text:
- Internet

OpenAI takes aim at Google with limited roll out of SearchGPT
OpenAI said it has opened sign-ups for the new tool, which is currently in the prototype stage and is being tested with a small group of users and publishers.
OpenAI said on Thursday it is selectively rolling out SearchGPT, an artificial intelligence-powered search engine with real time access to the information from the internet.
This move positions the Microsoft-backed startup directly against Google, the dominant search engine, as well as newer services like the search-focused AI chatbot Perplexity.
Shares of Google's parent company, Alphabet, extended a decline to end of over 3% lower after OpenAI's announcement.
OpenAI said it has opened sign-ups for the new tool, which is currently in the prototype stage and is being tested with a small group of users and publishers.
"While this prototype is temporary, we plan to integrate the best of these features directly into ChatGPT in the future," OpenAI said in a blog post, without giving more details or a timeline.
SearchGPT will provide summarized search results with source links in response to user queries. They will also be able to ask follow-up questions and receive contextual responses.
The company will also give publishers access to tools for managing how they appear in SearchGPT results.
The SearchGPT tool signals a closer collaboration between publishers and OpenAI, following content licensing agreements with major organizations like Associated Press, News Corp, and Axel Springer.
Major search engines have been trying to integrate AI into search since ChatGPT first launched in November 2022. Microsoft, through its early investment, adopted OpenAI technology for its Bing search engine, while Google rolled out AI-powered summaries for the wider public at its developer conference in May.
In June, Google Search held a 91.1% market share, down from 92.6% a year earlier, primarily due to increased usage of Microsoft Bing, according to web analytics firm Statcounter.
Google did not respond to a Reuters query on the potential impact of SearchGPT on its business.
Reuters had earlier reported on OpenAI's plans around AI search in May.

title: ‘Family Ties’ star Justine Bateman says Hollywood's use of new tech is 'motivated by greed'
text:
Justine Bateman continues to push back against AI’s infiltration of Hollywood.
The former "Family Ties" actress and filmmaker is launching a new film festival, the CREDO 23 Film Festival, requiring that entrants not use AI in their submissions.
"As we've seen over the last year, we've had a lot of streamers, embracing AI studios, embracing AI, and more recently, film festivals embracing AI. And I just feel like the use of generative AI is, it's theft, and you're never going to find out what you can really do. It's just a regurgitation of the past. You're sort of circling the drain," Bateman told Fox News Digital of her inspiration behind the festival.
She continued, "It's not the future. It's something that is going to increasingly occur in the future, but it's not the future of filmmaking. The future of filmmaking is whatever this next genre is going to be. You know, we haven't really had a new genre in the arts of any real wide significance since the '90s. So, I think we're long due for that. And I believe it's going to happen on the other side of this AI inferno."
WHAT IS ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE (AI)?
Bateman laid out how she sees the next few years in Hollywood, with AI making major gains despite current provisions and protections.
"I think the use of general AI will take over our business, and it will pull too many of the jobs in our pipeline out and then consequently collapse the structure of our business, which is just sort of corporate physics. That's just what happens," the "Desperate Housewives" actress said. "And I think the audiences will be taken with it and, like the fact that they can face replace themself on, [for example] Luke Skywalker in their viewing of ‘Star Wars’ at night or get films that are customized to their own viewing history, that'll be treated like Kleenex. [Studios] won't bother to copyright those. That'll just be – that's something you got to watch that day, and they can make you 45 more the next day."
She also sees an inevitable pushback against AI as well, especially as it begins to move into other industries and people’s everyday lives.
"I think they'll get to a point where the audiences will start feeling sick about it, and be bored with it, and also feel sick about how generative AI is infecting the rest of their lives, [their] education, insurance companies, your banks, everything. And at the same time, filmmakers will have had to differentiate themselves from what I can do in making really new material, making films that I can't do cheaper and quicker. And I think when you bring those two things together, where the audience is going to get to and where the filmmakers are going to get to, I think you'll have a new genre in the arts, and I'm really excited about that."

Bateman did advise that anyone working in film now should "try to make as much money as you can in the next two years. And/or get to know the producers and directors who are using full crews, like myself, there are many others who are not using generative AI, and work with them. Because everything is shifting and changing, motivated by greed."
"And that's why it's being used," she added. "It is not being used because it makes better films. It's being used because it makes volume content production faster and cheaper."
Bateman started CREDO 23 last year, an organization of people "that hold filmmaking sacred, and understand their responsibility to preserve the art form," as stated on their website.
Joining Bateman on the council are actress Juliette Lewis, "Mad Men" showrunner Matt Weiner, "Handmaid’s Tale" showrunner Reed Morano, and costume designer Arianne Phillips.
"[When] I founded CREDO 23, I was, at the time, talking to quite a few people about how disconcerting the involvement of AI was in our business. And so of those people I was speaking to, I asked a few of them if they'd be on the council with me . . . and they happily accepted," Bateman said. "So, it's great to have their input and, and I respect all of them so much as artists. It's a great group."
WATCH: JUSTINE BATEMAN EXPLAINS WHAT INSPIRED HER NEW NO-AI FILM FESTIVAL
The "Violet" director added that the council will also make up some of the programmers for the festival, which begins accepting submissions on August 1 through October 31. The event will kick off next year, March 28-30, at American Legion, Post 43, in Hollywood.
"It's not the future. It's something that is going to increasingly occur in the future, but it's not the future of filmmaking."
The event also promises grants, created from the profits of the festival, to participants.
"All the money that we pull in, through the various means, submissions, sponsorships, whatever, everything in excess of operating costs is going to be given to the filmmakers so that they can make more films," Bateman said.
CREDO 23 offers filmmakers the opportunity to add a stamp to the credits of their films, certifying that they have not used AI in any way, particularly generative AI, as well as minimal CGI use, and hiring union crews.
"The response to the film festival has been fantastic. People are really excited about it. It's not only, you know, refusing the use of AI, it's looking for fresh, really fresh, new filmmaking."

She added, "I want to be doing films that are the next wave of filmmaking. What did we do during our time as filmmakers? Did we just regurgitate the past? Or did we bring something new? And…new in the way that independent film was new. At some point, musicals were new. At some point, blockbusters were new, at some point, film noir was new. So what are we contributing to it? And it's certainly not going to be regurgitating material that has been stolen from all the other filmmakers in the last 100 years, which is what generative AI is."
Bateman has been speaking out against the use of AI since at least last year, when the technology came into heavy focus during the writers’ and actors’ strikes last summer.
"I think AI has no place in Hollywood at all. To me, tech should solve problems that humans have," Batemen told Fox News Digital last May at the beginning of the writers’ strike. "Using ChatGPT or any … software that's using AI to write screenplays, using that in place of a writer is not solving a problem. We don't have a lack of writers. We don't have a lack of actors. We don't have a lack of directors. We don't have a lack of talented people."
The strikes lasted until the fall for both unions, and resulted in some key provisions for both actors and writers to protect their livelihoods from being replaced by AI.
JUSTINE BATEMAN RIPS AI USE IN HOLLYWOOD, SAYS TECHNOLOGY IS 'GETTING AWAY FROM BEING HUMAN'
However, in June, The Hollywood Reporter shared a report that many in the entertainment industry are quietly using AI behind the scenes.
David Stripinis, a VFX professional who has worked on films like "Avatar," "Man of Steel" and several Marvel titles, told the outlet, "There are tons of people who are using AI, but they can’t admit it publicly because you still need artists for a lot of work. And they’re going to turn against you. Right now, it’s a PR problem more than a tech problem."
"There's definitely people using it. And I say, do whatever you got to do. For me, it's an anathema to actually moving forward as an artist. So I won't ever use it for anything," Bateman told Fox News Digital.
She continued, "I don't care how long it takes instead, or how many CGI artists I would have to hire instead. I just don't care. I'm not going to use stolen work. I'm not going to stunt my own growth as an artist, which is how I see it. So it makes no difference to me if other people use it. But it's the opposite direction of where I'm going creatively and professionally."
'TOP GUN' PRODUCER SAYS HE DOESN'T BELIEVE CLAIMS AI WILL REPLACE KEY JOBS
Through her work, and now her film festival, Bateman is pushing back at the idea of movies and television as "content," saying last year, "even referring to films and series as content to begin with, I think is … insulting."
She also noted that people and audiences do genuinely appreciate the efforts that go into making a movie.

RIDLEY SCOTT WARNS AI WILL BE ‘TECHNICAL HYDROGEN BOMB’ IN FILM INDUSTRY
"People love to hear about what you went through to get there," she said, citing Tom Cruise’s incredible stunt work in the "Mission: Impossible" films as an example.
"They love hearing how other humans have managed to get something done. And you see something that's done with AI and you just [shrugging] shrug emoji. You know, it's nothing. It doesn't enrich us. It doesn't take us further. It doesn't. It doesn't make us happy," she said.
"It's not only more impressive if a person did it, but it's also more encouraging to the viewer. . . . That's really exciting to people when they see that you came up with this completely inventive way to get that shot."

Bateman continued, "I love hearing how humans managed to get something done, because that means so can you. And if you just heard that some AI algorithm chewed up a bunch of old work and spat something out. [It feels like a] shrug emoji, like it's really not impressive."
She added, "I think it's a parlor trick, and I'm not impressed with it, and I find it unexciting and depressing. I find it completely depressing. So I'm all in on human-made films, human-made for human viewing. And, I'm really excited about the future."

title: Council Post: AI: Looking Beyond The Hype
text:
Erik Jost, VP Modern Workplace, Black Box Corporation.
It's all we hear about these days. I recently attended a weeklong conference and trade show, and everything was AI. AI this, AI that. Upon closer look, however, it seemed like 80% of the solutions I saw were marketing hype, and only 20% had any real substance. It got to the point where I half-expected the giveaway pens to be touted as special AI pens that knew what I wanted to write before I put pen to paper.
Do you detect a hint of cynicism in my comments? Yes, there's no disputing that AI is the next hot thing. For example, ChatGPT gained 1 million users within the first five days of its release. On top of that, according to a Forbes Advisor survey of business owners, 97% think ChatGPT will help their business. They're using it to generate website copy and information summaries, translate copy, and fix coding errors.
No doubt, AI is a game changer. MIT research scientist Andrew McAfee once told Bernard Marr (via Forbes): "Once in a while, the technology comes along that is so powerful and so broadly applicable that it accelerates the normal march of economic progress. And like a lot of economists, I believe that generative AI belongs in that category."
According to the Forbes Advisor survey, the top AI applications are customer service (56%) and cybersecurity and fraud management (51%), with recruitment and talent sourcing (26%) and audience segmentation (24%) at the bottom. Consumers are on board with that, with 65% saying they trust businesses that use AI.
AI and GenAI will change the way we work and live, and everyone wants it now. However, before you jump on the GenAI bandwagon, you need to wade through all of the hype to find the real value for you. Everyone has pie-in-the-sky dreams for AI, but what is its real-world impact? AI can be a dream-come-true solution, or it can be your worst nightmare. It has landed some well-known companies in very public hot water.
If you think AI is disruptive now, just wait. In the very near future, that disruption is going to explode.
IDC's Ritu Jyoti said GenAI's "potential for innovation and disruption is on a scale comparable to the introduction of the internet and the smartphone." I agree. AI technology is powerful, but the technology and how we use is it not mature.
First, do your homework. Everyone wants a quick AI fix to their problem du jour. That's not going to happen. Here's how to look beyond the hype.
1. Think big picture. Identify the goals and value you want from AI. What business functions do you want to target? CX? Marketing? Sales? IT? Include your "wouldn't it be great if" ideas as well as those annoying everyday tasks. What can be improved immediately (such as repetitive coding jobs), and what's better saved for the long term (such as the personalization of the customer journey)?
Enlist key stakeholders, and be honest and objective. You don't want gripe sessions where every department blames the other for their woes and inefficiencies.
2. Think tech. Now that you've identified what you want to accomplish, you can turn to technology to find out how to do it. McKinsey labels three types of AI adopters—takers, shapers and makers. Takers buy off-the-shelf solutions. Shapers customize off-the-shelf solutions. Makers, as the name suggests, develop their own solutions.
Approximately 53% of respondents to a survey on AI adoption used off-the-shelf solutions with little or no customization. When it comes to implementation, off-the-shelf solutions could be integrated in under four months, while custom solutions can take five months or more.
3. Think price tag. How much of an investment are you willing to make? When you start looking at the costs of implementing an AI digital transformation strategy, you may be in for sticker shock. From what I saw at the trade show, nearly everyone is offering AI at cost or at greatly discounted prices, but think about what you're paying for. AI is changing at breakneck speed. What is considered to be state-of-the-art today may be old news in two months. Where does that leave you? How are you going to keep up? Some investments may be expensive rabbit holes.
4. Think everything else. How are you going to manage AI? Are you going to have an internal GenAI team? What about cybersecurity and privacy concerns? Who determines your data governance? How will GenAI change your business model? You've got a lot to think about. I'll take a look at these issues in another post.
AI is revolutionary. It will do amazing things and hopefully reduce our costs, improve productivity, streamline operations, enhance CX, elevate sales, and just make our lives easier overall. If you're not using it now, you will be soon. Just be smart about how you incorporate AI into your business. What you decide now can affect your operations for years to come.

title: Council Post: How AI In Franchising Can Enhance Customer Interactions And Streamline Operations
text:
Hao Lam, entrepreneur, author, speaker, founder of Adaptively Education and Best in Class Education Center.
Artificial intelligence (AI) is a transformative force, offering tools and technologies to revolutionize marketing strategies, enhance operational efficiency and streamline human resources. It’s estimated that 73% of US companies have already implemented AI in their operations, paving the way for significant growth and success. While many businesses have taken the leap toward innovation, franchise owners have immense potential to leap ahead by integrating AI effectively and embracing technology advancements.
Enhancing Your Marketing Impact Using AI Innovations In Franchising
As a coach and mentor to many new franchise owners within my education franchise company, I understand the unique challenges business owners face when starting their businesses, particularly in marketing. Attracting customers is crucial for any new business, and finding effective yet affordable marketing strategies is key.
From creating personalized content that resonates with your target audience to efficiently managing your social media platforms, AI can help you make significant strides in building your brand's presence. Using AI tools, you'll not only optimize your resources but also set a strong foundation for future growth and engagement.
Here are some ways your franchise business can weave AI into your marketing efforts:
Content Creation At Scale: AI tools can generate a variety of marketing materials, including tailored copy variations and engaging social media posts. This automation allows franchises to maintain a consistent and dynamic online presence with less human intervention.
Targeted Advertising And Campaign Optimization: AI can analyze customer data to pinpoint precise marketing targets, allowing you to craft customized advertising campaigns. AI also helps optimize these campaigns for better engagement and higher conversion rates, helping ensure your marketing efforts efficiently reach the most receptive audiences.
Enhanced Customer Insights And Personalization: AI can sift through customer interaction data to uncover patterns and preferences, enabling you to tailor your marketing more effectively. This personalization can improve customer experience, foster loyalty and boost sales by delivering the right message at the right time.
Maximizing Your Operational Efficiency Through AI In Franchising
Operational efficiency is crucial for the success of any franchise, and incorporating AI can take this to the next level. AI tools can handle customer support effortlessly and simplify many day-to-day management tasks. Task automation helps reduce errors and improve efficiency. By using AI to enhance your operational efficiency, you're not just streamlining processes—you're setting your franchise up for better performance and increased competitiveness, all with the ease and convenience of AI integration.
Here are several strategies for embedding AI into your franchise operations to boost efficiency:
AI-Powered Customer Support: Implement AI chatbots to offer 24/7 customer support. These bots can handle common inquiries and explain basic concepts, offering customers timely and consistent support.
Data Analysis And Performance Prediction: Utilize AI to analyze vast amounts of operational data and predict future trends based on historical performance. This predictive capability can guide decision-making and help preempt potential challenges.
Meeting Planning And Report Generation: Several AI tools can transcribe meetings and highlight key points, making information sharing more efficient and ensuring that important details are not overlooked.
Transforming Human Resources With AI
Human resources play a pivotal role in the growth and stability of any franchise, and AI has the power to transform this crucial area. By automating labor-intensive processes like candidate screening and training program customization, AI can alleviate many of the traditional challenges associated with human resources management, speeding up processes and enhancing accuracy and personalization. Integrating AI into your human resources practices means you're not just modernizing your approach—you're improving your franchise's capability to attract, train and retain the best talent, thereby enhancing the value of your human resources.
Here are several impactful ways to incorporate AI into your franchise's human resources operations to improve effectiveness:
Automated Candidate Screening: AI can quickly analyze résumés and cover letters to identify the most suitable candidates, significantly speeding up the hiring process and ensuring that only the most qualified individuals move forward.
Personalized Onboarding Training Programs: AI technologies can tailor your onboarding training efforts to individual employees, adapting to their learning styles and speeds. This AI application leads to more effective training outcomes and better-prepared employees upon the onset of their employment with your company.
Ongoing Employee Development: AI can help in the continual development of employees by suggesting personalized learning paths and resources based on their performance and career goals, fostering a culture of continuous improvement and professional growth.
Additional Considerations
While integrating AI into your franchise operations can offer significant benefits, it's important to approach its implementation with caution and awareness of potential drawbacks. Ethical and transparency issues are crucial considerations. For instance, when using AI for content creation, always ensure the reliability and accuracy of the information through diligent fact-checking and source citing.
Additionally, be mindful of the financial implications of AI technology. The costs of AI tool subscriptions can accumulate quickly, and there are substantial commitments related to training both the AI itself and your staff to maximize your investment and avoid underutilized resources.
Leveraging AI In Your Franchise For A Sustainable Future
As you lean into AI integration, your franchise business can enhance operations, offer superior customer service and create a more engaging and responsive working environment.
When you consider which areas of your franchise business should integrate AI, remember that the goal is to complement and enhance human efforts rather than replace them. AI is not here to take jobs but to make them more efficient and less repetitive. By pairing your company’s talent with AI tools, you'll improve efficiency and foster a more innovative and adaptable business model prepared to meet the challenges of the future head-on.

title: Council Post: How Companies Can Support Independent Content Creators Through AI Upheaval
text:
Michael Sanchez is the co-founder and Chief Executive Officer of Raptive (formerly CafeMedia and AdThrive).
The internet promised to offer the greatest information democratization in history. People across the globe would have the opportunity to access vast amounts of quality information, education, opinion and entertainment—and for free. Even better, the content would not just come from the big media gatekeepers but from any independent content creator with powerful ideas, unique perspectives or important insights.
That early promise has not been realized. Over the last two decades, social platforms have captured the lion’s share of attention—and economic value—in our media landscape. We understand the damage that has been done: invasion of privacy, division and disinformation, doom-scrolling, and the negative impact on our young people’s mental health.
There is a critical bright spot amidst the noise. At the same time, and against the odds, individual content creators emerged and became some of the most vital forces for quality content on the open internet. What began as individual bloggers expressing their passions and interests has become the beating heart of the internet, funded almost entirely by advertising. Today, in the U.S., web-first independent content creators writing about food, family, wellness, tech, travel and more attract audiences of millions of people per month.
I think content creators represent the best of the American dream. But today, this promise is being challenged. Big AI companies have trained their models on independent creators’ content. They are repurposing it in search experiences and other new services they are building using AI. This dynamic could impact the livelihoods of these entrepreneurs and diminish the value of the internet.
Why Smaller Content Creators Must Be Protected
Media companies like the New York Times and Alden Global Capital have entered the public debate arguing that AI companies have infringed upon their copyrights and that fair use does not apply. I wholly agree—the economic harm to media properties is clear and measurable. However, the rights of individual content creators need to be equally heard and protected in this debate.
I believe it’s critical that tech companies license the content they use—not just from established media like the Associated Press, Reddit, Dotdash Meredith and Axel Springer, but also from the high-quality, independent content creators who make up so much of their AI’s training data.
The Potential Impact On Livelihoods And The Promise of the Open Internet
Google’s newly named AI Overview raises some concerns. (Disclosure: My company is a Premier Google Certified Publishing Partner.) Google will now surface AI results drawn directly from the websites it trained on, potentially eliminating the need for a user to visit the original source. The impact could diminish website traffic by as much as 50% by my company's estimates, impacting creators’ ability to make a living.
The result of projects like this could be a diminished internet—not one of creativity and diverse voices. Before long, the AI platforms themselves could struggle to find original content to train on and include in search summaries.
If we don't prioritize creators, tech companies could capture all of the value at the cost of independent voices and our larger society. The loss of income could impact hundreds of thousands of jobs in the U.S. alone. Unique and diverse voices could be silenced, reducing the depth of content and original thought in the world today. People could lack access to exciting and informative alternatives.
How We Can Support Creators
For AI to generate meaningful and equitable value in media, creators need to be active participants in the ecosystem. I think AI companies must provide creators with control and compensation so they can continue to participate fairly in the online economy. Google has said it believes AI Overviews will increase the amount of traffic being sent to publishers’ websites but has so far not shared any data. I encourage them to be transparent and show us the amount of traffic going to websites from the AI Overviews experience, and share the impact of its evolving roll-out.
I recommend AI companies compensate individual content creators proportionally based on their contribution to the models in their commercial enterprises. They should ensure that creators do not lose search traffic and that they’re included in any economic gains derived from their content. Opting out of Google search is currently the only way creators can stop AI Overviews from using their content without consent and without compensation, which is not a viable solution.
Executives at all organizations can be vocal in their support of quality content sites and the need for fair compensation. Make it clear to large tech companies that a balanced media ecosystem is crucial to all industries that have a content or advertising presence online. For the sake of fair competition and diverse and trustworthy information online, we can all be vocal about our desire to support content creators and media companies in all sectors. If big tech companies are able to divert web traffic and advertising revenue, businesses of all kinds could lose a major channel for reaching audiences.
For example, any company using search marketing or digital advertising should be clear with companies incorporating AI that they don’t want the media ecosystem to be diminished by the new tech.
To build stability and fairness across all levels of the industry, leaders can support laws that enforce content creators’ right to control and compensation. Legislators and regulators must protect competition and, where needed, reflect creators' interests in new frameworks for the booming AI sector.
Finally, courts can clarify current laws and statutes to reflect the dramatic changes AI brings to content, media, data and copyright. A clear statement on fair use and its applicability to the AI sector and training models is essential.
AI is potentially the most powerful, transformational technology ever. Let's work together to ensure its benefits are fully realized, its risks are wisely managed and the content creators who form the basis of it all are not left behind.

title: Council Post: What Businesses Can Learn From The Financial Services Industry Contending With Artificial Intelligence
text:
Tom Padgett is President of the Smarsh Enterprise business, which serves large global banks and financial services organizations.
Many companies are grappling with how to deal with artificial intelligence. However, given the regulatory scrutiny of financial services, the stakes are often higher. That puts a premium on leaders in the industry being able to cut through the hyperbole and find out how to reap the greatest rewards of this fast-evolving technology while minimizing the risks.
Some technology experts say that generative AI—which can create human-like responses to natural language queries—is the greatest invention since humans harnessed fire. Others warn that it's the beginning of our end. Then there's the group residing somewhere in the middle, and others who contend it's a fad.
Time will determine which view is correct. (As a leader in an organization that has been delivering AI-powered regulatory technology solutions for large global banks for over a decade, you can guess where my view aligns). What is certain is that no firm wants to become an example of how AI went wrong.
Approach AI as both a blessing and a curse.
The most immediate benefit of generative AI is creating efficiencies. I think every business, no matter the industry, should be looking for ways to maximize productivity and gain strong insights into its own data. Doing so can improve sales processes and HR functions, allow for better stakeholder communication or help recruit top talent.
Financial services is no different. Yet what makes the industry unique is that firms are bound by regulations requiring the preservation and oversight of business communications—resulting in the storage of large amounts of data. Firms must also be able to defend and explain the AI used.
That's both a blessing and a curse. Storing massive quantities of sensitive communications data amounts to a huge responsibility. One misstep could result in a seven-figure regulatory fine, reputational damage or both. Yet, the upside is that the same data is immeasurably valuable when a layer of AI can be applied to understand patterns, behaviors and intent that can help the organization operate efficiently, reduce risk and make decisions faster—and more accurately.
Other businesses may not have the regulatory obligations that forced them to confront the same dynamic… yet. I think they should treat AI as if they do because how they manage their data and train their large language models could have enormous implications.
Proceed with caution.
Today, with AI beneficiaries driving huge gains for investors, many organizations want to claim they have the most cutting-edge AI solutions. In the rush to do that, some skip an essential step: protecting themselves.
So, what happens is they adopt random, knee-jerk steps that get them close to where they want to be as quickly as possible. A better plan is to build a long-term AI strategy that safeguards the business, partners and, importantly, customers.
Firms have a duty to investors and the global financial system to use AI responsibly. AI is a serious opportunity with serious implications. If done too quickly, or with the wrong partner, a lackluster implementation of AI could spell disaster.
Companies must be very selective about who they work with as they seek to develop innovative solutions. No business is likely to build all the necessary tools in-house while staying focused on its core competencies.
Watch out for red flags.
AI is imperfect, especially at this stage in its development. For instance, AI-generated stock recommendations pose a significant risk in financial services, with companies having to validate them, which is a challenge. Businesses in other industries no doubt have similar hurdles.
Also, generative AI can produce outcomes based on confidential information about customers and employees, such as names, addresses and social security numbers. Making sure this private data is excluded from a model’s data set requires robust disclosures and guardrails.
Another issue is us: humans. Since generative AI typically relies on restricted data pools, it is possible to game it to produce false, misleading and irrelevant outcomes despite many of them initially seeming valid.
Additionally, people can skew the original training data or algorithms. Experts say biases can lead to generative AI sometimes associating women and racial minorities with common, often negative stereotypes.
Beyond the technology, another concern is "AI whitewashing." In an era when the term "artificial intelligence" has become a buzzword, some companies fall into the trap of telling the market what it wants to hear.
Executives must resist the urge to exaggerate the relevance of their company's data pools and the capabilities of their generative AI tools because those things could land them in regulatory hot water. The SEC, in fact, already has warned firms against making false and misleading statements.
Balance and responsibility are key right now.
Chief technology, security, compliance and legal officers generally make the decisions regarding company data and AI. Now, more of the C-suite, including CEOs at some of the largest global companies, are being kept up at night with the challenges and opportunities of the game-changing technology.
The reason for this shift is closely tied to its promises of achieving more with less and the perceived business potential. On the flipside, AI has made managing risk much more complex. For one, the sheer amount of data demands a sound strategy, especially for highly regulated businesses like financial services.
AI has endless possibilities, with the potential to save companies millions of dollars and supercharge growth. That said, numerous landmines exist. How leaders deal with them will go a long way toward determining how their firms perform in the years to come.
Executives now must balance regulatory pressure and uncertainty, investor confidence and firm best interest, and scaling innovation amid a sea of “AI whitewashing.” It’s a complex challenge, one that financial services is uniquely positioned to tackle before the rest of the world catches up.
This is a critical moment for organizations to decide how, when and why to use AI, but they must do so responsibly. Those who do it right will win. Those who don’t may cease to exist.

title: Council Post: How LLMs Are Transforming The Customer Support Industry
text:
Varun Vummadi is the cofounder and CEO of Giga ML.
Companies strive to provide excellent service to keep their customers satisfied. However, traditional customer support methods often struggle to keep up with the demand of queries. Long wait times for calls and poor service quality are just a few of the challenges that businesses face.
Large language models (LLMs) are already transforming the industry. Many current AI assistants are primarily used for chatting with documentation, which is a niche use case. Chatting with documentation literally means uploading the documents and chatting with them.
The real potential of LLMs lies in their ability to go beyond document lookup. Soon, LLMs will be booking appointments, canceling orders and even processing refunds based on uploaded images. LLMs can be trained to replace some of your customer support agents, which allows your staff to focus on more complex requests.
The Utility Of AI Assistants In B2B And B2C Customer Support
In B2C customer support, agents often need to reference various documents such as user manuals, policy documents and FAQs. Instead of manually searching, a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system helps retrieve the data and generate a response in real-time. This speeds up the process of providing customer support, but as we all know, chatbots often have limited capabilities. AI agents have begun making a splash across the industry lately. Why?
B2B scenarios are generally a lot more complex than B2C, where RAG AI is already deployed. In B2B, there’s not usually a specific policy; agents proceed with existing knowledge and discuss issues with expert team members to solve the problem. Human agents also bring emotional intelligence, which is crucial for resolving issues that require empathy and understanding. This is particularly important in situations where customers are frustrated or upset. Training an AI agent for your B2B customer support requires the same level of training as a typical human agent.
The true utility of AI in customer support for both B2B and B2C is alleviating human issues, such as burnout and stress, by taking on the most repetitive and straightforward tasks. RAG systems can efficiently handle routine tasks and queries in B2B, but human agents are indispensable for managing exceptions and providing a higher level of customer service. AI agents in B2C should allow human agents to focus on more complex and rewarding problems, reducing their workload and enhancing their job satisfaction.
Seamless Integration Of AI Customer Support Agents
Klarna's successful integration of AI customer support agents is a great example of the power of AI agents. They collaborated closely with OpenAI to develop a solution which resulted in their AI doing the work of 700 customer service agents. Klarna's experience highlights the importance of close collaboration with AI experts. While most companies will not be able to secure a collaboration with OpenAI, comprehensive testing and training human agents to work alongside AI allows for a successful integration.
You should follow several steps to ensure a smooth integration of AI customer support agents. First, assess your needs and set clear goals for AI integration. Evaluate the existing support infrastructure to pinpoint areas where AI can be most beneficial. Next, choose the right AI solution that fits these needs, ensuring compatibility with your existing systems.
The easiest method of integration in B2B is using AI agents that replicate humans. The process involves adding the AI as a customer support agent, much like adding a typical human agent. How do you train a customer support agent? You provide information and policies. Training an AI agent is no different.
Clearly defining customer care policies ensures that the AI provides responses consistent with the company's standards. You will upload relevant documents and data that the AI will need to interact with. Importantly, AI should have the same level of data access as a human agent to protect against privacy breaches. If you are working with an AI provider, it is essential to select one that has strict data protection policies.
Once training is complete, you will log in your AI agents as you would any customer support agent. The AI will handle customer requests according to the workflows you trained it on. This approach guarantees that the AI operates within the policies and mimics human actions.
The testing phase follows. Extensive testing should be conducted by your AI provider to ensure the AI interacts correctly with customers and performs tasks accurately. CSAT scores are an excellent metric for tracking the performance of your system in the longer term.
The key to harnessing the full potential of AI in customer support lies in a strategic approach. Companies must invest in training programs and policies so their AI systems are aligned with their customer service standards. By handling routine tasks, AI allows human agents to focus on more complex issues such as customer satisfaction and support quality. With careful implementation, businesses can achieve a balance where AI and human agents work together to deliver exceptional customer experiences.

title: Council Post: You Can’t Ignore It: The Power Of AI And Data In Reputation Performance Management
text:
Joe Burton is the CEO of Reputation.
Today’s consumers take the driver’s seat in their buying journey. Traditional marketing and sales strategies are often no longer enough to grow and sustain a customer base as consumers are now leveraging public and qualitative data at every touchpoint.
This shift means brands must meet consumers where they are by finding new ways to understand how they feel at every stage of their journey. Reputation performance management—the act of developing a strong online presence and asking consumers for feedback—is an effective way to lean into this dynamic. Although daunting, especially with multiple locations, it can prove to be an essential tool for running an effective business today.
Artificial intelligence (AI) helps harness the power of data in reputation performance management and allows this to happen at scale. This helps enable the delivery of better experiences directly based on consumer feedback, driving loyalty and boosting the bottom line.
Today, we’ll explore the importance of AI and data in reputation performance management, ways businesses can leverage AI for organizing and analyzing consumer feedback, and tips for leaders to inspire action and innovation.
AI And Data: Keys To Delivering On Brand Promise
Reputation performance management is the practice of managing and delivering on your brand promise by knowing each customer personally—like a small-town store. This is achievable by closing the feedback loop, ensuring consumers feel heard and have their needs addressed. It’s what transforms a brand into a community or movement.
That type of transformation can be time-consuming and costly, as it’s no longer possible for most businesses to know every customer. Years ago, this would have required someone to manually manage every component of your organization’s online presence while also sifting through feedback. However, today this can be managed at scale by using AI to optimize the use of resources and identify where human interaction can be best inserted in the customer journey. This can enhance human relationships while fostering trust and transparency both online and offline.
Three Practical Tips For Leveraging AI And Data
Utilizing AI and data to manage your online reputation requires both time and capital, but it's an investment with a strong ROI. Organizations prioritizing reputation management and looking to embrace AI to manage, organize, and understand their data can personalize at scale and quickly adapt to consumer needs and preferences while effectively allocating resources.
Whether you’re just starting to manage your online reputation or looking to further optimize and scale an existing program, here are three use cases for AI and data in reputation performance management.
1. Managing Online Presence
One critical component of a strong reputation performance management program is your brand’s online presence. As AI-powered search engines become increasingly common, organizations must create engaging, up-to-date content across all digital channels. This includes websites, social media pages and every Google Business Profile listing associated with the business. Implementing a proactive online review program is also essential to maintaining this positive digital footprint.
AI can help create content, streamline processes and provide consistency. However, human involvement is still crucial to ensure the final product resonates with the target audience and feels authentic to the business. By combining AI capabilities with human insights, brands can effectively manage their online presence and strengthen their reputation.
2. Sentiment Analysis And Trend Detection
AI technologies, like natural language processing (NLP), help brands analyze consumer sentiment data from public and private sources such as reviews, surveys and social media posts. This 360-degree view of how the consumer is feeling about their buying journey provides powerful insights that enable you to make meaningful improvements to your business.
Additionally, monitoring consumer sentiment identifies emerging trends and patterns in consumer behavior, allowing you to anticipate shifts in preferences, seasonal trends and potential market growth opportunities. This proactive approach helps ensure your business stays ahead of the curve and remains competitive in the marketplace.
3. Closing The Feedback Loop And Personalizing Experiences
Managing data from a wide range of sources and using AI to monitor and analyze it helps close the feedback loop and creates personalized experiences at scale. Automating certain tasks—such as responding to positive online reviews—frees up employees to focus on addressing product or service issues.
This can also provide richer consumer insights, enabling the creation of personalized experiences that foster customer loyalty. By identifying common trends in the buying journey and segmenting customers into distinct groups based on preferences and demographics, brands can understand and manage feedback data to enhance consumer personalization and elevate their overall customer experience.
How Leaders Can Foster AI-Driven Reputation Management
AI is an incredible tool, but implementing it requires a cohesive effort from the C-suite down to frontline employees. Leaders must paint a vision and provide examples of how AI can move the needle for consumers and the business. They must also cultivate a culture of learning and experimentation where employees feel safe to fail and learn from mistakes.
To succeed with AI analytics, you must experiment and iterate. The first attempt rarely yields the desired results, but continuous learning and adaptation will refine your strategies. Leaders must set this learning culture, ensuring employees are comfortable being wrong and eager to find new solutions. I would suggest fostering a more forward-looking culture by taking the following steps:
1. Define your vision and provide examples of how AI can benefit the business.
2. Champion a culture of learning by creating a safe environment for experimentation, encouraging teams to iterate and improve.
3. Give your teams autonomy by providing the necessary resources to explore and implement AI-driven solutions.
We’ve only scratched the surface in realizing AI and data’s power for reputation performance management, but they are already proving to be indispensable tools, especially when striving to bring a small-town feel to thousands of customers.
This landscape will only evolve with advanced LLMs, so my advice to fellow C-suite leaders right now is to set the vision and champion a culture of learning. Your teams will drive growth when harnessing the full potential of AI-driven reputation performance management.

title: Council Post: Mastering Adaptive Leadership With Real-World Insights
text:
Amalia Goodwin, Managing Director Slalom Consulting. AI strategy leader, organizational transformation expert, author, and public speaker.
AI is here now, as are its effects on our work and daily lives. Tech giants offering fast-paced releases are pushing organizations, governments and the world into deciding how we collectively want to incorporate AI into our lives. Whether you're a startup set to disrupt every industry or a legacy organization determining how it will use AI to stay competitive, you've likely faced the question of how to responsibly incorporate AI and integrate this pace of change in your company's day-to-day work.
Staying ahead of the pace of change is not easy for any company, and it is common to feel as though we're falling behind the competition due to AI. But I take comfort in knowing that even a leading AI tech company has faced challenges with this rapid change, and they still came out ahead. Let's take a closer look at the case study of Microsoft and what lessons we can learn for our own businesses.
Adaptive Leadership Displayed At Microsoft
Recent news stories stemming from discovery documents in a Google lawsuit have highlighted that Microsoft was “caught off guard” by advancements in natural language processing and LLM models. What I see in this coverage is a master lesson in adaptive leadership—an important skill for staying competitive in a fast-changing landscape.
Adaptive leadership is a practical framework for assisting leaders and organizations in changing environments. It involves not only anticipating and reacting to changes but also managing and leading through them in innovative and inclusive ways. From what we can see in the news coverage, Microsoft demonstrated key adaptive leadership skills that business leaders in any industry can develop. I believe that in the face of the uncertainty we are currently experiencing due to technological advancements, economic fluctuations and global affairs, it is important for leaders to be willing to change and develop these leadership skills to bring our organizations into the future.
The recent actions of Microsoft embody the model of adaptive leadership in two key areas:
1. Leading With Vulnerability
Microsoft's internal acknowledgment that they were behind in a critical technology and that this technology is a game changer required a culture of leading with vulnerability and safety. They admitted they were behind the competition, expressed concern and focused on addressing the problem and finding a solution rather than blaming individuals. Microsoft may have been caught off guard this time, but the rapid pace of technological change makes it likely that we all will face similar challenges at some point.
In my experience, this approach is important for success in a disruptive technological landscape. As a business leader, ask yourself these questions:
• Have you created an environment where your team members feel safe sharing risks and opposing points of view?
• How often do you hear opposing ideas from your team members?
A practical way to apply these questions in your workplace is by incorporating a "What Could Go Wrong" session into your team processes. This session should be implemented after a team agrees to a course of action, allowing them to get together and brainstorm what could go wrong with that course and what they will do if they see indicators that they may be on the wrong track. I have found that holding these sessions, as well as rewarding and celebrating team members who come up with the most out-of-the-box or thoughtful ideas, is a great way to encourage more of this forward-thinking behavior in a team's day-to-day work.
2. Willingness To Change Course And Innovate
When Microsoft executives realized the significance of the new technology and that they were lagging behind competitors, they acted. Although we don't know all the details, we know that the team aligned to a new course of action and was able to quickly move forward and form a relationship with OpenAI.
This decision to pivot and invest in a new direction is critical to adaptive leadership. Leaders must be willing to continually explore new developments and change course if necessary. This can be challenging when emotional attachments and budget investments are involved, but it's essential for staying competitive.
The outcome for Microsoft—a steady rise in stocks after announcing its investment in AI—demonstrates that acknowledging you are behind and changing course can allow you to still come out ahead. To determine if your own company has a similar mindset, ask these questions:
• Are your leaders scanning what your competition is doing to understand the impact to your business? How willing are you to change course and invest in a different direction from your current strategy?
• What information, data or support would you need to lead your organization on a different path?
A great way to encourage a mindset of expecting and being ready for change is by incorporating a "What's Next?" session into your monthly meeting cadence. Ask each team member to suggest what they think is coming up next in terms of innovation or disruption. This can not only encourage adaptive thinking but also help you gain insights into what your team members are seeing competitors and adjacent industries doing that could be useful for helping your company stay competitive.
Embracing Adaptive Leadership For Future Success
Adaptive leadership is an effective strategy for navigating the complexities of today's business landscape, especially with the rapid development of AI. While Microsoft found themselves behind, they were able to regroup and make a strategic pivot, securing a leading position in the AI space. I believe this example underscores the importance of recognizing risks and making bold decisions to stay ahead of the competition.
By adopting principles of adaptive leadership, business leaders can better navigate the uncertainties of the future, driving innovation and maintaining a competitive edge. How will you recognize risk and make strategic decisions to lead?

title: Council Post: Recognizing Emerging AI Trends In Data Science
text:
Shashidhar Reddy Keshireddy is the Director of Data Integration Specialist at CEPTUA IT INC.
Emerging AI trends are pushing the boundaries of data science, offering innovative approaches to long-standing integration challenges. Recognizing these trends can better position leaders for alleviating data science learning curves.
I believe business and tech leaders must recognize emerging AI trends in data science because these trends not only drive innovation but also provide a competitive edge by enabling more accurate predictions and better decision-making. With the global data science platform market size forecast to reach $322.9 billion by 2026 (up from $95.3 billion in 2021), staying informed and adapting to these advancements means leaders can position their organizations for success in an increasingly complex, data-rich environment.
Emerging AI Trends In Data Science
AI and data science are intrinsically linked. Data science provides vast datasets, while AI offers tools to analyze and interpret this data, transforming it into actionable insights.
This synergy is crucial for predictive analytics, where identifying patterns and trends within data allows for future outcomes to be predicted. However, integrating these fields presents challenges, including data silos, inconsistent data formats and the sheer volume of data. As a data integration specialist, here are the AI trends I'm seeing take shape in data science:
1. Standardizing Data Formats With Automated Machine Learning (AutoML)
Inconsistent data formats can complicate data integration. AutoML tools preprocess data, converting it into standardized formats. AutoML automates the end-to-end process of applying machine learning to real-world problems, from data preprocessing and feature selection to model selection and hyperparameter tuning.
Simplifying the machine learning pipeline through AutoML makes advanced analytics accessible, speeding up model development and reducing time to insight. At Ceptua IT, we implemented AutoML to streamline our analytics processes, speeding up project timelines by up to 30%.
2. Gaining Clarity Through Explainable AI (XAI)
XAI aims to make AI decision-making processes transparent and understandable to humans. Increased transparency can build trust and facilitate the adoption of AI-driven decisions, especially in regulated industries. We implemented XAI for a financial client, which allowed us to gain the trust of their risk management team, leading to broader adoption of our AI tools.
3. Implementing Federated Learning To Break Down Data Silos
Data silos prevent comprehensive analysis and limit predictive model accuracy. Federated learning enables the use of diverse datasets without centralizing them. This allows you to train AI models across multiple decentralized devices or servers holding local data samples without exchanging the data. This addresses privacy concerns and broadens data integration across industries. Federated learning enabled us to develop predictive models using patient data from multiple hospitals safely and without data breaches.
4. Handling Data Volume With Edge AI
Increasing data volume can overwhelm centralized systems. Edge AI processes data locally, enhancing scalability by deploying AI algorithms on local devices (edge devices) rather than relying on centralized cloud computing. This approach can reduce latency and bandwidth usage, enabling more immediate insights to act on. In a manufacturing project, we deployed edge AI to specifically reduce downtime with an eye toward saving costs in operational delays, which can be costly.
5. Using Graph Analytics To Enhance Predictive Models
Traditional methods may miss complex relationships within data. Graph analytics has emerged as a way to uncover these relationships, improving predictive power. Graph analytics leverages graph theory to explore relationships within data and enhances predictive accuracy, especially in domains like fraud detection and recommendation systems. We've utilized graph analytics in our retail projects with a focus on improved recommendation systems, which allowed us to increase our sales conversion rates by 25%.
Conclusion
Emerging AI trends aim to address key integration challenges, enabling organizations to achieve predictive success, make more informed decisions and drive innovation. Leaders who embrace these trends and consider how integrating them into their strategies could be well-positioned to thrive in this dynamic landscape.

title: Public-Private Collaboration Leads To Effective AI Procurement
text:
For years, governments have increasingly relied on commercial technologies to serve their constituents. Today, they are finding more ways to leverage emerging technologies, particularly artificial intelligence (AI), to drive mission outcomes. From predictive analytics assisting in crime prevention to chatbots handling public service inquiries to models that identify suicide risk among veterans, AI is transforming how governments operate and interact with citizens.
As these technologies rapidly evolve, government procurement processes must keep pace to ensure access to cutting-edge commercial solutions. The successful widespread adoption of AI by governments hinges on strong collaboration with the technology industry.
The Private Sector's Vital Role
AI's innovative capabilities are set to revolutionize government operations, driving efficiency and unlocking new ways to connect with citizens. Tech companies, as developers and deployers of AI, possess firsthand knowledge of these capabilities. Moreover, their agility and investment in research and development often surpasses that of government entities, allowing for rapid creation and iteration of technologies tailored to specific governmental needs.
However, AI presents unique challenges for government customers. These include competition concerns, data access issues, and the imperative to protect citizens' rights and safety. The best way to address these challenges and ensure a federal AI landscape that works for all is through increased public-private cooperation and information sharing.
The private sector can provide insights into the latest AI advancements, potential risks, and practical implementation challenges. Meanwhile, the public sector must ensure that policies align with public interests, ethical standards, and legal frameworks. This synergy is crucial for responsible and effective AI adoption in government.
Innovative Procurement Strategies
To facilitate successful AI procurement, the federal government must leverage all available innovative acquisition tools and authorities. In many cases, AI can and should be procured like commercial software. However, unique government requirements and/or gaps in existing commercial contracting methods may require governments to employ innovative methods to incentivize private sector research and development.
Non-traditional federal contracting methods particularly well-suited for AI include:
- Pilot programs: Allowing agencies to test AI solutions before full-scale implementation.
- Cooperative agreements: Enabling collaboration between government and private entities on AI projects.
- Commercial Solutions Opening (CSO) Authority: Facilitating shared government and private sector investment in commercial capabilities.
- Other Transaction Authority (OTA): Providing flexibility in contracting for prototype projects.
- Challenge-based procurement: Incentivizing innovative solutions through competitions.
- Incremental development and modular contracting: Breaking AI projects into manageable, iterative phases.
Federal stakeholders also need to consider developing cross-functional teams to ensure a coordinated approach to market research, defining requirements, crafting testing/evaluation strategies, and acquiring and deploying AI solutions within federal agencies in a manner that appropriately considers the multiple technical, legal, privacy, security, and other concerns associated with using this transformative emerging technology.
The Importance of Uniform Definitions
Throughout this process, the effective government adoption of AI will depend on a shared set of definitions. Uniform definitions allow for consistency across agencies and even global governments, facilitate collaboration between public and private entities, and prevent misunderstandings that could lead to errors in the implementation and management of IT (Information Technology) projects and policies.
While there is no universally accepted set of AI terminology, adopting common definitions for key AI-related terms, concepts, and technologies is crucial. This shared language will help the public and private sectors communicate more consistently and effectively about the procurement and use of AI.
Public-private collaboration can help address these concerns by combining the tech industry's technical expertise with the government's commitment to public interest and regulatory knowledge. For instance, collaborative efforts can focus on developing AI systems that are not only efficient but also transparent and explainable. This approach ensures that AI-driven government services maintain public trust while leveraging modern technology.
Looking Ahead
The future of AI in government is promising but complex. As AI capabilities expand, so too will the need for robust public-private collaboration. This partnership will be crucial in navigating emerging challenges, from quantum computing's impact on AI to the ethical implications of increasingly autonomous systems to the long-term sustainability of technologies requiring unprecedented computing power.
By fostering a collaborative environment, governments can harness AI's transformative power to enhance service delivery and strengthen bonds with their constituents. This approach not only drives innovation but also ensures that AI development aligns with public values and needs.
As we move forward, the key to success lies in maintaining open dialogue, sharing expertise, and working together towards common goals. Through strong public-private collaboration, we can build AI-powered governments that are not only more efficient and effective but also more responsive and accountable to the people they serve.

title: ServiceNow Stock Tops $800 As Generative AI Boosts Backlog
text:
About two years ago, CEO Bill McDermott told me ServiceNow’s stock should trade at $800 a share.
On July 25, shares of the Santa Clara, Calif.-based provider of workflow software surpassed that goal — ending the day at about $829. This marks a 21% increase for 2024 and a 73% increase since April 27, 2022 when McDermott told me he thought the company’s stock should trade at $800 a share.
Can ServiceNow stock keep rising? Here are three reasons that could happen:
- Strong demand for Now Assist, the company’s generative AI offering;
- A bigger than expected contract backlog; and
- A standout ability to monetize generative AI internally and for customers.
While the abrupt departure of chief operating officer and president, CJ Desai is disturbing, his acting successor could help keep that market momentum going.
ServiceNow Beats Expectations In Second Quarter Report
Here are the key numbers that ServiceNow reported:
